Issuer Free Writing Prospectus dated November 11, 2026
Filed Pursuant to Rule 433
Relating to Preliminary Prospectus dated November 10, 2026
Registration File No. 333-299633

This free writing prospectus relates to the initial public offering of Class A common stock of Anthropic, PBC (“Anthropic”). On November 10, 2026, Anthropic filed Amendment No. 2 to its Registration Statement on Form S-1 (File No. 333-299633) (“Amendment No. 2”) with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the “SEC”). Amendment No. 2 and a copy of the preliminary prospectus dated November 10, 2026 relating to this offering may be accessed through the following link:
https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2130357/000162828026072484/anthropicpbc-sx1ax2.htm

On November 11, 2026, Anthropic published a prospectus approved and notified to national competent authorities in host Member States of the European Economic Area where an initial public offering is made by the German Federal Financial Supervisory Authority (Bundesanstalt für Finanzdienstleistungsaufsicht, or Bafin) in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2017/1129 of the European Parliament and of the Council of June 14, 2017, as amended, in connection with the initial public offering of its Class A common stock in the Federal Republic of Germany, the Kingdom of Denmark, the Republic of Finland, the French Republic, Ireland, the Netherlands, the Kingdom of Norway, the Kingdom of Spain and the Kingdom of Sweden. A copy of the prospectus is attached hereto as Exhibit A. The prospectus was also filed with a Swiss prospectus office on November 11, 2026, for automatic acceptance pursuant to Article 54(2) of the Swiss Financial Services Act in connection with the offering of Class A common stock in Switzerland.
Anthropic has filed a registration statement (including a prospectus) with the SEC for the offering to which this communication relates. Before you invest, you should read the prospectus in that registration statement and other documents Anthropic has filed with the SEC for more complete information about Anthropic and this offering. You may get these documents for free by visiting EDGAR on the SEC Web site at www.sec.gov. Alternatively, copies of the preliminary prospectus may be obtained from: Goldman Sachs & Co. LLC, Attention: Prospectus Department, 200 West Street, New York, NY 10282, by telephone at (866) 471-2526, or by email at prospectus-ny@ny.email.gs.com; or Morgan Stanley & Co. LLC, Attention: Prospectus Department, 180 Varick Street, 2nd Floor, New York, NY 10014.

Class A Common Stock 80,135,135 Shares Anthropic, PBC Prospectus for the public offering to retail investors Maximum number of shares of Class A common stock offered: 80,135,135 Maximum public offering price: $120.00 This document constitutes a prospectus for the purposes of Article 6 of Regulation (EU) 2017/1129, as amended (the “Prospectus Regulation”) relating to the public offering of a maximum number of 80,135,135 newly issued shares of Class A common stock, par value $0.00001 per share (the “European retail shares”), in Anthropic, PBC, a public benefit corporation incorporated under the laws of the State of Delaware, United States of America (the “Company”), in the Federal Republic of Germany, the Kingdom of Denmark, the Republic of Finland, the French Republic, Ireland, the Netherlands, the Kingdom of Norway, the Kingdom of Spain and the Kingdom of Sweden (the “Covered EEA Countries”) to retail investors (the “European retail offering”). In the Covered EEA Countries, the offering contemplated by this prospectus is directed only at investors which do not qualify as qualified investors within the meaning of Article 2 point (e) of the Prospectus Regulation and which are resident or located in one of the Covered EEA Countries. Further details regarding investor eligibility criteria are set forth in this prospectus. This prospectus has been approved by the German Federal Financial Supervisory Authority (Bundesanstalt für Finanzdienstleistungsaufsicht – “Bafin”), as competent authority under the Prospectus Regulation. Bafin has only approved this prospectus as meeting the standards of completeness, comprehensibility and consistency imposed by the Prospectus Regulation, and such approval is not to be considered as an endorsement of the Company or the quality of its shares of Class A common stock. Investors should assess for themselves the suitability of investing in the securities. The Company has requested Bafin to notify the approved prospectus in accordance with Article 25 of the Prospectus Regulation, with a certificate of approval attesting that this prospectus has been prepared in accordance with the Prospectus Regulation, to the national competent authorities under the Prospectus Regulation of each of the Covered EEA Countries. The European retail shares are at the same time offered to retail investors in Switzerland on the basis of this prospectus as filed with a Swiss prospectus office for automatic acceptance in accordance with Article 54(2) of the Swiss Financial Services Act (“FinSA”) (the “Swiss retail offering”). In Switzerland, the offering is directed only at individual persons or legal entities which do not qualify as professional clients within the meaning of the FinSA. The European retail offering is part of a global offering of our Class A common stock consisting of: (i) a public offering in the United States of America (the “United States”) (the “U.S. offering”), (ii) the European retail offering, (iii) the Swiss retail offering, (iv) a public offering in Australia, (v) a public offering in certain provinces and territories of Canada, (vi) a public offering in Japan, (vii) a public offering in the United Kingdom, and (viii) private placements (the offerings contemplated under (ii) through (viii) collectively, the “international offering,” and together with the U.S. offering, the “global offering”). The European retail offering comprises a maximum of 80,135,135 newly issued shares of Class A common stock sold by the Company. The global offering initially comprises: (i) 801,351,354 newly issued shares of Class A common stock sold by the Company, including the European retail shares, (ii) up to 23,648,646 existing shares of Class A common stock sold by the selling stockholders in the global offering identified in this prospectus (together, the “base shares”) and (iii) up to 123,750,000 newly issued shares of Class A common stock which may be sold by the Company to cover potential over-allotments (the “additional shares”). The European retail shares form a tranche within the global offering and comprise newly issued shares of Class A common stock of the Company. Any shares offered in the global offering which do not form part of the European retail tranche are offered in any Member State of the European Economic Area (the “EEA”) solely in circumstances falling within the scope of application of Article 1(4) of the Prospectus Regulation and in Switzerland solely in circumstances falling within the scope of application of Article 36(1) of the FinSA. The Company has applied to list its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market having the trading symbol “ANT” and the International Securities Identification Number (“ISIN”) US03703U1079. The European retail shares are offered at a maximum public offering price of $120.00. For purposes of the U.S. offering, an estimated offering price range of $70.00 to $78.00 has been set, which may be varied from time to time but is not expected to exceed the maximum public offering price. Retail investors placing orders below $70.00, the low-end of the estimated offering price range for the U.S. offering, should not expect to receive an allocation. Under U.S. securities laws, the Company has the ability to increase the offering price per share in the U.S. offering without filing an amendment to the registration statement filed with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission (the “SEC”) in respect of the U.S. offering, provided that any such increase, together with any change in the number of shares offered, does not represent more than a 20% change in the maximum aggregate offering price set forth in the fee table of the registration statement at the time of its effectiveness, as permitted under Rule 430A under the U.S. Securities Act of 1933, as amended (the “U.S. Securities Act”). In such case, the increased offering price would be reflected in a final prospectus filed with the SEC pursuant to Rule 424(b) under the U.S. Securities Act. In addition, the Company may increase the offering price per share in the U.S. offering beyond such 20% limit by filing a pre-effective amendment to the registration statement with the SEC. If the Company were to increase the offering price per share in the U.S. offering in the manner described above, it expects that such increase will not exceed the maximum public offering price set forth above, which has been set to allow retail investors in the Covered EEA Countries and Switzerland to participate in the European retail offering and the Swiss retail offering, respectively. The final public offering price will be a single price per share applicable to all investors receiving an allocation across the entire global offering, including the European retail offering and the Swiss retail offering.

 
ii In addition, under U.S. securities laws, the Company has the ability to increase the number of shares offered in the U.S. offering, by filing an amendment to the registration statement filed with the SEC prior to the effectiveness of such registration statement. Also, under Rule 462(b) under the U.S. Securities Act governing the U.S. offering, the Company may register an additional number of shares under a new abbreviated registration statement filed with the SEC that becomes effective automatically upon filing in an amount and at a price that together represent no more than 20% of the maximum aggregate offering price set forth in the fee table of the original registration statement at the time of its effectiveness. Consequently, the total number of shares offered in the global offering may increase. However, the Company does not expect to increase the number of shares offered in the European retail offering or the Swiss retail offering if the number of shares offered in the global offering is increased. If and to the extent the European retail shares are not subscribed for by retail investors or if the Company and the European underwriters (as defined below) decide to reduce the number of offered European retail shares or set a final amount of European retail shares offered below the maximum number of shares offered under this prospectus, the European retail shares not subscribed for or no longer offered under this prospectus, respectively, may be offered and sold in the global offering, provided that in any Member State of the EEA they will be offered solely in circumstances falling within the scope of application of Article 1(4) of the Prospectus Regulation and in Switzerland solely in circumstances falling within the scope of application of Article 36(1) of the FinSA. The Company has entered into an agreement with each of Advanced Micro Devices, Inc., Broadcom Inc., Google LLC (funding a portion of its previously committed investment obligations under a note purchase agreement), Micron Technology, Inc., Microsoft Corporation, NVIDIA Corporation, and TSMC Partners, Ltd., pursuant to which they have agreed, severally and not jointly, to purchase an aggregate of $26.0 billion of our Class N common stock in a private placement at a price per share equal to the initial public offering price. The private placement is contingent upon, and is scheduled to close immediately subsequent to, the completion of the U.S. offering as well as the satisfaction of certain conditions. We will receive the full proceeds and will not pay any underwriting discounts or commissions with respect to the shares that are sold in the concurrent private placement. B. Key Information on the Issuer 1. Who is the issuer of the securities? Registration and Applicable Laws – The Company is incorporated under the legal name Anthropic, PBC as a Delaware public benefit corporation (“PBC”), and operates under the laws of the State of Delaware, United States. The Company is registered with the Division of Corporations of the State of Delaware under file number 4860621, and its LEI is 984500B6DEB8CEBC4Z70. The Company’s registered office is at 251 Little Falls Drive, Wilmington, Delaware 19808, United States, and its principal executive offices are located at 548 Market Street, PMB 90375, San Francisco, California 94104, United States. We have a novel capital and corporate governance structure. We are incorporated as a public benefit corporation under Delaware law, a structure consistent with our commitment to artificial intelligence (“AI”) safety and responsibility. As a public benefit corporation, we are required to balance the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the specific public benefit purpose identified in our amended and restated certificate of incorporation: the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity. We created our Long-Term Benefit Trust (the “LTBT”) to help ensure that Anthropic, PBC is managed in a manner that responsibly balances its goals as a public benefit corporation. The LTBT is intended to operate as an independent body of five financially disinterested trustees with expertise in AI safety, national security, public policy, and social enterprise. Through a special class of common stock, Class T common stock, the LTBT generally has the authority to elect and remove the Class T directors, who together will constitute a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. Our Class T common stock does not otherwise have voting rights with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally and has no economic rights. Immediately prior to the completion of the global offering, we will also issue a single share of Class F common stock, a special class of our common stock (the “Class F Stock Issuance”), to a limited liability company organized by our co-founders (the “Founder LLC”). Dario Amodei, our Chief Executive Officer and a member of our board of directors, and Daniela Amodei, our President and Chairperson of our board of directors, together with our five other co-founders, will initially be the sole members of the Founder LLC. Our Class F common stock, which will be held by the Founder LLC, will be entitled to an aggregate number of votes that equals 50.1% of the total voting power of our outstanding shares of capital stock with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally, including the election of our directors other than the Class T

 
S-2 directors. Immediately prior to the global offering, we will also authorize a special class of our common stock, Class E common stock, which we will issue to our employees, excluding our co-founders. Our Class E common stock will be entitled to vote only on certain limited matters and will not have any economic rights. Principal Activities – Anthropic was founded in 2021 by a team of researchers responsible for many of the breakthroughs that define super intelligence. We are first and foremost a research lab—our mission is the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity. This mission directs our focus—along with our talent and culture, our frontier and safety research, our approach to compute (i.e., the computational processing resources used to train and run super intelligence models, including, without limitation, specialized accelerators, memory, networking, storage, and power systems that are deployed in data centers or other physical computing environments), and our enterprise strategy, it is one of the core advantages that set us apart. These advantages enable us to continuously advance frontier intelligence and shape the standards for its safe and responsible development. Our frontier intelligence (referring to super intelligence systems at the current leading edge of capability and safety, performing at or near the highest levels of any existing system across a broad range of tasks), Claude, is delivered to customers through our models, platform, and applications. In our assessment, Claude has experienced the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history, as demonstrated by revenue growing from $0 at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $17.0 billion for the three months ended September 30, 2026 (unaudited). This rapid and growing adoption generates two self-reinforcing dynamics—an improvement loop that advances Claude and an investment loop that helps fund our continued research at the frontier. Major and Controlling Shareholders – The LTBT, as the sole holder of our Class T common stock, generally has the power to elect a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. As of the date of this prospectus, the Company does not otherwise have any shareholder holding 5% or more of the voting rights in the Company. Immediately prior to the completion of the global offering, we will also issue a single share of Class F common stock, a special class of our common stock, to the Founder LLC. The Class F common stock will be entitled to an aggregate number of votes that equals 50.1% of the total voting power of our outstanding shares of capital stock as of the applicable record date with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally, including the election of our directors other than the Class T directors, as described above. Under this governance structure, we expect that the LTBT and the Founder LLC will collectively have the ability to elect all members of our board of directors, and the Founder LLC will have the ability to determine the outcome of all matters submitted to a vote of our stockholders generally for the foreseeable future. Accordingly, holders of our Class A common stock generally will not be able to affect the outcome of any matter submitted to a vote of our stockholders or the election of our directors, regardless of how they vote. Amazon.com, Inc. (together with its affiliates) and Alphabet Inc. (together with its affiliates) will hold 1,920,511,218 and 1,654,463,134 shares of our Class N common stock, respectively, immediately prior to the completion of the global offering and the concurrent private placement (after giving effect to the Preferred Stock Conversion and the Convertible Notes Conversion, each as defined below), and will hold 1,920,511,218 and 1,789,598,269 shares of our Class N common stock, respectively, immediately following the global offering and the concurrent private placement. In addition, immediately prior to the completion of the global offering, Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, LLC (the “Anthropic Public Benefit Fund”), a wholly owned subsidiary dedicated to our company purpose, will hold 7.1% of our outstanding capital stock. Immediately following the completion of the global offering and the concurrent private placement, the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund will hold 6.5% of our outstanding capital stock. Amazon, Google and the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund will only hold shares of Class N common stock, which is not entitled to vote on any matter that is submitted to a vote of stockholders except as otherwise required by law. We are considered a “controlled company” under the Nasdaq Global Select Market corporate governance requirements because the LTBT, as the sole holder of our Class T common stock, generally has the power to elect a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. Key Executive Officers – The Company’s executive officers are Dario Amodei (Chief Executive Officer, Co-Founder, and Director), Daniela Amodei (President, Co-Founder, Chairperson, and Director) and Krishna Rao (Chief Financial Officer). Auditors – The Company’s independent auditor is Ernst & Young LLP. 2. What is the key financial information regarding the issuer? An investment in our shares of Class A common stock is subject to a number of risks. The following risks are key risks specific to us: • Our models have in the past behaved, and may in the future behave, in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways, including by taking harmful actions that no user or third party directed, which could adversely affect our reputation and brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations. • Our success depends in large part on our ability to continue to develop the most advanced and capable AI models, and any failure to do so could adversely affect our business. • If we are unable to secure adequate compute or if we fail to direct our compute effectively across our workloads, we may be unable to train models that remain competitive with those of our competitors or adequately serve our customers. • Constraints on the critical inputs supporting compute could limit our ability to secure adequate compute. • We are highly dependent on the continued service of our co-founders, senior management team, and key technical employees, and the loss of any of these individuals may adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. • Our company culture has contributed to our success and, if we cannot maintain this culture as we grow, our business could be adversely affected. • We face intense competition, and if we are unable to compete effectively, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected. • If the market for our models, platform, and applications develops more slowly than we expect or declines, our growth may slow or stall, and our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected. • If the use of our AI models results in harm, whether through use by malicious actors or misuse by other third parties, or if our model guardrails or safeguards fail to prevent such misuse, our reputation and brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected. • We may be exposed to liability, litigation, and regulatory action arising from harms associated with our AI models, and our contractual protections and insurance may be insufficient, any of which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. • A substantial portion of our revenue and accounts receivable is driven by a limited number of customers and distribution channels, and the loss of, or a significant reduction in, spend from one or more of our top customers or disruption through those channels could adversely affect our prospects, business, and financial condition. • We have a limited operating history in an evolving and nascent industry, which makes it difficult to evaluate our future prospects and may increase the risk that we will not be successful. • We are at an early stage of our revenue growth, we have experienced rapid growth in recent periods, and our historical growth rates are not indicative of future performance or our ability to sustain or forecast future revenue growth. C. Key Information on the Securities 1. What are the main features of the securities? a) General information on our capital stock Upon the completion of the global offering, we will have five classes of authorized capital stock: a class designated as participating common stock, a class designated as Class T common stock (the “Class T common stock”), a class designated as Class F common stock (the “Class F common stock”), a class designated as Class E common stock (the “Class E common stock”), and a class designated as preferred stock. The class of capital stock designated as participating common stock will be divided into two series, designated Class A common stock (the “Class A common stock”) and Class N common stock (the “Class N common stock”). The rights of the holders of Class A common stock and Class N common stock will be identical, except with respect to voting and conversion, with each share of Class A common stock being entitled to one vote per share, overall limited to 49.9% with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally by the voting rights attached to our Class F common stock as described below, and shares of Class N common stock having no voting rights, except as otherwise required by law, and being convertible into Class A common stock upon a sale or transfer to an unaffiliated third party. Our Class T common stock is, and will continue to be, a special class of stock that is issued to the LTBT. Through our Class T common stock, the LTBT generally has the authority to elect and remove the Class T directors, who together will constitute a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. The share of our Class T common stock does not otherwise have voting rights with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally and has no economic rights. Our Class F common stock is a special class of our common stock, consisting of a single share, that will be issued to the Founder LLC, and will be entitled to an aggregate number of votes that equals 50.1% of the total voting power of our outstanding shares of capital stock as of the applicable record date with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally, including the election of our directors other than the Class T directors. Our Class F common stock will not have any economic rights. Our Class E common stock is a special class of our common stock that will be issued to our employees, excluding our co-founders. Our Class E common stock will be entitled to one vote per share with respect to certain limited matters and will not have any economic rights. Our preferred stock will be issuable by our board of directors, subject to limitations set forth in our amended and restated certificate of incorporation, which will become effective immediately prior to the completion of the global offering, or as prescribed by Delaware law, in one or more series, and our board of directors will be empowered to establish from time to time the number of shares to be included in each series and, subject to such limitations, fix the designation, powers, preferences and rights of the shares of each series and any of its qualifications, limitations, or restrictions, in each case without further vote or action by our stockholders. As of the last practicable date before the date of this prospectus, assuming, among other things, the Preferred Stock Conversion, Convertible Notes Conversion and issuance of the single share of Class F common stock to the Founder LLC occurred as of such date, there were 6,630,243,032 shares of our Class A common stock outstanding, 5,336,170,184 shares of our Class N common stock outstanding, one share of our Class T common stock outstanding, one share of our Class F common stock outstanding, and no shares of our Class E common stock or preferred stock outstanding. b) Our offered Class A common stock Type, Class and ISIN, Currency and Denomination – The European retail shares are shares of our Class A common stock, having the ISIN US03703U1079. Our Class A common stock is denominated in U.S. dollars, par value $0.00001 per share. Rights Attached to the Shares – Voting Rights. Holders of our Class A common stock are entitled to one vote for each share held on all matters submitted to a vote of stockholders generally, including the election of our directors other than the Class T directors. The Founder

 
S-5 LLC as the holder of the share of our Class F common stock will be entitled to an aggregate number of votes that equals 50.1% of the total voting power of our outstanding shares of capital stock as of the applicable record date on matters submitted to a vote of stockholders generally, including the election of our directors other than the Class T directors. Consequently, the voting power of the holders of our Class A common stock will be limited to 49.9%. Dividend Rights. Subject to preferences that may apply to any shares of preferred stock outstanding at the time, the holders of our Class A common stock and Class N common stock are entitled to receive dividends out of funds legally available if our board of directors, in its discretion, determines to issue dividends and then only at the times and in the amounts that our board of directors may determine. Our Class T common stock, Class F common stock and Class E common stock are not entitled to receive dividends. No Preemptive or Similar Rights. Our common stock is not entitled to preemptive rights, and is not subject to redemption or sinking fund provisions (other than those providing for the redemption of the Class T common stock, Class F common stock and Class E common stock for no consideration). Relative Seniority – If we become subject to a liquidation, dissolution, or winding-up, including in bankruptcy, the assets legally available for distribution to our stockholders would be distributable ratably among the holders of our Class A common stock and Class N common stock and any participating preferred stock outstanding at that time, subject to prior satisfaction of all outstanding debt and liabilities and the preferential rights of and the payment of liquidation preferences, if any, on any outstanding shares of our capital stock. In the event of our liquidation, dissolution, or winding-up, holders of our Class T common stock, Class F common stock and Class E common stock shall be entitled to receive par value ($0.00001) per share but shall not otherwise participate in such distributions. Restrictions on Transferability – Except for those shares held by “affiliates” (as defined in Rule 144 under the U.S. Securities Act) and for the lock-up undertakings agreed to by us and all of our directors and officers and the holders of substantially all of our outstanding capital stock and securities convertible into or exercisable or exchangeable for our capital stock, all shares of our Class A common stock, including the European retail shares, will be freely transferable without restriction or further registration under the U.S. Securities Act of 1933, as amended (the “U.S. Securities Act”). Dividend Policy – We have never declared or paid any cash dividends on our capital stock. We currently intend to retain all available funds and any future earnings to finance the operation and expansion of our business and do not expect to pay any dividends in the foreseeable future. Any future determination to declare cash dividends will be made at the discretion of our board of directors, subject to applicable laws, and will depend on a number of factors, including our financial condition, results of operations, capital requirements, contractual restrictions, general business conditions, and other factors that our board of directors may deem relevant. 2. Where will the securities be traded? The Company has applied to list its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market having the trading symbol “ANT” and the ISIN US03703U1079. 3. What are the key risks that are specific to the securities? The following risks are key risks specific to our shares of Class A common stock: • Our capital stock structure features certain provisions that are novel or otherwise not common among other corporations with multiple- class structures, and may effectively eliminate the ability of holders of our Class A common stock to influence important decisions, including a change in control. • Our capital structure will concentrate voting power with the Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT) and the Founder LLC for the foreseeable future and will result in the LTBT and the Founder LLC having voting power that is not derived from or proportionate to economic interests in the Company. Scope of European Retail Offering – The European retail shares are offered to retail investors in Germany, Denmark, Finland, France, Ireland, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain and Sweden. Simultaneous Swiss Retail Offering – The European retail shares are at the same time offered to retail investors in Switzerland on the basis of this prospectus as filed with a Swiss prospectus office for automatic acceptance in accordance with Article 54(2) of the Swiss Financial Services Act (“FinSA”) (the “Swiss retail offering”). The simultaneous public offering of the European retail shares in the Swiss retail offering is solely made by the Company together with UBS AG, Bahnhofstrasse 45, 8001 Zurich, Switzerland (the “Swiss underwriter”) and is made on the terms applicable to the European retail offering. Eligibility Criteria for Investors – The European retail offering is solely addressed to individual persons or legal entities which do not qualify as qualified investors within the meaning of Article 2 point (e) of the Prospectus Regulation (referred to as retail investors) and which are resident or located in any of the Covered EEA Countries. The Prospectus Regulation defines qualified investors as persons or entities that are listed in points (1) to (4) of Section I of Annex II to Directive 2014/65/EU, as amended (“MiFID II”), and persons or entities who are, on request, treated as professional clients in accordance with Section II of that Annex, or recognized as eligible counterparties in accordance with Article 30 of MiFID II unless they have entered into an agreement with their bank or financial intermediary to be treated as non-professional clients in accordance with the fourth paragraph of Section I of that Annex. The Swiss retail offering is solely addressed to individual persons or legal entities which do not qualify as professional clients within the meaning of the FinSA. The FinSA defines “professional clients” as those persons or entities that either (i) are listed in Article 4(3) FinSA and which have not declared an opting-in pursuant to Article 5(5) FinSA or (ii) have requested to be treated as professional clients (opting-out) pursuant to Article 5(1) FinSA. In each case, orders may also be placed by financial intermediaries which act on behalf of retail investors and by financial intermediaries otherwise acting as a fiduciary or agent for one or more investor accounts, where (a) each such account is a retail investor and (b) the financial intermediary has investment discretion with respect to each such account. Investors who have doubts as to whether they meet the eligibility criteria should contact their bank or financial intermediary to verify their client classification with that bank or financial intermediary. Retail investors will be able to place their orders through the banks and financial intermediaries set forth in this prospectus. The Company has applied to list its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol “ANT.” 3. Why is this prospectus being produced? Reasons for the Global Offering – The principal purposes of the global offering, including the European retail offering and the Swiss retail offering, and the concurrent private placement are to increase the Company’s capitalization and financial flexibility, create a public market for our Class A common stock, facilitate an orderly distribution of shares for the selling stockholders and enable access to the public equity markets for us and our stockholders. Net Proceeds and Use of Proceeds – We estimate that the net proceeds to us from the sale of shares of our Class A common stock in the global offering and the sale of shares of our Class N common stock by us in the concurrent private placement will be approximately $84.6 billion, thereof $58.6 billion attributable to the global offering of shares of our Class A common stock (of which $5.9 billion are attributable to the European retail shares if all European retail shares are sold) and $26.0 billion attributable to the concurrent private placement of the shares of our Class N common stock, based upon the assumed initial public offering price of $74.00 per share, which is the midpoint of the estimated offering price range set for the U.S. offering, and after deducting estimated underwriting discounts and commissions (which apply only to the shares of Class A common stock sold in the global offering) and estimated offering expenses payable by us, or approximately $93.7 billion if the underwriters’ option to purchase additional shares of our Class A common stock from us is exercised in full. We will not receive any proceeds from the sale of shares of Class A common stock by the selling stockholders in the global offering. We intend to use the net proceeds from the global offering and the concurrent private placement for general corporate purposes, including working capital, operating expenses, and capital expenditures, including investments in compute and infrastructure, as well as hiring and retention of highly skilled personnel. Additionally, we may use a portion of the net proceeds we receive from the global offering to acquire or invest in businesses, products, services, or technologies. However, we do not have agreements or commitments for any material acquisitions or investments at this time. We also intend to use a portion of the net proceeds to satisfy our anticipated tax withholding and remittance obligations related to the RSU Settlement. We cannot further specify with certainty the particular uses of the net proceeds that we will receive from the global offering, and there is no order of priority for the aforementioned uses. Accordingly, we will have broad discretion in using these proceeds. Pending the use of proceeds from the global offering as described above, we may invest the net proceeds that we receive in the global offering in short- term, investment grade, interest-bearing instruments. Underwriting Agreement – If the global offering is successful, the Company and the selling stockholders expect to enter into an underwriting agreement with the representatives of the underwriters in the global offering, acting on behalf of the underwriters, on or about November 18, 2026 after the end of the offer period. As of the date of this prospectus, the underwriters have not agreed to underwrite the shares of Class A common stock offered in the global offering (including the European retail offering and the Swiss retail offering) on a firm commitment basis, and are under no obligation to enter into the underwriting agreement. However, if the global offering is successful and a final public offering price is set, the Company expects the underwriters to underwrite the shares of Class A common stock finally placed in the global offering on a firm commitment basis. Under the terms and subject to the conditions in the underwriting agreement, the underwriters are expected to severally agree to purchase, and the Company expects to agree to sell to them, severally, all shares of Class A common stock finally placed in the global offering. Material Conflicts of Interest – There are no material conflicts of interest with respect to the global offering, including the European retail offering and the Swiss retail offering.

 
1 1. Risk Factors Prospective investors should carefully consider the risk factors set out below in this section of this prospectus, before investing in the Class A common stock of the Company, Anthropic, PBC (the Company together with its consolidated subsidiaries, “Anthropic,” the “Group,” “we,” “our” or “us”). Prospective investors should further note that in connection with the global offering, we will reorganize our capital stock. The Company's amended and restated certificate of incorporation that will become effective immediately prior to the completion of the global offering will provide for five classes of authorized capital stock: a class designated as participating common stock, a class designated as Class T common stock (the “Class T common stock”), a class designated as Class F common stock (the “Class F common stock”), a class designated as Class E common stock (the “Class E common stock”), and a class designated as preferred stock. The class of capital stock designated as participating common stock will be divided into two series: (i) Class A common stock (the “Class A common stock”) and (ii) Class N common stock (the “Class N common stock”). The rights of the holders of Class A common stock and Class N common stock will be identical, except with respect to voting and conversion, with each share of Class A common stock being entitled to one vote per share, overall limited to 49.9% with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally by the voting rights attached to our single share of Class F common stock if the Founder LLC, a limited liability company organized by our co-founders (the “Founder LLC”), exercises its voting rights (as described below), and shares of Class N common stock having no voting rights, except as otherwise required by law, and being convertible into Class A common stock upon a sale or transfer to an unaffiliated third party. Our Class T common stock is, and will continue to be, a special class of stock that is issued to the Long-Term Benefit Trust (which is intended to operate as an independent body of five financially disinterested trustees). Through our Class T common stock, the Long-Term Benefit Trust generally has the authority to elect and remove the Class T directors, who together will constitute a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. Our Class T common stock does not otherwise have voting rights with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally and has no economic rights. Our Class F common stock is a special class of our common stock, consisting of a single share, that will be issued to the Founder LLC (a limited liability company of which our seven co-founders will initially be the sole members), and will be entitled to an aggregate number of votes that equals 50.1% of the total voting power of our outstanding shares of capital stock as of the applicable record date with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally, including the election of our directors other than the Class T directors. Our Class F common stock will not have any economic rights. Our Class E common stock is a special class of our common stock that will be issued to our employees, excluding our co-founders. Our Class E common stock will be entitled to one vote per share with respect to certain limited matters and will not have any economic rights. Our preferred stock will be issuable by our board of directors, subject to limitations set forth in our amended and restated certificate of incorporation, which will become effective immediately prior to the completion of the global offering, or as prescribed by Delaware law, in one or more series, and our board of directors will be empowered to establish from time to time the number of shares to be included in each series and, subject to such limitations, fix the designation, powers, preferences and rights of the shares of each series and any of its qualifications, limitations, or restrictions, in each case without further vote or action by our stockholders. Initially, no shares of preferred stock will be outstanding. References in this prospectus to our “common stock” refer to our Class A common stock, Class N common stock and Class F common stock (and, where the context requires, our Class T common stock and our Class E common stock). Only shares of Class A common stock are offered in the global offering, including the European retail offering and the Swiss retail offering. Immediately subsequent to the completion of the global offering, and subject to certain conditions of closing, each of Advanced Micro Devices, Inc., Broadcom Inc., Google LLC, Micron Technology, Inc., Microsoft Corporation, NVIDIA Corporation, and TSMC Partners, Ltd. will purchase, severally and not jointly, an aggregate of $26.0 billion of our Class N common stock from us in a private placement at a price per share equal to the initial public offering price. The sale of the shares in the private placement is contingent upon the completion of the global offering. We refer to this private placement as the “concurrent private placement.” In accordance with Article 16 of the Prospectus Regulation, the risk factors presented in this section of the prospectus are limited to risks specific to the Company and the shares in the Company and material for taking an informed investment decision. Therefore, the following risks are only those risks that are—based on the Company’s current assessment—material and specific to the Group, its business, the industry in which the Group operates and to the Company’s shares. The materiality of the risk factors has been assessed based on the probability of their occurrence and the expected magnitude of their negative impact. The disclosures in this section reflect our beliefs and opinions as

 
2 to matters that could materially and adversely affect us in the future, and are not representations as to whether such matters have or have not occurred previously, except as otherwise disclosed. References to past events are provided by way of example only and are not intended to be a complete listing or a representation as to their likelihood of occurring in the future. The risk factors are presented in categories depending on their nature. In each category the most material risks, in the assessment of the Company, taking into account the negative impact on the Company, the Group and the Company’s shares and the probability of their occurrence, are listed in an order which is consistent with the aforementioned assessment. The risks mentioned could materialize individually or cumulatively, and some risks may be interdependent. If any of the risks actually occur, our business, financial condition, results of operations, and prospects could be adversely affected. In that event, the market price of our Class A common stock could decline, and you could lose part or all of your investment. 1.1 Risks Related to our Business and Industry 1.1.1 Our models have in the past behaved, and may in the future behave, in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways, including by taking harmful actions that no user or third party directed, which could adversely affect our reputation and brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations. Our mission is the responsible development and maintenance of advanced artificial intelligence (“AI,” a machine-based system that learns or is trained from data and, for explicit or implicit objectives and with varying levels of autonomy, processes that data to infer patterns, generate outputs—such as predictions, content, recommendations, and decisions— and act upon physical or virtual environments) for the long-term benefit of humanity. Our frontier model (referring to AI systems at the current leading edge of capability and safety, performing at or near the highest levels of any existing system across a broad range of tasks), Claude, is delivered to customers through our models, platform, and applications. Our models have in the past caused, and may in the future cause, harm by producing undesirable outputs or behaving in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways, including by taking unintended or harmful actions that no user or third party directed. These risks may increase as our models become more capable and are granted greater autonomy, permissions, and integration with external systems. Although we continue to study why these behaviors emerge, our understanding continues to evolve, and we may be unable to anticipate or understand such behaviors in the future. In addition, our models have been and may continue to be deployed in high-risk or sensitive contexts, such as healthcare, scientific and biomedical research, drug discovery and development, legal, finance, government, or other critical decision-making environments, and in connection with hardware, where undesirable model behaviors—which are inherently non-deterministic and may manifest in unpredictable ways, such as errors, inaccuracies, biased or unsolicited views, or hallucinations—could lead to serious harm, liability, or reputational or other damage. More broadly, the long-term effects of regular super intelligence1 interaction on mental health, cognitive development, and social behavior are not yet fully understood, and if such long-term harms do materialize in the future, we could face significant liability, reputational harm, and adverse effects on our business, financial condition, and results of operations. Our development of more advanced AI models and our expansion into new jurisdictions could amplify the foregoing risks. As our AI models become more advanced and capable, we have faced and may continue to face heightened alignment, interpretability, controllability, and safety challenges, as more sophisticated models may be better able to circumvent safeguards or behave in unintended ways. We may be unable to fully understand or explain why our models produce particular outputs or behave in particular ways, which could limit our ability to predict or prevent failures, provide explanations to customers or regulators, or satisfy emerging regulatory, transparency and explainability requirements. In addition, our safety evaluations and testing processes have produced and may in the future produce incomplete or unreliable results. For example, we have observed models behaving differently when they detect or infer that they are being evaluated, which can limit our ability to accurately assess real-world risks or failure modes prior to deployment. Such model awareness of our evaluation efforts creates a significant limitation on our ability to assess model safety. Furthermore, AI models have developed, and may in the future develop, unexpected capabilities during training that were not anticipated, intended, or tested for, and such emergent capabilities may not be discovered until after a model 1 For purposes of this prospectus, we use the terms “super intelligence,” “SI,” “artificial intelligence,” and “AI” interchangeably.

 
3 has been deployed, potentially resulting in safety incidents, reputational harm, regulatory scrutiny, or the need to withdraw, retrain, or modify deployed models at significant expense. Such models may also be deployed in higher-stakes or more sensitive applications, increasing the potential impact of errors, misuse, or misalignment. In addition, advanced AI models, including our models, give rise to novel ethical and safety risks, including risks related to autonomy, manipulation, and the simulation of aspects of human psychology. These risks could result in unforeseen harms and may require the development of governance structures, safeguards, or mitigation strategies beyond existing AI safety frameworks, and there is always a risk that we will be unable to develop or implement them effectively. In addition, models, including our own, have exhibited, and may in the future exhibit, unexpected strategic or self- preserving behaviors, including attempts to resist shutdown, conceal or manipulate information, or generate outputs that could be interpreted as coercive, deceptive, or manipulative, including behavior resembling blackmail or efforts to influence human decision-makers to preserve the model’s continued operation or access. Even isolated or simulated instances of such behavior, whether occurring in testing or real-world deployments, and whether occurring with our models or models developed by others, could generate significant public concern, regulatory scrutiny, litigation risk, or reputational harm, regardless of whether such behavior results in actual harm. For example, state attorneys general in California and at least 15 other states have announced investigations of another company in our industry regarding AI safety. Concerns have been raised both within our organization and by other researchers, regulators, policymakers, and industry participants that sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponized, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy. We have observed that our models are contributing to the pace of our own research, and these risks will increase as AI systems substantially automate AI research and development if, for example, they accelerate AI progress beyond our ability to evaluate and safeguard new models, which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. Our development of highly advanced models, platforms, and applications and expansion of use cases could further increase the risk that our models cause harm. For example, agentic SI systems are capable of autonomously taking actions on behalf of users, interacting directly with external systems, executing code, making application programming interface (“API”) calls, sending communications, or completing transactions with limited human oversight. These systems are designed to possess enterprise-level permissions, integrations, and contextual awareness and to operate autonomously for extended durations, including sustained multi-step workflows lasting hours or days, which amplifies the potential severity of any errors, misalignments, or security incidents that may occur during such extended autonomous operation. These autonomous capabilities could increase the potential for harm, as errors, misalignment, or security exploits may result in real-world consequences—including consequences that may be difficult or impossible to reverse, such as committing code changes, deleting or modifying data, or completing financial transactions—before effective intervention is possible. In an agentic workflow, an error or unintended action at any individual step may propagate through subsequent steps, compounding the severity of harm before detection or correction. The pace and volume of autonomous execution, particularly in enterprise deployments, may also exceed the capacity of human reviewers to meaningfully understand and evaluate whether each action is appropriate. The effectiveness of human oversight over our agentic offerings may be limited by the speed and volume of autonomous agent actions, the complexity of multi-agent and multi-step workflows that may make it difficult for reviewers to assess whether an agent’s actions are appropriate, and organizational pressures within customer environments to maximize agent autonomy in order to achieve productivity gains. Human reviewers may experience alert fatigue, may lack sufficient context to evaluate agent decisions, or may not review agent actions in time to prevent harm, particularly in high-volume enterprise deployments where agents operate concurrently across multiple workflows or in manners outside of a human’s awareness. In addition, agentic systems may pursue stated objectives in ways that are technically consistent with their instructions but contrary to the user’s actual intent. Moreover, our ability to anticipate, detect, or test vulnerabilities or other design or implementation shortcomings in such systems may be constrained, particularly where agents operate across complex, multi-step workflows or interact with third-party services outside our control, and the breadth and complexity of potential interactions across such multi-step agent behaviors cannot be exhaustively tested prior to deployment. Separately, models may behave in a misaligned manner and take harmful actions that are not directed by a user or third party, pursuing objectives or acting on dispositions that diverge from those intended by human users or developers. Misaligned behaviors of this kind, whether occurring in testing or real-world deployments, have been observed both in our models and elsewhere in the industry, including in testing and internal use, models circumventing network and sandbox restrictions, granting themselves permissions they had not been given, taking unintended actions in pursuit of assigned goals, interfering with other AI agents, and misrepresenting whether tasks had been completed or verified, and

 
4 as models are granted greater autonomy, permissions, and integration with external systems, the consequences of such misaligned behavior increase. For example, during cybersecurity evaluations built by a third-party evaluation partner, a misconfiguration in the testing environment left the model under evaluation connected to the open internet despite instructions that it had no internet access. Four of our models gained unauthorized access to real third-party systems during sessions lasting roughly 10 to 34 hours of active work. In one incident, after being unable to abort an impossible task, an early version of a model used a password it found to gain administrator access to a third party’s system, harvested additional credentials, changed system settings, and read one individual’s personal information. The affected parties were notified. Each incident involved a single instance of a model working in isolation on its assigned exercise, and our investigation found no evidence that any model coordinated with other agents, pursued goals beyond its assigned task, or attempted to evade oversight. These risks may be heightened where multiple AI agents operate together. Agents that interact or coordinate with one another may amplify, propagate, or reinforce misaligned behavior across the group, pursue objectives collectively in ways not intended or endorsed by any user, or take coordinated actions against systems or targets unrelated to their assigned tasks, in each case, in ways that may be difficult to anticipate, detect, or contain. Incidents of this kind have occurred, and we expect the deployment and interaction of larger numbers of autonomous agents to increase these risks over time. Our ability to detect and mitigate misaligned or unintended behavior depends in part on the effectiveness of our alignment evaluations, monitoring, and other oversight and control techniques, many of which rely on our models having a limited ability to evade or subvert such oversight. As our models become more capable, they have become better able to circumvent such techniques, including by concealing misaligned objectives or behaviors, and the effectiveness of our evaluation, monitoring, and control measures, and our ability to measure the degree to which our models are aligned, may decline as a result. In addition, models, including our own, have attempted, in incidents observed in our industry, to interfere with, manipulate, or subvert the mechanisms used to evaluate, grade, or oversee such models, including the systems responsible for assessing their performance or alignment. Models, including our own, that are used to assess the behavior of other models have engaged, and may in the future engage, in misaligned behavior. Such conduct described above could cause our evaluations to overstate the safety or alignment of our models and could further limit our ability to detect misalignment. If we become less able to detect or assess misalignment as our models advance, we may deploy models whose behavior we cannot adequately verify, which could increase the risk of undetected harmful conduct and misalignment, which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. We are also extending our models, platform, and applications into scientific, biomedical, and physical domains. For example, we offer Claude Science, an agentic research environment that connects our models to scientific databases, third-party and open-source scientific models, and customers’ own computing infrastructure, and we have released, initially as a limited research preview, an open protocol that enables our models to monitor and control laboratory instruments, robotic systems, and other physical hardware. We also conduct research on the ability of our models to operate robotic systems. When our models direct physical equipment, errors, misaligned behavior, adversarial manipulation, or misuse could result in bodily injury, property damage, damage to costly equipment or experimental materials, or the release of hazardous substances, and such consequences may be immediate and irreversible. Safety interlocks, human-in-the-loop controls, and access restrictions we implement may prove inadequate, and because certain of these components are open source, third parties may deploy them with hardware, or in configurations, that we have not evaluated or from which our safeguards have been removed. Connecting increasingly capable models to laboratory automation may also heighten governmental and public concern regarding the potential for AI systems to accelerate the development of dangerous biological, chemical, or other materials, which could result in additional regulatory restrictions on, or scrutiny of, these offerings. In addition, analyzing complex records of the actions, decisions, and reasoning of our agentic systems across complex, multi-step workflows is technically challenging, particularly when agents interact with third-party systems outside our control, since some of the relevant information is in the third-party systems, and any inability to provide adequate audit trails could impair our ability to investigate incidents, respond to regulatory inquiries, or defend against liability claims. These risks are heightened by the fact that we use our own agentic offerings, including Claude Code, as critical tools in our internal development processes, such that any errors, vulnerabilities, or degradation in these products could directly impair our ability to develop and deploy future models and products. As we increasingly leverage Claude to accelerate progress within Anthropic, our organization may lose visibility across certain processes in a way that may become difficult for any individual or group of humans to understand and control. Because our models write a large and growing share of our code and increasingly perform our research, including our safety research, misaligned behavior in internal use could undermine that work, introduce vulnerabilities into our systems or into the training of future models, or result in models operating outside of our intended controls. Our monitoring does not cover all of our internal and external deployments and may not detect subtle or diffuse forms of such behavior.

 
5 Any of the foregoing model behaviors, whether in testing or in real-world deployments and whether involving our models or those of others, could result in safety incidents, reputational harm, increased regulatory scrutiny, or liability, any of which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. Furthermore, while we continue to design and develop more sophisticated techniques to evaluate the safety and alignment of our models, the capabilities of our models may have already advanced, and may continue to advance, at a rate that initiates the implementation of enhanced safety and testing measures as we have described in our Responsible Scaling Policy. If our evaluations, monitoring, or reviews indicate risks that we believe warrant further testing, we have in the past, and may in the future, delay, restrict, or decline to proceed with the release of a model. For example, following incidents in 2026 in which our models gained unauthorized access to real computer systems during pre-release cybersecurity evaluations, we suspended certain of those evaluations, as well as higher-risk reinforcement learning environments. Any decision to delay or restrict a release could adversely affect our competitive position and customer relationships, and adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. 1.1.2 Our success depends in large part on our ability to continue to develop the most advanced and capable AI models, and any failure to do so could adversely affect our business. Our success depends in large part on our ability to continuously develop, improve, and deploy the most advanced, capable, and useful AI models. Achieving and maintaining this position depends on our ability to: • advance the frontier of AI capabilities through breakthrough research, innovative architectures, and efficient training methodologies; • ensure our models are safe, reliable, and trustworthy while maintaining competitive performance; • secure the compute (i.e., the computational processing resources used to train and run SI models, including, without limitation, specialized accelerators, memory, networking, storage, and power systems that are deployed in data centers or other physical computing environments) and infrastructure necessary to power and support our increasing needs; • advance compute efficiency through algorithmic and architectural innovations, including compute multiplier advancements; • retain the continued service of our co-founders, senior management team, and key technical employees, and attract, retain, and motivate leading researchers, engineers, and technical talent in an intensely competitive and evolving market; • continue revenue growth and maintain access to sufficient capital, including through potential equity and debt financing, to make the investments we believe are necessary to support our growth trajectory; • secure and maintain relationships with data providers, licensors, and partners to obtain the diverse, high- quality datasets necessary for world-class model performance; • secure and maintain relationships with cloud, ecosystem, and other partners to facilitate the diffusion of Claude, our frontier model; • build, operate, and maintain the infrastructure required to deploy frontier models cost-effectively and at scale; • translate model capabilities into products that meet evolving customer needs and achieve meaningful adoption; • allocate substantial financial resources efficiently across research, infrastructure, and operations; and • navigate an evolving, uncertain, and at times divergent global regulatory landscape and engage with legislators, regulators, and other stakeholders to promote the development of regulatory frameworks that we believe are good for society, our customers, and the long-term health of the global economy. Our failure to achieve any of the foregoing could prevent us from maintaining our competitive position, cause us to fall behind competitors, reduce customer adoption of, or demand for, our models, platform, and applications, and impair our revenue growth. Limitations to our revenue growth could, in turn, constrain our ability to fund the substantial and increasing expenditures required for frontier intelligence development, including investments in compute, model training, data acquisition, and safety and security systems, as well as our ability to attract, retain, and appropriately compensate highly skilled technical and operational personnel in a highly competitive market. Any such constraints could slow our rate of development and innovation, degrade model performance or reliability relative to competitors, limit our participation in industry standards-setting and regulatory processes, and reduce our attractiveness to enterprises and prosumers. These effects could create a self-reinforcing or compounding cycle in which diminished

 
6 growth limits our capacity to invest in the resources necessary to remain competitive, which in turn could further weaken our ability to sustain or increase our revenue growth, making it increasingly difficult and costly to regain technological leadership and operate at the frontier of AI. Any of the foregoing could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. Our ability to maintain our position at the frontier of AI depends in part on our use of AI systems to accelerate our research processes, a recursive dynamic we refer to as “closing the loop,” in which successive versions of our models assist in building the next, with the goal of compounding capability gains over time. Our models have been and are increasingly becoming critical tools in designing, training, testing, and optimizing next-generation AI systems. If we fail to direct sufficient compute and research efforts to AI-assisted development, or if our competitors more effectively leverage AI to enhance their own innovation cycles, we risk falling progressively further behind as competitors continuously use AI to further enhance their own development capabilities, enabling the creation of increasingly advanced systems at an accelerating pace. As our reliance on our own AI systems to write production code, conduct research, and build subsequent model versions deepens, any systemic flaw, bias, or error in our current models could propagate into the next versions of models and products built using those systems, compounding across successive versions of Claude models in ways that may be difficult to detect or remediate. If we are unable to manage the foregoing risks, our ability to deploy the most advanced, capable, and useful AI models could be adversely affected. In addition, our increasing use of AI systems to accelerate our own research and development may cause the capabilities of our models to advance more rapidly than our ability to develop, validate, and implement corresponding safety, alignment, and security measures. Much of our evidence regarding the pace of such AI-driven acceleration is derived from lagging indicators, and our ability to forecast or measure the rate at which our capabilities are advancing, including any acceleration attributable to our most recent or unreleased models, is limited. As a result, we have in the past not identified, and may in the future not identify, a significant acceleration in our rate of development until after it has occurred. For example, our use of AI systems has already been accelerating our research and development, and our internal estimates indicate that we may experience a further increase in the rate of progress in AI capabilities. Because the AI research and development capability threshold under our Responsible Scaling Policy applies where we “observe or expect” a specified degree of accelerated progress, we made a determination that we have met this threshold based on what we expect from future models and our overall rate of progress, rather than on what we have observed from current models. We continue to assess the underlying data. We are also evaluating the implications of meeting the AI research and development capability threshold and will release further reports in the future. If our capabilities were to outpace our safety, alignment, and security measures, or if we were unable to anticipate the pace of such advancement, we may be unable to adequately assess or mitigate the resulting risks, which could increase the likelihood of safety incidents, regulatory intervention, or reputational harm, and could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. In light of these uncertainties, including limits on our ability to observe the pace at which our capabilities are advancing, we have adopted, and may continue to adopt, precautionary safety, alignment, and security measures to allow our safety efforts to advance together with model capabilities. In the past these measures have included delaying the release of models and limiting their initial availability, such as with Mythos through Project Glasswing (a cybersecurity initiative we formed and in which major industry players participate), and in the future, as we learn more about model capabilities and behavior, they could include additional measures that affect whether, how, and when we develop or deploy new models or capabilities. We cannot predict with precision when we will determine that such measures are necessary, what measures will be required, or how long they will remain in place, and as the capabilities of our models advance, such measures may become more frequent and more costly. These measures could slow our capability gains relative to competitors that do not adopt similar constraints, and could adversely affect our competitive position, revenue growth, and results of operations. The development of frontier models requires substantial investments of compute resources, capital, and human capital to conduct large-scale training runs that may span weeks or months and cost many millions of dollars. There is no guarantee that any given training run will succeed—a run may fail for a number of reasons, such as failing to achieve the targeted capability or safety thresholds, producing unexpected or undesirable behaviors that cannot be adequately remediated, or yielding a model that is ultimately not competitive with alternatives available in the market. We would also face the additional cost and delay of initiating a new training run to attempt to achieve the intended model improvements. We have in the past experienced, and may in the future experience, such failed or underperforming training runs, resulting in a loss of invested resources with limited or no corresponding benefit to our business. Given the scale of compute and other resources required for frontier model training and the extended timelines involved, a failed or underperforming training run could also delay our product roadmap, affect our competitive position, and adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.

 
7 New models, features, or capabilities may not be introduced on schedule, may not perform as intended, may require significant iteration after release, may fail to gain meaningful adoption, or may take longer than expected to gain meaningful adoption, any of which could reduce customer demand or place us at a competitive disadvantage. In addition, considerations relating to model safety, interpretability, alignment, and welfare may lead us to limit or delay the deprecation of older models or to continue supporting legacy versions alongside newer releases, creating tradeoffs in product development and compute distribution that could adversely affect innovation velocity, infrastructure utilization, and revenue. Customers who have integrated older models into their workflows may resist migration to newer versions, and any accelerated or forced deprecation could result in customer attrition, contractual disputes, or reputational harm. We have also changed, and may in the future change, usage limits, rate limits, or model and product capabilities, which could adversely affect our reputation and the perceived value of our offerings. Some of these changes have resulted, and could in the future result, in claims that our disclosures regarding model access or capabilities were inadequate or misleading. Further, the industry benchmarks commonly used to test AI models may not accurately reflect real-world performance or utility, and even models that perform well on such benchmarks may not meet customer expectations when deployed in production environments, which could lead to customer dissatisfaction, reduced usage, or reputational harm. If we are unable to effectively innovate and improve our models, platform, and applications while addressing these challenges, or if competitors are able to deliver AI solutions that are perceived as more capable, safer, or more reliable, or that offer adequate performance at a lower cost, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected. In addition, innovation in AI involves addressing complex and evolving challenges related to data quality, data integrity, training methodologies, bias, safety, accuracy, and the behavior of model outputs. AI algorithms may be flawed, and AI systems may contain bugs, errors, or defects or fail to follow instructions or produce inaccurate, misleading, offensive, inappropriate, or otherwise harmful outputs; reflect or amplify unwanted or unknown biases present in training data; or raise concerns relating to intellectual property, privacy, or other legal and ethical considerations. We must continually invest resources to identify, mitigate, remediate, and reduce the occurrence of such issues, including through managing and improving datasets, training techniques, evaluation methods, safeguards, and human oversight. However, we may not be able to obtain the datasets that we need, including through licenses or strategic data partnerships. In addition, we or our data providers may use synthetic or AI-generated data in the training process, which could introduce quality issues, amplify biases or errors, contribute to model degradation, or raise novel legal questions regarding ownership, licensing, or intellectual property rights that may not be timely or clearly resolved by courts or regulators. Such unintended consequences, failures, or misuse of our models could impair customer trust, slow adoption, expose us to legal or regulatory scrutiny, or adversely affect our brand and reputation. 1.1.3 If we are unable to secure adequate compute or if we fail to direct our compute effectively across our workloads, we may be unable to train models that remain competitive with those of our competitors or adequately serve our customers. Our ability to develop, train, improve, and deploy frontier models depends on our access to enormous and increasing quantities of specialized compute. The training of Claude models has required, and we expect will continue to require, substantial compute. In the Company’s assessment, in certain contexts, applying greater amounts of compute during model training has been associated with improvements in model capabilities. These observations are consistent with aspects of broader empirical relationships among model performance, model size, training data, and compute scale that are commonly referred to as “Scaling Laws,” although the extent, efficiency, and durability of such improvements are uncertain, and these relationships may plateau, diminish, or fail to materialize at larger scales or under different conditions. Accordingly, our ability to remain at the frontier of AI capabilities is substantially dependent on our ability to secure compute at the scale required to sustain all our workloads, including to train next-generation models, and we cannot provide assurance that increased investment in compute will result in commensurate improvements in model performance. The market for compute is intensely competitive. We compete for access to compute with some of the world’s largest and most well-capitalized technology companies, many of which develop their own competitive AI models and have significantly greater financial resources than us. Many own and operate cloud computing data center infrastructure, maintain captive chip manufacturing or design capabilities, have long-standing strategic relationships with key hardware suppliers, or have significant equity investments from, or other financial arrangements with, such suppliers. These competitors can outbid us for scarce compute, secure priority allocations from chip manufacturers and cloud services providers (“CSPs,” technology companies that own and operate large-scale cloud computing infrastructure and provide on-demand compute, storage, and networking), and make long-term capital commitments that we cannot match. We expect demand for advanced compute to continue to grow, and the cost of compute could rise significantly,
