These risks may cause us to limit or modify our public advocacy, our participation in industry safety and standard-setting initiatives, and our communications with other developers of frontier models, which could adversely affect our ability to pursue collaborative approaches to AI safety that we believe are important to our mission. The results of any such claims, lawsuits, arbitration proceedings, government inquiries and investigations, executive and administrative orders and directives, or other legal, regulatory, and administrative actions and proceedings cannot be predicted with any degree of certainty. Any claims, lawsuits, investigations, orders, directives, regulatory actions, or proceedings against us, whether meritorious or not, could adversely affect our revenue, cause potential customers to pause sales discussions, cause existing customers to delay, pause, or cancel contracts or seek to modify their contracts, undermine our ability to pursue future contracts, damage our relationships with partners and customers, adversely affect our institutional standing, undermine investor confidence, limit our ability to sell our models, platform, and applications in certain industries, result in costly litigation or regulatory or other defense, adversely affect our reputation, require significant management attention, consume significant time, and divert significant resources. Determining reserves for our pending litigation or other disputes is a complex and fact-intensive process that requires significant subjective judgment and speculation. It is possible that a resolution of one or more such proceedings could result in substantial damages, settlement costs, fines, and penalties that could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. Because of the potential risks, expenses, and uncertainties of litigation or other dispute resolution processes, we may, from time to time, settle disputes, even where we have meritorious claims or defenses, by agreeing to settlement agreements, as we did, for example, in Bartz. Moreover, as in Bartz, insurance may not fully cover such claims, provide sufficient payments to cover all the costs to resolve one or more such claims, or continue to be available on terms acceptable to us. A claim brought against us that is uninsured or underinsured could result in unanticipated costs. These proceedings could also result in harm to our reputation and brand, sanctions, consent decrees, injunctions, or other orders requiring a change in our business practices. Further, under certain circumstances, we have contractual and other legal obligations to indemnify and to incur legal expenses on behalf of our business and commercial partners and current and former directors and officers. Any of these consequences could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. 1.3.2 We are subject to anti-corruption and anti-bribery laws, anti-money laundering laws, and similar laws. We are required to comply with the United States Foreign Corrupt Practices Act of 1977, the United Kingdom Bribery Act 2010, and other anti-corruption and anti-bribery laws, anti-money laundering laws, and similar laws in the United States and non-U.S. countries where we have operations and conduct business. Anti-corruption and anti-bribery laws, which have been enforced aggressively and are interpreted broadly, prohibit companies and their employees, agents, intermediaries, and other third parties from, among other things, promising, authorizing, making, or offering improper payments or other benefits to government officials and other persons in the public and private sector. We leverage third parties, including intermediaries and agents, to conduct our business and to sell our models, platform, and applications, and in connection with lobbying and other activities. We and these third parties have in the past and may in the future have direct or indirect interactions with officials and employees of government agencies, including state-owned or state-affiliated entities, and we potentially could be held liable for the corrupt or other illegal activities of third-party business partners and intermediaries, our employees, representatives, contractors, partners, agents, and other third parties, even if we do not explicitly authorize such parties’ activities. We cannot ensure that our policies and procedures to address compliance with these anti-corruption and anti-money laundering laws will be effective, or that all of our employees, representatives, contractors, partners, agents, intermediaries, or other third parties have not taken, or will not take, actions that violate these laws, for which we may be ultimately held liable.

 
67 As we increase our non-U.S. sales and business, our risk of violating these laws may increase. Non-compliance with applicable anti-corruption and anti-bribery laws, anti-money laundering laws, and similar laws could subject us to criminal or civil sanctions, settlements, prosecution, loss of export privileges, suspension or debarment from U.S. government contracts, other enforcement actions, disgorgement of profits, significant fines, damages, other civil and criminal penalties or injunctions, whistleblower complaints, adverse media coverage, and other consequences. Any investigations, actions, or sanctions could adversely affect our reputation, business, financial condition, and results of operations. Responding to any investigation or action could result in a significant diversion of management’s attention and resources and significant defense costs and other professional fees. 1.3.3 Governmental trade controls, including export and import controls, sanctions, customs requirements, and related regimes, could subject us to liability or loss of contracting privileges or limit our ability to compete in certain markets. Our models, platform, and applications are subject to U.S. export controls, and our current or future models, platform, and applications may be controlled under the Export Administration Regulations administered by the U.S. Department of Commerce or, in more limited circumstances, under the International Traffic in Arms Regulations (the “ITAR”) administered by the U.S. Department of State. Because the capabilities of our AI models are currently evolving rapidly through ongoing training and frequent model development, and because the export control treatment of AI technologies under relevant laws is developing, the classification of, and controls related to, our models, platform, applications, and technologies under these regimes are inherently uncertain and are likely to change over time. Certain of our models, platform, and applications, and the underlying technology and source code associated with our models, platform, and applications, may require authorization for export, re-export, or transfer in-country, and for individuals of certain nationalities to access such technology or source code, including within the United States. In particular, our core models, platform, and applications leverage encryption for data protection, and some of our future models, platform, and applications may be able to produce export-controlled software, which may subject exports, re-exports, and transfer of such models, platform, and applications to export authorization requirements. Our commercially available models, platform, and applications generally can be exported without an export license. However, some exports may require us to obtain authorization from the cognizant government agency. In certain contexts, the provision of our models, platform, and applications may constitute export of defense articles or defense services subject to the ITAR, which can be exported only if we obtain required export licenses or other government authorizations. Compliance with applicable export controls may delay the introduction or sale of our models, platform, and applications outside the United States, restrict our customers’ ability to deploy our models, platform, and applications globally, inhibit our ability to engage in certain research and development activities, limit the performance of our models, platform, and applications, or prohibit exports to certain jurisdictions altogether. Such restrictions have already affected our offerings directly. For example, in June 2026, the U.S. Department of Commerce imposed worldwide export restrictions on our Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models. To ensure compliance, we disabled Fable 5 and Mythos 5 for all of our customers; access to our other models was not affected. We redeployed the Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models after we updated our safeguards in coordination with the U.S. government and our industry partners and once the U.S. Department of Commerce lifted its restrictions. Similar export controls could recur, could remain in place longer, or could extend to additional models or capabilities. In addition, future updates to our safeguards or other remedial measures may not be sufficient to obtain relief from such restrictions or relief may not be granted on a similar timeline or at all. The restrictions imposed in June 2026 and potential restrictions in the future may also limit our ability to recruit talent, to fully utilize our existing workforce, to continue to improve our models, and to make our products available internationally. Any such restrictions could adversely affect our financial results; impair the research, compute, and development investment our models represent; and cause us to lose customers, partners, and market share, including to competitors not subject to similar restrictions. Further, our activities are subject to economic, financial, and trade sanctions administered by the United States and other countries. Economic, financial, and trade sanctions restrict or prohibit providing certain services and engaging in certain transactions or other activities or dealings with individuals, entities, organizations, governments, territories, and countries targeted by or the subject of these sanctions. These restrictions, as well as other applicable international trade rules, are subject to change with little to no notice. In addition, U.S. law increasingly authorizes the U.S. government to restrict or review the use of hardware, software, and services originating from, or linked to, countries it designates as adversaries, including such technology incorporated into the supply chains for the data centers and compute infrastructure on which we depend. Such restrictions could narrow our choice of suppliers, delay our infrastructure projects, or increase our costs, and any non-compliance could result in penalties, loss of contracting privileges, or reputational harm.

 
68 We take various steps to comply with applicable export controls and sanctions, including: maintaining a global trade policy and a supported regions policy, implementing IP-based geo-blocking controls that restrict access from certain jurisdictions to our models, platform, and applications, conducting restricted party screening of certain customers and vendors, and including sanctions and export compliance provisions in our customer terms of service and vendor agreements. However, we cannot guarantee the compliance measures and internal controls we have adopted will prevent violations of applicable export controls and sanctions. Our compliance measures and internal controls have not always been and may not always be fully effective, and we have in the past voluntarily disclosed, and may in the future voluntarily disclose, instances of non-compliance to the relevant authorities. We cannot guarantee that our measures will prevent future violations or keep pace with the changing substance, application, and interpretation of export controls and sanctions. In addition, third parties have in the past and may in the future take action to circumvent our compliance measures and controls in order to gain access to our products and services. If we misclassify a product or service, export, re-export, transfer, or provide access to a product, or provide services in violation of applicable export controls or sanctions, or otherwise fail to comply with applicable export controls or sanctions, we could be subject to criminal or civil sanctions, settlements, prosecution, loss of export privileges, suspension or debarment from U.S. government contracts, other enforcement actions, disgorgement of profits, significant fines, damages, other civil and criminal penalties or injunctions, whistleblower complaints, adverse media coverage, and other consequences. Any investigations, actions, or sanctions could adversely affect our reputation, business, financial condition, and results of operations. Responding to any investigation or action could result in a significant diversion of management’s attention and resources and significant defense costs and other professional fees. Decreased use of our models, platform, and applications by customers outside the United States or a limitation on our ability to export, provide access to, or sell our models, platform, and applications to customers and other parties outside the United States may cause our revenue from such unsupported jurisdictions to decline and otherwise adversely affect our business and financial condition. If we or our business partners or counterparties, including licensors and licensees, prime contractors, subcontractors, sublicensors, vendors, customers, or contractors, violate export controls or sanctions, including by failing to obtain appropriate import, export, or re-export licenses or permits, or if we fail to secure such contractual commitments from such parties, we may also be adversely affected through reputational harm as well as other negative consequences, including government investigations or penalties. Negative consequences stemming from violations or apparent violations of export controls or sanctions may include the loss of the right to sell our models, platform, and applications or services to the U.S. government, or to other U.S. or non-U.S. public bodies, or a reduction in our ability to compete for such sales opportunities involving government agencies or other public bodies. Further, ensuring that we are complying with applicable export controls and sanctions regulations may be time-consuming and could result in the delay or loss of sales opportunities in connection with particular transactions. Also, in addition to the United States, various countries regulate the import and export of certain encryption and other technology and have enacted laws that could limit our ability to distribute our models, platform, and applications or could limit our customers’ abilities to implement our models, platform, and applications in those countries. For example, following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, the United States and other countries imposed financial and trade sanctions and export controls against Russia, Belarus, and certain regions of Ukraine, and the United States and other countries could impose wider sanctions and export restrictions and take other actions should the conflict further escalate. Any new export restrictions, new legislation, changes in sanctions, or shifting approaches in the enforcement or scope of existing regulations, or in the individuals, entities, governments, territories, countries, or technologies targeted by or subject to such regulations could result in decreased use of our models, platform, and applications by existing customers outside of the United States, reduced adoption of our models, platform, and applications by new customers with non-U.S. operations, limited expansion into new markets, and decreased revenue. 1.3.4 To continue to grow our business, we will need to continue to expand internationally, and our non-U.S. operations and sales to customers outside of the United States expose us to risks inherent in international expansion, sales, and operations. We are a U.S.-headquartered company with extensive U.S. operations, as well as subsidiaries and operations in several other countries and regions, including the United Kingdom, the EU, Canada, and Asia-Pacific, and we expect that our future growth will depend in part on expanding our operations, customer base, and market presence in additional jurisdictions. Operating in non-U.S. markets requires significant resources and management attention and subjects us to regulatory, economic, and political risks that are different from those in the United States. As we continue to expand

 
69 internationally, we have faced and will continue to face risks in doing business internationally that could adversely affect our business, including: • the need to localize and adapt our models, platform, and applications for specific countries, including translation into foreign languages and associated expenses; • privacy laws, export controls, sanctions, and other national security regulations that impose different and potentially conflicting obligations with respect to how personal data is processed or require that customer data be stored in a designated territory; • laws in certain jurisdictions that may compel our personnel, vendors, or facility operators to provide governmental authorities with access to our systems, data, or other information, in some cases without notice to us and with limited means of recourse; • national security-driven data security regulations. For example, the Department of Justice issued a final rule, effective in April 2025, that places limitations, and in some cases prohibitions, on certain transfers of covered data to partners, service providers, vendors, employees, and investors located in China or with other specified links to China (and other designated countries). We may be required to re-examine current contracts or engage in new contract negotiations with third parties that aid in processing data on our behalf or otherwise have access to covered data. These rules also may broadly require us to extract promises from other third-party service providers that they will not transfer data we share with them onward to parties linked to countries of concern; • import regulations, including U.S. and non-U.S. governments’ restrictive trade policies, customs duties and other parallel regulations, tariffs, and countermeasures; • AI, data-related, cybersecurity, and digital service laws and regulations (such as the EU AI Act, NIS2, the EU Digital Services Act, the UK Online Safety Act 2023, and the EU Data Act) that are rapidly evolving, require continuous monitoring to maintain compliance, and often provide for substantial penalties in the event of a violation; • difficulties in staffing and managing non-U.S. operations, including the complexity of engaging in various employer-of-record arrangements that are geographically dispersed and the risk that these arrangements, or any failure to establish local employing entities on a timely basis, may not comply with local employment, labor, or tax laws, exposing us to fines, penalties, reclassification, or back-payment claims; • difficulties of maintaining our culture across various jurisdictions; • regulatory and other delays and difficulties in setting up non-U.S. operations, including delays in forming, registering, and obtaining governmental approvals for local subsidiaries, delays in establishing local banking, payroll, and benefits arrangements, and difficulties relating to safety of personnel and information, any of which could delay local hiring efforts; • the potential need for reviews by the U.S. government or non-U.S. governments of certain transactions with non-U.S. entities; • different pricing environments, longer sales cycles, longer accounts receivable payment cycles, and collections issues; • new and different sources of competition; • weaker protection for, and practical difficulties in enforcing, intellectual property and other legal rights outside of the United States compared to protections available domestically; • laws and business practices favoring local competitors; • compliance challenges related to the complexity of multiple, conflicting, and changing governmental laws and regulations, including copyright, employment, tax, privacy, and data protection laws and regulations, export controls, and sanctions; • parties outside the United States seeking to circumvent sanctions and export controls; • increased financial accounting and reporting burdens and complexities; • increased costs in establishing infrastructure across various jurisdictions;

 
70 • declines in the values of foreign currencies relative to the U.S. dollar; • restrictions on the transfer of funds; • potentially adverse tax consequences; • the cost of and potential outcomes of any claims or litigation; • future accounting pronouncements and changes in accounting policies; • changes in tax laws or tax regulations; and • regional and local economic and political conditions. Entry into certain transactions with non-U.S. entities or persons may be subject to government regulations and review, including review by U.S. or non-U.S. government entities related to contemplated or past foreign direct investment (“FDI”). In recent years, many countries around the world have adopted FDI regulatory regimes that seek to scrutinize investments into, and acquisitions of, domestic companies by non-domestic parties, granting governments broad discretion to review contemplated and past investment and acquisition transactions. These FDI regimes may restrict our ability to attract investments, invest in or fund partners outside of the United States that build or operate data centers or supply infrastructure for us, or acquire promising new technologies, companies, and talent in countries around the world, potentially limiting our ability to carry out our business strategy. More broadly, increasing geopolitical tensions, shifting national security priorities, and evolving technology-focused trade, export control, investment, and data-governance regimes may result in restrictions, heightened scrutiny, or other limitations on our ability to operate, sell products, partner with customers, or deploy our models in certain jurisdictions or with certain counterparties. Governments may adopt or expand policies aimed at protecting domestic technology ecosystems, restricting the cross-border flow of data, or limiting access to AI systems, which could reduce our addressable market, increase compliance costs, or require operational changes. In particular, the U.S. government has increasingly scrutinized AI companies’ exposure to Chinese state actors, and future executive orders, legislation, or regulatory actions could restrict our ability to serve customers or users connected to China, impose new compliance obligations, lead us to implement anti-abuse mechanisms or other technical access restrictions, or limit the deployment of our models in ways that reduce our addressable market. Any escalation of U.S.-China tensions, retaliatory measures by either government, or failure or perceived failure by us to prevent non-U.S. state-actor access to or misuse of our technology could subject us to regulatory action, reputational harm, and adverse effects on our business, financial condition, and results of operations. As we continue to expand our business globally, our success will depend, in large part, on our ability to anticipate and effectively manage these risks. These factors and others could adversely affect our ability to increase non-U.S. revenue and, consequently, could materially impact our business. The expansion of our existing non-U.S. operations and entry into additional non-U.S. markets will require significant management attention and financial resources. Our failure to successfully manage our non-U.S. operations and the associated risks effectively could limit the future growth of our business. 1.3.5 Increasing scrutiny and changing expectations from regulators, our investors, customers, and employees with respect to ESG may result in additional compliance risk and costs and may impact our reputation and business. Companies across many industries are facing increasing scrutiny related to their environmental, social, and governance (“ESG”) practices and reporting, both in the United States and internationally. For example, new U.S. and non-U.S. laws and regulations relating to ESG matters, including environmental sustainability and climate change, are under consideration, being adopted, or being rolled back or revised, which may impact our necessary disclosures and increase compliance costs. Further, there is particular focus on concerns relating to AI and its impact on society and the environment, including the power-intensive nature of the industry, public concern regarding high consumption of water, and reliance on critical minerals and rare elements in the manufacture of chips. Some investors may use these non-financial performance factors to guide their investment strategies and, in some cases, may choose not to invest in us if they believe our policies and actions relating to ESG are inadequate. Our sustainability initiatives, goals, or commitments could be difficult to achieve or costly to implement. Moreover, compliance with recently adopted and potential upcoming ESG requirements, including California legislation that requires various climate-related disclosures, the EU’s Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive and Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive, and the United Kingdom’s Streamlined Energy and Carbon Reporting framework will require the dedication of significant time and resources. At the same time, anti-ESG sentiment has

 
71 gained momentum across the United States, particularly at the federal level, and the federal and certain state governments have enacted or proposed “anti-ESG” policies or legislation or have issued related legal opinions. Such policies, legislation, initiatives, and scrutiny could expose any sustainability, employment, governance, or other corporate practices we adopt to the risk of litigation, antitrust investigations or challenges by federal or state authorities, and result in injunctions, penalties, and reputational harm. Additionally, if our competitors’ corporate social responsibility performance is perceived to be better than ours, potential or current investors may elect to invest with our competitors instead. Our business may face increased scrutiny related to these activities and our related disclosures, including from the investment community and the local communities in which we operate, and our failure to achieve progress or manage the dynamic, and at times conflicting, public sentiment and legal landscape in these areas on a timely basis, or at all, could adversely affect our reputation, business, and financial condition. Further, we may experience backlash from customers, government entities, advocacy groups, employees, or other stakeholders who disagree with our actual or perceived positions, or with our lack of position on social, environmental, governance, political, public policy, economic, geopolitical, or other sensitive issues. Any perceived lack of transparency about these matters could adversely affect our brand and reputation, our employees’ engagement and retention, and the willingness of our customers and partners to do business with us. Both advocates and opponents of ESG-related matters are increasingly resorting to a range of activism forms, including media campaigns and litigation, to advance their perspectives. To the extent we are subject to such activism, it may require us to incur costs or otherwise adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. 1.3.6 If we or our payment processing partners fail to manage the risks related to our payment processing activities, we could be subject to fines, regulatory scrutiny, disruptions to our business, or reputational harm. A portion of our customers authorize us to bill their credit card accounts through our third-party payment processing partners for our paid subscriptions. We have experienced, and expect to continue to experience, fraudulent activity, including the creation of accounts using false identities and the use of stolen or otherwise unauthorized payment credentials, which has resulted, and may in the future result, in losses, including payment processing fees, chargeback fees, and fines and penalties imposed by our payment processors or card networks, for which we may not be reimbursed. We maintain fraud-detection and identity-verification measures, but these measures have not identified, and may not identify, all such activity. Further, our customers provide us with credit card billing information online, and we do not verify the physical identity of cardholders or conduct additional verification beyond what we collect online, which increases our risk of exposure to fraudulent activity. We also incur chargebacks when customers or card issuers claim that a transaction was unauthorized or otherwise improper. If the volume of chargebacks were to become excessive, we could be subject to higher processing fees, additional fines, fraud mitigation requirements, or the termination or suspension of our ability to accept certain payment methods, including credit cards, through one or more payment processors. In addition, payment processors, card networks, and financial institutions periodically revise their rules, standards, and practices, including data protection and documentation standards, required to utilize their services. Our compliance with these evolving requirements, and the continued compliance of our third-party payment processing partners, may require additional operational resources and expense. Failure by us or our payment processing partners to comply with applicable standards could result in fines, increased scrutiny, disruptions to our business and our ability to process payments for our intelligence service, or reputational harm. 1.4 Risks Related to Tax and Accounting Matters 1.4.1 Changes in tax laws or regulations could be enacted, or existing tax laws or regulations could be applied to us or our customers in a manner that could increase the costs of our models, platform, and applications and adversely affect our business. We operate in multiple jurisdictions and are subject to tax laws and regulations of U.S. federal, state, and local and non- U.S. governments. Income, sales, use, or other tax laws, statutes, rules, regulations, or ordinances could be enacted or amended at any time (possibly with retroactive effect) and could be applied solely or disproportionately to models, platforms, and applications provided over the internet. These enactments or amendments could reduce our sales activity due to the inherent cost increase the taxes would represent and ultimately harm our results of operations and cash flows. Further, the application of U.S. federal, state, local, and non-U.S. tax laws to services provided electronically is unclear and continuously evolving. Existing tax laws, statutes, rules, regulations, or ordinances could be interpreted or applied adversely to us, possibly with retroactive effect, which could require us or our customers to pay additional tax amounts, as well as fines or penalties, and interest for past amounts. If we are unsuccessful in collecting such taxes due from our

 
72 customers, we would be held liable for such costs, thereby adversely affecting our results of operations and harming our business. As we expand the scale of our non-U.S. business activities, any changes in the U.S. or non-U.S. taxation of such activities may increase our worldwide effective tax rate and harm our business, financial condition, and results of operations. We may be subject to taxation in several jurisdictions around the world with increasingly complex tax laws, the application of which can be uncertain. In addition, our hiring of personnel and engagement of third-party employer-of-record providers in non-U.S. jurisdictions, as well as our data center and other infrastructure activities outside the United States, have created, and may in the future create, permanent establishments or other taxable presence in those jurisdictions, which could subject us to additional income, withholding, and indirect taxes, as well as interest, penalties, and additional compliance obligations. In advance of forming and obtaining approvals for local operating entities, we have entered into, and expect to enter into, additional letters of intent, leases, and other agreements relating to our international compute and infrastructure activities through interim contracting arrangements with existing entities, and we may be unable to transfer these arrangements to local entities on a timely basis or at all. Any prolonged reliance on these interim arrangements, or any failure to migrate them to local entities, could increase our exposure to permanent establishment or other taxable-presence determinations and could result in non-recoverable value-added or similar indirect taxes, which could be material in certain jurisdictions. Although we have not been required to pay income taxes, other than in immaterial amounts in certain jurisdictions to date, the amount of taxes we pay in these jurisdictions could increase substantially as a result of changes in the applicable tax principles, including increased tax rates, new tax laws, or revised interpretations of existing tax laws and precedents, which could adversely affect our liquidity and results of operations. For example, a number of countries and organizations, such as the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (“OECD”), have proposed changes to existing tax laws or new laws that could impact our tax obligations, including a framework that imposes a 15% global minimum tax, which has been implemented into the domestic laws of some jurisdictions in the EU, among other jurisdictions, and is being considered for implementation by other countries. On January 5, 2026, the OECD announced a “side-by-side” elective safe harbor that exempts electing U.S.-parented multinational entities from certain provisions of the global minimum tax for fiscal years beginning on or after January 1, 2026. In addition, the authorities in these jurisdictions could review our tax returns and impose additional tax, interest, and penalties, and the authorities could claim that various withholding requirements apply to us or our subsidiaries or assert that benefits of tax treaties are not available to us or our subsidiaries, any of which would harm us and our results of operations. 1.4.2 Our business, financial condition, and results of operations may be adversely affected if we are required to collect sales or other related taxes for subscriptions to our models, platform, and applications in jurisdictions where we have not historically done so. We collect sales tax in a number of jurisdictions. Sales, use, value-added, digital services, and similar tax laws and rates vary by jurisdiction. One or more states or countries may seek to impose incremental or new sales, use, or other tax collection obligations on us. A successful assertion by a state, country, or other jurisdiction that we should have been or should be collecting additional sales, use, or other taxes could, among other things, result in substantial tax payments, create significant administrative burdens for us, discourage potential customers from subscribing to our models, platform, and applications due to the incremental cost of any such sales or other related taxes, or otherwise harm our business, financial condition, and results of operations. Further, certain jurisdictions in which we operate have enacted a digital services tax, which is generally a tax on gross revenue generated from users or customers located in those jurisdictions, and other jurisdictions are considering enacting similar laws. Any successful action by taxing authorities to compel us to collect and remit sales, use, value-added, digital services, and similar taxes, either retroactively, prospectively, or both, may adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. 1.4.3 Our ability to use our net operating loss carryforwards and certain other tax attributes may be limited. We have incurred substantial net operating losses (“NOLs”) during our history. In general, under Sections 382 and 383 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, as amended (the “U.S. Code”), a corporation that undergoes an “ownership change” is subject to annual limitations on its ability to utilize its pre-change U.S. federal NOL carryforwards and certain other tax attributes, including tax credit carryforwards, to offset its future taxable income or tax liabilities. For these purposes, an ownership change generally occurs if the percentage of a corporation’s stock (by value) owned by one or more “5-percent shareholders” increases by more than 50 percentage points over a rolling three-year period. We have experienced ownership changes in the past, and we may experience ownership changes in the future, including as a result of the global offering or subsequent shifts in our stock ownership, some of which may be outside our control. NOLs and other tax attributes of companies we have acquired are, and of companies we may acquire may be, subject to similar limitations. Similar provisions of state tax law and the tax laws of non-U.S. jurisdictions may also limit our ability

 
73 to utilize state and non-U.S. NOL carryforwards and other tax attributes. In addition, certain states, including California, have suspended or otherwise limited the use of NOL carryforwards and other tax attributes, which could accelerate or permanently increase our state income tax liabilities. Separately, under current law, U.S. federal NOLs arising in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2017 may be used to offset only 80% of taxable income in any year, whether or not an ownership change occurs. As a result of the foregoing, even if we attain profitability, we may be unable to use all or a material portion of our NOLs and other tax attributes, which could adversely affect our future cash flows and results of operations. 1.4.4 Our corporate structure and intercompany arrangements are subject to the tax laws of multiple jurisdictions, and we could be required to pay additional taxes, which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. As we continue to expand our non-U.S. operations, we are, and may increasingly be, required to report taxable income in various jurisdictions around the world based on our business activities in those jurisdictions. Our corporate structure and associated transfer pricing policies reflect the functions, risks, and assets of the entities involved in our intercompany transactions. However, our tax position is subject to various risks, including increases in tax rates, new or revised tax laws (which may apply retroactively), and new interpretations of existing tax laws and policies by taxing authorities or courts, any of which could increase our overall tax obligations. Our intercompany transactions are subject to complex transfer pricing rules administered by tax authorities in the jurisdictions in which we operate, many of which apply divergent, and sometimes conflicting, legal standards. Tax authorities may take inconsistent positions regarding the application of the arm’s-length principle, the characterization or valuation of our intellectual property, or the pricing of intercompany services and other transactions. If a tax authority successfully challenges our transfer pricing or the allocation of income and expenses among jurisdictions, we could be required to reallocate income or pay additional taxes, interest, and penalties. If the jurisdiction from which income is reallocated does not agree with the adjustment, we could also be subject to double taxation. In addition, certain of our cross-border contracting arrangements, including infrastructure-related agreements entered into by U.S. entities pending the formation of local subsidiaries, may give rise to non-recoverable value-added or similar indirect taxes or other tax costs, which could be material depending on the jurisdiction. Although we believe our tax positions are reasonable, our tax reserves are adequate, and our transfer pricing practices reflect arm’s-length terms, tax authorities may disagree with our assumptions, judgments, and estimates. If a tax authority were to prevail in asserting that our intercompany arrangements do not satisfy applicable transfer pricing requirements, we could be required to pay additional taxes, interest, and penalties that exceed our reserves. Such an outcome could increase our effective tax rate, reduce our cash flows, and adversely affect our ability to achieve and sustain profitability. 1.4.5 If our judgments or estimates relating to our critical accounting policies prove to be incorrect, our results of operations may be adversely affected. The preparation of financial statements in conformity with U.S. GAAP requires management to make judgments in applying our accounting policies and to make estimates and assumptions that affect the amounts reported on our consolidated financial statements and accompanying notes. We base our estimates in part on historical experience, market observable inputs, if available, and various other assumptions that we believe to be reasonable under the circumstances. Significant accounting policies, estimates, and assumptions used in preparing our consolidated financial statements include, but are not limited to, revenue recognition, stock-based compensation, common stock valuations, fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs, leases, income taxes, and loss contingencies. In addition, we engage in complex and novel transactions and may be required to consolidate certain assets or entities on our financial statements, which may involve significant judgment and could result in volatility in our reported results of operations. Our results of operations may be adversely affected if our assumptions change or if actual circumstances differ from those in our assumptions, which may cause our results of operations to fall below the expectations of securities analysts and investors and cause a decline in the market price of our Class A common stock. 1.4.6 If we fail to maintain an effective system of disclosure controls and internal control over financial reporting, our ability to produce timely and accurate financial statements or comply with applicable regulations may be impaired, which may adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. As a public company, we will be subject to the reporting requirements of the U.S. Exchange Act, the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, and the listing standards of the Nasdaq Global Select Market. The Sarbanes-Oxley Act and related U.S. Exchange Act rules require, among other things, that we maintain effective disclosure controls and procedures and internal control

 
74 over financial reporting. We are continuing to develop and refine our disclosure controls and other procedures that are designed to assure that information required to be disclosed by us in the reports that we will file with the SEC is recorded, processed, summarized, and reported within the time periods specified in SEC rules and forms and that information required to be disclosed in reports under the U.S. Exchange Act is accumulated and communicated to management, including our principal executive and financial officers, to allow timely decisions regarding disclosure. We are also continuing to improve our internal control over financial reporting. We have expended, and anticipate that we will continue to expend, significant resources to maintain and improve the effectiveness of our disclosure controls and procedures and internal control over financial reporting. Our current controls and any new controls that we develop may become inadequate because of changes in the conditions in our business. Further, weaknesses in our disclosure controls, procedures, or internal control over financial reporting may be discovered in the future. Any failure to develop or maintain effective controls, or any difficulties encountered in their implementation or improvement, may adversely affect our results of operations or cause us to fail to meet our reporting obligations and may result in a restatement of our financial statements for prior periods. We also rely on distribution partners and other third-party service providers to process and store data underlying our financial reporting. Our ability to maintain effective internal controls therefore depends in part on the design and operating effectiveness of controls maintained by these third parties, and our ability to audit or remediate deficiencies in such third-party control environments is limited. Any failure to implement and maintain effective internal control over financial reporting may also adversely affect the results of periodic management evaluations and annual independent registered public accounting firm attestation reports regarding the effectiveness of our internal control over financial reporting that we will eventually be required to include in our periodic reports that will be filed with the SEC. Ineffective disclosure controls and procedures and internal control over financial reporting may also cause investors to lose confidence in our reported financial and other information, which would likely adversely affect the market price of our Class A common stock. In addition, if we are unable to continue to meet these requirements, we may not be able to remain listed on the Nasdaq Global Select Market. We are not currently required to comply with the SEC rules that implement Section 404 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and are therefore not required to make a formal assessment of the effectiveness of our internal control over financial reporting for that purpose. As a public company, we will be required to provide an annual management report on the effectiveness of our internal control over financial reporting commencing with our second annual report on Form 10-K. 1.4.7 We are exposed to fluctuations in interest rates and currency exchange rates, which could negatively affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. We hold a significant amount of cash, cash equivalents, and investments, a substantial portion of which is invested in instruments with variable or market-based interest rates. As a result, our investment income is sensitive to changes in prevailing interest rates. A decline in interest rates could reduce the income we earn on these investments, which could adversely affect our financial condition and results of operations. In addition, volatility in interest rates may impact the fair value of our investment portfolio and could affect our overall financial performance. Our sales are currently denominated in U.S. dollars, euros, and British pounds, and will likely be denominated in other currencies in the future. Because we report our results of operations and revenue in U.S. dollars, we are exposed to foreign currency translation risk and may in the future face additional foreign currency risks. For example, a strengthening of the U.S. dollar compared to these foreign currencies could increase the real cost of our models, platform, and applications to non-U.S. customers, which could reduce demand for our models, platform, and applications and adversely affect our results of operations. In addition, as our non-U.S. operations expand, an increasing portion of our operating expenses may be denominated in foreign currencies and subject to fluctuations due to changes in foreign currency exchange rates. If we are not able to effectively manage these risks, including through any hedging activities, our financial condition and results of operations could be adversely affected. 1.5 Risks Related to our Governance Structure 1.5.1 Our capital stock structure features certain provisions that are novel or otherwise not common among other corporations with multiple-class structures, and may effectively eliminate the ability of holders of our Class A common stock to influence important decisions, including a change in control. We have a novel capital and corporate governance structure that has no direct public company precedent. We are incorporated as a PBC under Delaware law. As a PBC, we are required to balance the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose identified in our amended and restated certificate of incorporation. In addition, the LTBT possesses certain rights that are designed to

 
75 help ensure that we are managed in a manner that responsibly balances our goals as a PBC. Through a special class of common stock, Class T common stock, the LTBT generally has the authority to elect and remove the Class T directors, who together will constitute a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. The LTBT is intended to operate as an independent body of five financially disinterested voting trustees of the LTBT (“Trustees”), and our Class T common stock has no economic rights. As a result, the LTBT may have interests that differ from yours, and it may exercise its power in a way with which you disagree or in a way that may be adverse to your interests. Immediately prior to the completion of the global offering, we will also issue a single share of Class F common stock, a special class of our common stock, to the Founder LLC. Our seven co-founders will initially be the sole members of the Founder LLC. Upon the incapacity or death of any of our co-founders, a successor member may be admitted to the Founder LLC until the tenth anniversary of the completion of the global offering. We refer to our seven co-founders and any successors in the Founder LLC as “Continuing Founders.” Our Class F common stock will be entitled to an aggregate number of votes that equals 50.1% of the total voting power of our outstanding shares of capital stock as of the applicable record date with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally, including the election of our directors other than the Class T directors. Immediately prior to the global offering, we will also authorize a special class of our common stock, Class E common stock, which we will issue to our employees, excluding our co-founders. Our Class E common stock will be entitled to vote only on certain limited matters and will not have any economic rights. Under this governance structure, we expect that the LTBT and the Founder LLC will collectively have the ability to elect all members of our board of directors, and the Founder LLC will have the ability to determine the outcome of all matters submitted to a vote of our stockholders generally for the foreseeable future. Accordingly, holders of our Class A common stock generally will not be able to affect the outcome of any matter submitted to a vote of our stockholders or the election of our directors, regardless of how they vote, unless a majority of the Continuing Founders cannot agree on how our Class F common stock will be voted (in which case our Class F common stock will generally be voted proportionately with the votes of our Class A common stock cast on the matter). Our governance structure is likely to have the effect of limiting the likelihood of an unsolicited merger proposal, unsolicited tender offer, or proxy contest for the removal of directors. As a result, our governance structure may make it more difficult to replace our directors and management and may have the effect of depriving our stockholders of an opportunity to sell their shares at a premium over prevailing market prices. We cannot predict whether our structure will result in lower demand for our Class A common stock, increased volatility, adverse publicity, or other adverse consequences. In particular, the absence of judicial precedent interpreting this structure increases the risk and unpredictability of governance-related litigation, and courts may interpret the obligations inherent in our structure in ways that we might not anticipate. 1.5.2 Our capital structure will concentrate voting power with the Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT) and the Founder LLC for the foreseeable future and will result in the LTBT and the Founder LLC having voting power that is not derived from or proportionate to economic interests in the Company. Our Class T common stock will generally entitle the long-term benefit trust (the “LTBT”) to elect and remove the Class T directors, who together will constitute a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. Our Class T common stock will remain outstanding indefinitely, subject to the right of our board of directors and the Trustees or specified majorities of our Class A common stock, Class E common stock and Class F common stock to amend or terminate the terms of the LTBT or the rights of our Class T common stock or to redeem our Class T common stock (such time as no share of Class T common stock is outstanding, the “Class T Sunset Time”). The Class T common stock may also be transferred without restriction upon the receipt of the same approvals required to amend, terminate, or redeem it. We intentionally structured the Class T common stock in this manner to preserve long-term flexibility if circumstances change. If the Class T common stock were transferred to a person or entity that is not affiliated with the LTBT or is not otherwise required to consider the Company Purpose, for so long as we remain a PBC, all of our directors, regardless of how they are elected, would continue to be obligated to act in accordance with Delaware law and our certificate of incorporation, bylaws, and other governing documents as then in effect, including those provisions relating to our public benefit purpose. The Long-Term Benefit Trust Amended and Restated Trust Agreement limits Trustee compensation to a reasonable cash amount fixed annually by the Trustees. Trustee compensation will not vary with or be conditioned upon the profits or any action or inaction of the Company. The policies of the LTBT prohibit a Trustee from directly purchasing or holding any of our securities. Our Class F common stock, of which a single share will be issued, will entitle the Founder LLC to an aggregate number of votes that equals 50.1% of the total voting power of our outstanding shares of capital stock as of the applicable record date with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally, including the election of our directors other than the Class T directors. Our Class F common stock will remain outstanding until the earlier of (i) the completion of a 450-day

 
76 transition period commencing when there have been fewer than three Continuing Founders (not including any successor member who is a non-qualifying member as defined in the Founder LLC limited liability company agreement (the “Founder LLC Agreement”)) for 90 consecutive calendar days (the “Class F Transition Period”), and (ii) the time when there is no Class F common stock outstanding, including as a result of a redemption thereof agreed to by a supermajority of the Continuing Founders, which is the total number of Continuing Founders entitled to vote on the matter minus one; provided that if there are fewer than three Continuing Founders, such vote must be unanimous (“Supermajority”), or upon the dissolution of the Founder LLC (the “Class F Sunset Time”). Upon the completion of the global offering, based on beneficial ownership as of September 30, 2026, our co-founders will collectively hold approximately (i) 11.2% of the total voting power of our outstanding capital stock with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally, excluding through their interests in the Founder LLC, and (ii) 61.3% of the total voting power of our outstanding capital stock with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally, including through their interests in the Founder LLC. The voting powers of the LTBT and the Founder LLC are not derived from or proportionate to economic interests in the Company and will not be subject to dilution or the loss of rights upon the issuance of additional shares of Class A common stock (including upon conversion of any Class N common stock) or any other shares of our capital stock. Moreover, the LTBT, Founder LLC, and our individual co-founders may have interests that differ from yours and may vote in a way with which you disagree and that may be adverse to your interests. For example, while the LTBT, Founder LLC, and our co-founders share a long-term commitment to our mission that may benefit stockholders who share our public benefit goals, the separation between voting power and economic interests may result in such persons exercising their influence in a manner that prioritizes actions or outcomes they believe to be consistent with the Company Purpose and the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct over the pecuniary interests of our other stockholders. This divergence of voting power from economic interests in the Company is likely to persist for the foreseeable future and will not be subject to dilution based on additional issuances of our capital stock or reduction for sales or dispositions of our capital stock by our individual co-founders. 1.5.3 Our governance structure and the adoption of our amended and restated certificate of incorporation may negatively affect the decision by certain institutional investors to purchase or hold shares of our Class A common stock. Certain aspects of our governance structure, such as our multi-class capital structure, may limit the ability of certain institutional investors to invest in us as a result of their investment policies or may make such an investment less attractive to the portfolio managers of certain institutional investors. In addition, our multi-class capital structure may make us ineligible for inclusion in indices, and as a result, mutual funds, exchange-traded funds, and other investment vehicles that attempt to passively track these indices would not invest in our stock. These policies may depress our valuation compared to those of other similar companies that are able to be included in such indices. 1.5.4 We are considered a “controlled company” within the meaning of the Nasdaq Global Select Market corporate governance requirements, and, as a result, we qualify for, and currently rely on, exemptions from certain corporate governance requirements. We are considered a “controlled company” within the meaning of the Nasdaq Global Select Market corporate governance requirements because the LTBT, as the sole holder of our Class T common stock, generally has the power to elect a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. As a result, we may elect not to comply with certain corporate governance requirements, including: • the requirement that a majority of our board of directors consist of independent directors; • the requirement that our board of directors have a nominating and corporate governance committee that is comprised entirely of independent directors with a written charter addressing the committee’s purpose and responsibilities; and • the requirement that we have a compensation committee that is comprised entirely of independent directors with a written charter addressing the committee’s purpose and responsibilities. If we elect not to comply with certain requirements, you will not have the same protections afforded to stockholders of companies that are subject to all of the Nasdaq Global Select Market corporate governance requirements. Although we qualify as a “controlled company,” we do not expect to rely on this exemption except with respect to our nominating and corporate governance committee (“NGC”), which will not consist entirely of independent directors. Our board of directors currently consists of a majority of independent directors and our audit and compensation committees

 
77 currently consist entirely of independent directors. In the event that we cease to be a “controlled company” and our Class A common stock continues to be listed on the Nasdaq Global Select Market, we will be required to comply with the provision that our NGC be comprised entirely of independent directors within the applicable transition period. 1.5.5 We operate as a Delaware public benefit corporation. As a public benefit corporation, we cannot provide any assurance that we will achieve the Company Purpose. As a PBC, we are intended to produce a public benefit or benefits and to operate in a responsible and sustainable manner, balancing our stockholders’ pecuniary interests, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose identified in our amended and restated certificate of incorporation. We cannot assure you that we will achieve the Company Purpose or that the expected positive impact from being a PBC will be realized, which could adversely affect our reputation, business, financial condition, and results of operations. As a PBC, we are required, under Section 366 of the Delaware General Corporation Law (“DGCL”) and pursuant to our amended and restated bylaws, to disclose to stockholders a report at least biennially on our overall performance in promoting the public benefit identified in our amended and restated certificate of incorporation and the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct and on our assessment of our success in achieving the Company Purpose and in promoting those interests. If we are not timely or are unable to provide this report, or if the report is not viewed favorably by parties doing business with us, regulators, others reviewing our credentials, or other stakeholders, including holders of our Class A common stock, our reputation as a PBC may be adversely affected. 1.5.6 Our focus on the long-term best interests of the Company as a PBC, and the duty of our directors to balance the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those stakeholders materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose, may conflict with short-, medium-, or long-term financial interests and business performance, which may negatively impact the value of our Class A common stock. We have made, and may in the future make, decisions that we believe balance the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose set forth in our amended and restated certificate of incorporation, even if such decisions may negatively impact the short-, medium-, or long-term performance of our business, financial condition, and results of operations or the short-, medium-, or long- term performance of our Class A common stock. This may impact the value of our Class A common stock and make owning our Class A common stock less appealing to investors who are focused on returns. Our decisions and actions in pursuit of long-term success may not result in the long-term benefits we expect, which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations, as well as the market price of our Class A common stock. Such decisions and actions may include changes to our models, platform, and applications; limitations on certain uses of our models, platform, and applications; moderating the pace of the development of our models for safety-related reasons; adjustments to the timing of new offerings; changes in how we deliver customer support; investments in our relationships with partners and employees; investments in and introductions of new models, platforms, and applications; investments in social impact initiatives consistent with our public benefit objectives; and changes in our approach to working with local or national jurisdictions on laws and regulations governing our business. Our policies, including those on usage, currently prohibit, or may be revised in the future to prohibit, certain usage or other actions, which may have adverse commercial consequences to us. For example, our usage policy prohibits the use of our models, platform, and applications to develop or operate fully autonomous weapons or to conduct mass surveillance, including mass domestic surveillance, and we have declined to permit such uses based on the Company Purpose, notwithstanding the revenue those or similar uses could generate. Maintaining these limitations has had, and may continue to have, adverse commercial and financial consequences. We have also restricted or delayed the availability of certain capabilities for safety reasons. For example, we initially released our Mythos model only as a gated research preview through Project Glasswing rather than making it broadly available to the public. Similarly, we have chosen not to develop certain commercially attractive offerings, such as image and video generation models, in order to direct our compute toward our research and safety priorities. Our public advocacy, and the decisions we make to moderate the pace of AI development, delay or restrict the release of models or features, or forgo commercial opportunities for safety-related reasons, may not maximize stockholder value, could have a negative impact on the value of our Class A common stock, and could result in litigation. Each of these decisions reflects our directors’ balancing of the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose. While we believe these decisions are consistent with the Company Purpose, as a result of these decisions, we may forgo revenue, customers, or growth opportunities that a corporation managed solely to maximize stockholder value might pursue.

 
78 Further, while directors of traditional corporations typically have a fiduciary duty to focus on maximizing stockholder value, directors of a PBC have a duty to consider not only the stockholders’ financial interests but also the company’s specific public benefit purpose and the best interests of those stakeholders materially affected by the company’s actions. Thus, our directors are not merely permitted, but obligated, to consider the Company Purpose and the interests of other stakeholders. Under Delaware law, directors are shielded from liability for breach of these obligations if they make informed and disinterested decisions that serve a rational purpose. In the event of a conflict among the interests of our stockholders, the Company Purpose, or the interests of our other stakeholders, our directors must only make informed and disinterested decisions that serve a rational purpose; thus, we cannot guarantee that such a conflict would be resolved in favor of our stockholders’ monetary interests, which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations and cause the market price of our Class A common stock to decline. In addition, there is very limited judicial precedent interpreting the balancing requirement applicable to PBCs under Delaware law, particularly for companies with significant scale or visibility, or with a scope of PBC purpose similar to ours. As a result, the scope of directors’ obligations, the standards by which their decisions may be reviewed, and the nature and availability of stockholder remedies in connection with alleged failures to responsibly balance these interests remain uncertain. Future judicial interpretations of these provisions could be more expansive than we currently anticipate and could result in increased litigation risk, greater scrutiny of board decision-making, or outcomes that differ from our expectations. Additionally, as a PBC, we are less vulnerable to an unsolicited takeover effort than a traditional company would be and, therefore, your ability to realize your investment through an acquisition may be limited. We may also not be an attractive target for activists or hedge fund investors because new directors must consider and give appropriate weight to the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose, and stockholders may be able to enforce this obligation through litigation. Further, by requiring that our board of directors consider additional stakeholders and the Company Purpose, and not just maximizing stockholder value, Delaware law could make it easier for our board of directors to reject a hostile bid, even where the acceptance of such a bid would provide the greatest short-term financial yield to investors. In addition, we intend to direct a meaningful portion of our resources toward our public benefit initiatives, which may include contributions to nonprofit organizations, research institutions, underserved communities, and other third parties that may not otherwise have access to frontier intelligence capabilities. These initiatives, which include the contribution of 846,840,960 shares of our Class N common stock, representing 5% of our fully diluted shares as of June 30, 2026 (assuming full conversion of the Amazon Notes), to Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, LLC (the “Anthropic Public Benefit Fund”), our wholly owned subsidiary dedicated to the Company Purpose (such issuance, the “Initial Public Benefit Issuance”) and any future contributions up to an additional 2% of our then-outstanding equity (plus any shares subject to options, RSUs, and other convertible securities and any shares held by the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund) to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund (or other designee) each time our share price appreciates 50% above the prior share price milestone, beginning with our initial public offering price, under a framework approved by our board of directors (the “Public Benefit Issuances”), have been, and may continue to be substantial in scale, and we expect to significantly grow these efforts over time. The benefits of such expenditures may be difficult or impossible to measure in financial terms and may not result in any direct or measurable benefit to our business or our stockholders. The amount of resources directed toward these initiatives may, in any given period, reduce our revenue, increase our expenses, or otherwise affect our results of operations. 1.5.7 As a Delaware public benefit corporation, we may be subject to increased litigation concerning our board of directors’ obligation to balance our stockholders’ pecuniary interests, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose, the occurrence of which may have an adverse impact on our business, financial condition, and results of operations. Section 367 of the DGCL provides that stockholders of a Delaware PBC with shares listed on a national securities exchange may only file an action to enforce the statutory balancing requirement imposed on the board of directors by the DGCL if they, individually or collectively, own the lesser of at least two percent of the corporation’s outstanding shares or shares of the corporation with a market value of at least $2,000,000 as of the date the action is instituted and, in the case of a derivative action, such stockholders satisfy any other conditions applicable to filing a derivative action. This potential liability for enforcement of the statutory balancing requirement does not exist for traditional corporations. Therefore, we may be subject to the possibility of increased litigation, which would require the attention of our management, and, as a result, may adversely affect our management’s ability to effectively execute our strategy. There is limited judicial precedent for this type of balancing litigation, which may create uncertainty around the scope of our directors’ obligations or the remedies available to stockholders. Additionally, any such litigation may be costly, which may adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.

 
79 1.5.8 Our amended and restated bylaws will designate a state or federal court located within the State of Delaware as the exclusive forum for substantially all disputes between us and our stockholders, and also provide that the federal district courts will be the exclusive forum for resolving any complaint asserting a cause of action arising under the U.S. Securities Act of 1933, as amended, each of which may limit our stockholders’ ability to choose the judicial forum for disputes with us or our directors, officers, stockholders, or employees. Our amended and restated bylaws, which will become effective immediately prior to the completion of the global offering, will provide that, unless we consent in writing to the selection of an alternative forum, the Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware (or, if the Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware does not have jurisdiction, another State court in Delaware or the federal district court for the District of Delaware) will, to the fullest extent permitted by law, be the sole and exclusive forum for (i) any derivative action or proceeding brought on our behalf, (ii) any action asserting a claim of breach of a fiduciary duty owed by any of our current or former directors, stockholders, or officers or other employees to us or our stockholders, (iii) any action arising pursuant to any provision of the DGCL, or as to which the DGCL confers jurisdiction upon the Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware, (iv) any action arising pursuant to or to interpret, apply, enforce, or determine the validity of our amended and restated certificate of incorporation, or our amended and restated bylaws, or (v) any action asserting a claim governed by the internal affairs doctrine, except for, in all cases, any claim as to which such court determines that there is an indispensable party not subject to the jurisdiction of such court (and the indispensable party does not consent to the personal jurisdiction of such court within 10 days following such determination). Section 22 of the U.S. Securities Act of 1933, as amended (the “U.S. Securities Act”) establishes concurrent jurisdiction for federal and state courts over U.S. Securities Act claims. Accordingly, both state and federal courts have jurisdiction to hear such claims. To prevent having to litigate claims in multiple jurisdictions and the threat of inconsistent or contrary rulings by different courts, among other considerations, our amended and restated bylaws will also provide that, unless we consent in writing to the selection of an alternative forum, the federal district courts of the United States will, to the fullest extent permitted by applicable law, be the sole and exclusive forum for resolving any complaint asserting a cause or causes of action arising under the U.S. Securities Act against any person in connection with any offering of our securities, including, without limitation, any auditor, underwriter, expert, control person, or other defendant. Unless we consent in writing to the selection of an alternative forum, the United States District Court for the District of Delaware will, to the fullest extent permitted by applicable law, be the sole and exclusive forum for the resolution of any derivative action or proceeding brought to enforce any duty or liability created by the U.S. Exchange Act or the rules or regulations thereunder. All other claims arising under the U.S. Exchange Act may be brought in any federal court of competent jurisdiction. Any person or entity purchasing, holding, or otherwise acquiring any interest in any of our securities shall be deemed to have notice of and consented to the foregoing bylaw provisions. Although we believe these exclusive forum provisions benefit us by providing increased consistency in the application of Delaware law and federal securities laws in the types of lawsuits to which each applies, the exclusive forum provisions may limit a stockholder’s ability to bring a claim in a judicial forum of its choosing for disputes with us or our current or former directors, officers, stockholders, or other employees, which may discourage lawsuits with respect to such claims against us and our current and former directors, officers, stockholders, or other employees. Our stockholders will not be deemed to have waived our compliance with the federal securities laws and the rules and regulations thereunder as a result of our exclusive forum provisions. 1.5.9 Provisions in our amended and restated certificate of incorporation and amended and restated bylaws could make a merger, tender offer, proxy contest, or other significant corporate transaction difficult, potentially depressing the market price of our Class A common stock. Our amended and restated certificate of incorporation and amended and restated bylaws, which will become effective immediately prior to the completion of the global offering, will contain a number of provisions that may make the acquisition of our company more difficult. 81 1.6.2 The market price of our Class A common stock may be volatile, and you may lose all or part of your investment. We cannot predict the prices at which our Class A common stock will trade. These fluctuations may cause you to lose all or part of your investment in our Class A common stock. Factors that may cause fluctuations in the market price of our Class A common stock include the following: • price and volume fluctuations in the overall stock market from time to time, including fluctuations due to general economic uncertainty or negative market sentiment; • fluctuations in the trading volume of shares of our Class A common stock or the size of our public float; • short selling of our Class A common stock or related derivative securities; • actual or anticipated changes or fluctuations in our results of operations;
