Upon the conversion of shares of Class N common stock into Class A common stock, however, the resulting shares of Class A common stock will be entitled to one vote per share and the issuance of such shares will dilute the voting power of the existing holders of our Class A common stock. Any shares of Class N common stock that we issue in the future would have the same effect, diluting the economic interests of the holders of our Class A common stock while outstanding, as well as diluting their voting power upon conversion into Class A common stock. 1.6.5 Future issuances of our Class A common stock and Class N common stock will not dilute the voting power of our Class F common stock. Future issuances of our Class A common stock, including upon conversion of our Class N common stock, and our Class N common stock will not dilute the voting power of our Class F common stock because our Class F common stock, which consists of a single share held by the Founder LLC (a limited liability company of which our seven co-founders will initially be the sole members, see “1.5.1 Our capital stock structure features certain provisions that are novel or otherwise not common among other corporations with multiple-class structures, and may effectively eliminate the ability of holders of our Class A common stock to influence important decisions, including a change in control.”), is entitled to a fixed 50.1% of the total voting power of our outstanding shares of capital stock as of the applicable record date with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally. For example, if we were to issue 1,000,000 additional shares of Class A common stock, our Class F common stock would automatically be entitled to an incremental number of votes sufficient to cause the aggregate voting power of our Class F common stock to equal 50.1% of the total voting power of our outstanding shares of capital stock as of the applicable record date with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally, or approximately 1,004,008 additional votes. Any future issuances of additional shares of Class A common stock, including upon conversion of our Class N common stock, and Class N common stock will not be subject to approval by our stockholders except as required by the listing standards of the Nasdaq Global Select Market.

86 1.6.9 Non-U.S. holders of our Class A common stock are subject to currency exchange risk, and adverse currency movements could reduce the value of their investment. Our Class A common stock is, and is expected to continue to be, denominated and quoted for trading exclusively in U.S. dollars. Stockholders located outside the United States, including investors resident in member states of the European Union, will therefore be exposed to fluctuations in the exchange rate between the U.S. dollar and their local currency. Such fluctuations may adversely affect the value, expressed in a stockholder’s local currency, of (i) the proceeds received upon any sale, transfer, or other disposition of our Class A common stock, (ii) any dividends or other distributions we may pay in respect of our Class A common stock, and (iii) the overall return on investment realized by such stockholders. Depreciation of the U.S. dollar against an investor’s local currency would reduce the local currency value of any such sale proceeds or dividends, even if the U.S. dollar value thereof, or the U.S. dollar trading price of our Class A common stock, remains unchanged or increases. We do not, and do not intend to, enter into any currency hedging transactions or other arrangements designed to reduce or manage currency exchange risk on behalf of our non-U.S. stockholders, and we assume no obligation to do so. Accordingly, non-U.S. investors will bear the full currency risk associated with their investment in our Class A common stock, and any adverse movement in the applicable exchange rate will be borne entirely by such stockholders without any mitigation on our part. Any dividends or other cash distributions we declare on our Class A common stock will be declared and paid in U.S. dollars. The amount that a non-U.S. stockholder ultimately receives in its local currency will depend on the exchange rate prevailing at the time such dividend or distribution is converted, which may differ materially from the exchange rate prevailing at the time the dividend or distribution was declared or on the applicable record date. Non-U.S. stockholders may also incur currency conversion costs, including fees charged by banks or other financial intermediaries effecting the conversion, which would further reduce the net amount received. Because our Class A common stock is expected to be quoted and traded in U.S. dollars, non-U.S. stockholders who wish to sell their holdings of our Class A common stock will likely receive sale proceeds denominated in U.S. dollars and will bear the risk of converting those proceeds into their local currency at the exchange rate prevailing at the time of conversion. An unfavorable movement in the applicable exchange rate between the date of purchase and the date of sale, or between the date of sale and the date of conversion, could significantly reduce the return realized by such stockholders, or result in a loss, even where the U.S. dollar price of our Class A common stock has appreciated over the relevant period. Exchange rates between the U.S. dollar and other currencies, including the euro and other currencies of European Union member states, are influenced by a wide range of factors that are outside of our control, including changes in exchange controls or foreign exchange regulations, monetary and fiscal policy decisions by the U.S. Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank, or other central banks or governmental authorities, interest rate differentials, inflation, sovereign debt levels, and broader macroeconomic and geopolitical conditions in the United States, the European Union, and elsewhere. Any such developments could result in significant and unpredictable fluctuations in the applicable exchange rates, which could adversely affect the value of an investment in our Class A common stock for non-U.S. stockholders, including stockholders resident in the European Union.

None of the directors, officers or other executives of the Company are residents or citizens of the EEA. Investors may be unable to effect service of process within the EEA. Furthermore, since the Company’s assets are primarily located in the United States, any judgment obtained in the EEA against the Company may not be collectible in the EEA. Conversely, civil liabilities based on U.S. federal or state securities laws may not be enforceable in the Covered EEA Countries and Switzerland: Germany and Sweden: There is doubt as to the enforceability in Germany of civil liabilities based on U.S. federal or state securities laws, either in an original action or in an action to enforce a judgment obtained in U.S. federal or state courts. The United States and Germany currently do not have a treaty providing for the reciprocal recognition and enforcement of judgments, other than arbitration awards, in civil and commercial matters. Consequently, a final judgment by any U.S. federal or state court for payment, whether or not predicated solely upon U.S. federal or state securities laws, would not automatically be enforceable in Germany. In addition, in the past the recognition and enforcement of punitive damages has been denied by German courts as incompatible with the fundamental principles of German law. Moreover,

 
90 a German court may reduce the amount of damages granted by a U.S. court and recognize damages only to the extent that they are necessary to compensate actual losses or damages. The same considerations regarding enforceability of civil liabilities apply in Sweden. Denmark: There is doubt as to the enforceability in Denmark of civil liabilities based on U.S. federal or state securities laws, either in an original action or in an action to enforce a judgment obtained in U.S. federal or state courts. The United States and Denmark do not have a treaty providing for reciprocal recognition and enforcement of judgments, other than arbitration awards, in civil and commercial matters, and no executive order has been issued under the Danish Administration of Justice Act (Retsplejeloven) to provide for such recognition and enforcement in relation to the United States. Consequently, a final judgment by any U.S. federal or state court for payment, whether or not predicated solely upon U.S. federal or state securities laws, would not automatically be enforceable in Denmark, although the judgment may be submitted as evidence in a new action before a competent Danish court. Danish law does not recognize punitive or exemplary damages as a form of civil damages, as this is considered contrary to Danish public policy (ordre public), and such awards in actions brought in the United States or elsewhere are unlikely to be enforceable, or otherwise given effect, by Danish courts. Finland: There is doubt as to the enforceability in Finland of civil liabilities based on U.S. federal or state securities laws, either in an original action or in an action to enforce a judgment obtained in U.S. federal or state courts. The United States and Finland do not have a treaty providing for reciprocal recognition and enforcement of judgments, other than arbitration awards, in civil and commercial matters. Consequently, a final judgment by any U.S. federal or state court for payment, whether or not predicated solely upon U.S. federal or state securities laws, would not automatically be enforceable in Finland, although the judgment may be submitted as evidence in a new action before a competent Finnish court in which case the Finnish court may give such effect to the foreign judgment as it deems appropriate. Finnish law does not recognize punitive or exemplary damages as a form of civil damages, and punitive or exemplary damages may be considered contrary to the fundamental principles of the Finnish legal system. In addition, a Finnish court may reduce the amount of damages granted by a U.S. court and recognize damages only to the extent that they are necessary to compensate actual losses or damages. France: There is doubt as to the enforceability in France of civil liabilities based on U.S. federal or state securities laws, either in an original action or in an action to enforce a judgment of a U.S. court. The United States and France do not have a bilateral treaty providing for the reciprocal recognition and enforcement of judgments (other than arbitral awards) in civil and commercial matters. In the absence of such a treaty, a final and conclusive judgment from a U.S. court is not automatically enforceable in France and requires an enforcement order from a French court. A French court may grant such an order without re-examining the merits of the case, provided it finds that three general conditions are met: (i) the jurisdiction of the U.S. court, which is assessed by determining if the dispute had a “characterized link” with the United States and that French courts did not have exclusive jurisdiction over the matter; (ii) the judgment’s conformity with French international public policy, which includes both substantive and procedural aspects. Regarding substantive public policy, enforcement of a U.S. judgment awarding punitive damages may be denied if the amount is considered disproportionate to the actual loss suffered and the breach of contractual obligations. Procedural public policy essentially consists of principles protecting the fundamental rights of the defense; and (iii) the absence of fraudulent intent to circumvent French law. Ireland: There is currently no treaty in force between Ireland and the United States providing for the automatic, reciprocal recognition and enforcement of judgments (other than arbitration awards) in civil and commercial matters. As a result, a judgment of a U.S. federal or state court would not be automatically enforceable in Ireland, and would instead need to be enforced by means of a fresh action before the Irish courts. Before proceedings may be served on a U.S.-domiciled entity, leave of the Irish courts is required. An applicant must establish a prima facie case and a practical benefit to bringing the proceedings in Ireland. The existence of Irish assets against which the judgment could be enforced is the clearest example of such a benefit. If leave is granted and proceedings are served on the Company, the Irish courts would then consider whether the U.S. judgment should be enforced in accordance with Irish common law principles. Under those principles, an Irish court will generally recognize and enforce a foreign money judgment that is final and conclusive and for a definite sum, provided the foreign court is regarded as having had jurisdiction over the judgment debtor, and provided the judgment is not impeachable on grounds such as fraud, a breach of Irish principles of natural justice, or conflict with Irish public policy or incompatibility with an earlier judgment. There is no assurance that (i) leave would be obtained from the Irish courts to serve proceedings; or (ii) a U.S. civil judgment would satisfy the common law requirements for enforcement in Ireland in any given case. The Netherlands: There is doubt as to the enforceability in the Netherlands of civil liabilities based on U.S. federal or state securities laws, either in an original action or in an action to enforce a judgment obtained in U.S. federal or state courts. The United States and the Netherlands currently do not have a treaty providing for the reciprocal recognition

 
91 and enforcement of judgments, other than arbitration awards, in civil and commercial matters. However, a Dutch court may, without substantive re-examination on the merits, give binding effect to such a final and conclusive judgment, provided that it finds that the judgment: (i) was rendered by a court that established its jurisdiction on the basis of internationally accepted grounds; (ii) was rendered in proceedings that comply with Dutch standards of the proper administration of justice (behoorlijke rechtspleging); (iii) is not contrary to Dutch public policy (openbare orde); and (iv) is not incompatible with a prior judgment of a Dutch or foreign court rendered between the same parties on the same subject matter. In addition, in the past the recognition and enforcement of punitive damages has been denied by Dutch courts as incompatible with the substantial foundations of Dutch law. Moreover, a Dutch court may reduce the amount of damages granted by a U.S. court and recognize damages only to the extent that they are necessary to compensate actual losses or damages. Norway: There is doubt as to the enforceability in Norway of civil liabilities based on U.S. federal or state securities laws, either in an original action or in an action to enforce a judgment obtained in U.S. federal or state courts. The United States and Norway do not currently have a bilateral treaty providing for the reciprocal recognition and enforcement of civil judgments (other than arbitral awards) in civil and commercial matters. Accordingly, a final judgment by a Norwegian court against the Company would not automatically be recognized and enforced in the United States, and there is no certainty that U.S. courts would give effect to such a judgment. Conversely, a final judgment rendered by a U.S. court would not be automatically recognized and enforced in Norway. Whether a Norwegian court will recognize and enforce a foreign judgment will depend on a case-by-case assessment, and there is no assurance that such recognition or enforcement will be granted. Investors should be aware that awards of punitive or exemplary damages in actions brought in the United States or elsewhere may not be enforceable by Norwegian courts. Spain: There is doubt as to whether a lawsuit based upon U.S. federal or state securities laws, or the laws of any non- Spanish jurisdiction, could be brought in an original action in Spain, and whether a foreign judgment based upon such laws would be enforceable in Spain. In particular, the United States and Spain do not currently have a treaty providing for the reciprocal recognition and enforcement of judgments, and the same may apply to other non-Spanish jurisdictions. Accordingly, a judgment rendered by any U.S. federal or state court based on civil liability, whether or not predicated solely upon U.S. federal or state securities laws, enforceable in the United States, would not be directly recognized or enforced in Spain. Switzerland: There is doubt as to the enforceability in Switzerland of original actions, or actions for enforcement of judgments of U.S. courts, of civil liabilities to the extent predicated upon the federal and state securities law of the United States. Switzerland and the United States do not have a treaty providing for reciprocal recognition and enforcement of judgments, other than arbitration awards, in civil and commercial matters. The recognition and enforcement of a judgment of the courts of the United States in Switzerland is governed by the principles set forth in the Swiss Federal Act on Private International Law. This statute provides that the application of provisions of non-Swiss law by the courts in Switzerland shall be precluded if the result is incompatible with Swiss public policy. Also, mandatory provisions of Swiss law may be applicable regardless of any other law that would otherwise apply. The Swiss Federal Act on Private International Law provides in principle that a judgment rendered by a non-Swiss court may be enforced in Switzerland only if: the non-Swiss court had jurisdiction pursuant to the Swiss Federal Act on Private International Law; the judgment of such non-Swiss court has become final and non-appealable; the judgment does not contravene Swiss public policy; the court procedures and the service of documents leading to the judgment were in accordance with the due process of law; and no proceeding involving the same parties and the same subject matter was first brought in Switzerland, or adjudicated in Switzerland, or was earlier adjudicated in a third state and this decision is recognizable in Switzerland. Where a claim relating to the information contained in a prospectus is brought before a court, the plaintiff investor might, under the respective national legislation of the relevant member state of the EEA, have to bear the costs of translating the prospectus before the legal proceedings are initiated. 2.6 Presentation of Financial and Other Information 2.6.1 Note Regarding Financial Information The Company prepares its consolidated financial statements in accordance with U.S. GAAP. Strategy, Performance and Business Environment 4.1 Information about the Company and the Group The Company was founded and incorporated under the legal name Anthropic, PBC as a Delaware public benefit corporation on January 26, 2021, and operates under the laws of the State of Delaware, United States. The Company is registered with the Division of Corporations of the State of Delaware under file number 4860621, and its LEI is 984500B6DEB8CEBC4Z70. The Company’s registered office is at 251 Little Falls Drive, Wilmington, Delaware 19808, United States, and its principal executive offices are located at 548 Market Street, PMB 90375, San Francisco, California 94104, United States (telephone +1 (415) 326-6303). The Company as well as certain of its subsidiaries and associated companies primarily operate under the commercial name “Anthropic.” The Group’s website address is www.anthropic.com. Information contained on our website or linked therein or otherwise thereto does not constitute part of nor is it incorporated by reference into this prospectus. 4.1.1 Our Governance Structure and Its Goals Our novel capital and corporate governance structure has been carefully designed and differs significantly from that of other public companies. We strive to help bring humanity safely into an era where transformative super intelligence4 exerts tremendous and potentially decisive influence over a broad range of human undertakings. Operating as a PBC gives our board of directors the necessary latitude to balance the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose. In addition, a financially disinterested LTBT, which generally has the power to elect and remove a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors, is designed to supply both the incentives and insights for striking this balance appropriately. We also believe that our seven co-founders are distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission. 4.1.1.1 Public Benefit Corporation We are incorporated as a public benefit corporation (PBC) under Delaware law, a structure that enables our commitment to AI safety and responsibility. PBCs are a class of corporations that are intended to produce a public benefit and to operate in a responsible and sustainable manner. As a PBC, we are required to balance (i) the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, (ii) the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and (iii) the Company Purpose. This requires our board of directors to weigh multiple factors, including relevant long- and short-term externalities of decisions, alongside the pecuniary interests of our stockholders. To date, we have found that the safety and societal benefit of AI and consideration of the best interests of all key stakeholder groups have generally aligned with our long- term commercial success and stockholders’ long-term monetary interests. However, as a PBC, we may make decisions that we believe appropriately balance the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose, but that negatively impact the short-, medium-, or long-term performance of our business or the market price of our Class A common stock. There is limited judicial precedent interpreting the balancing requirement applicable to PBCs under Delaware law, and there is therefore uncertainty as to how a court would view our directors’ balancing of these potentially competing interests. For a discussion of these risks, see the sections titled “1.5.6 Our focus on the long-term best interests of the Company as a PBC, and the duty of our directors to balance the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those stakeholders materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose, may conflict with short-, medium-, or long-term financial interests and business performance, which may negatively impact the value of our Class A common stock.” and “1.5.7 As a Delaware public benefit corporation, we may be subject to increased litigation concerning our board of directors’ obligation to balance our stockholders’ pecuniary interests, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose, the occurrence of which may have an adverse impact on our business, financial condition, and results of operations.” In measuring our public benefit performance, our board of directors will consider the objectives set forth in our five mission pillars: that the technical problems of AI safety are solved, that AI safety is a universal practice backstopped by 4 For purposes of this prospectus, we use the terms “super intelligence,” “SI,” “artificial intelligence,” and “AI” interchangeably.

 
98 law, that AI strengthens democracy and global stability, that AI expands prosperity and human flourishing, and that AI’s benefits are shared by everyone. We may also address the additional interests of our customers, partners, employees, and other stakeholder constituencies that we may identify from time to time. Neither our amended and restated certificate of incorporation nor our amended and restated bylaws will require that we measure our public benefit performance against an objective third-party standard, and our board of directors will be responsible for establishing and overseeing the standards by which to measure our public benefit performance against these objectives. We currently expect that our objectives and standards will be qualitative in nature and may evolve over time as our business grows and as our understanding of our public benefit impact develops. As required by Section 366(b) of the DGCL, we will provide our stockholders no less than biennially with a statement assessing our promotion of the Company Purpose and of the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct. The statement will set out our objectives and standards and describe the actions we have taken. We intend to make the statement available to stockholders and the public through our website. We also expect to demonstrate our progress towards these goals by continuing to publish evidence-based research on our website regarding our work and its impact. 4.1.1.2 Long-Term Benefit Trust We created the LTBT, which was designed to ensure that we are managed in a manner that responsibly balances our tripartite goals as a PBC: (i) the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, (ii) the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and (iii) the Company Purpose. The LTBT is organized as a common law “noncharitable purpose trust” under Delaware law and governed by the Long-Term Benefit Trust Amended and Restated Trust Agreement (the “Trust Agreement”). The LTBT is intended to operate as an independent body of Trustees with expertise in AI safety, national security, public policy, and social enterprise. The LTBT’s arrangements are designed to minimize the LTBT’s and the Trustees’ exposure to our financial performance and grant the Trustees sufficient independence to ensure we are striking this balance appropriately. Through a special class of common stock, Class T common stock, the LTBT generally has the authority to elect and remove the Class T directors, who together will constitute a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. Class T common stock has no economic rights. Decisions regarding our business and affairs are made by our board of directors. While the LTBT has significant influence over our board of directors through its ability to generally elect and remove Class T directors, neither the LTBT nor the Trustees have decision-making authority in the day-to-day management or strategy setting of the Company. The LTBT’s role is to select directors who are well equipped to responsibly balance our tripartite goals as a PBC, and to support our management’s decision-making through advice and guidance. Certain actions, such as a merger, consolidation, or sale of all or substantially all of our assets, will require the approval of our board of directors pursuant to Delaware law, a majority of whom are elected by the LTBT. 4.1.1.2.1 Election and Removal of Directors As the sole holder of Class T common stock, the LTBT generally has the authority to elect and remove the Class T directors, who together will constitute a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. Our Class T common stock will not vote on the election or removal of directors elected by the holders of our Class A common stock and Class F common stock, who will be elected or removed solely by the holders of Class A common stock and Class F common stock, voting together. For a discussion of the members of our board of directors who are currently Class T directors and those who will be Class T directors upon the completion of the global offering, see the section titled “9.1 Management.” Prior to nominating or removing a director, the nominating party must provide at least 30 days’ notice to our nominating and corporate governance committee (“NGC”), which notice period is waivable by our NGC in its discretion. Following the completion of the global offering, our NGC will be composed of one Class T director and two directors who are not Class T directors and will act by majority vote. With respect to one of the Class T director seats (the “Specified Class T Director”), the LTBT’s ability to nominate that director, to remove that director without cause, or to change the director designated as the Specified Class T Director is subject to the concurrence of our NGC. If our NGC does not concur with such nomination, removal, or change in designation within 15 days of receiving notice, the matter will be submitted to a vote of the holders of our Class E common stock unless the LTBT elects to withdraw the notice. If submitted to a vote of the holders of Class E common stock, approval of the LTBT’s proposal will require a majority of the votes cast by our Class E common stock (subject to a quorum of a majority of outstanding Class E common stock). The LTBT may withdraw any notice of nomination, removal, or change in designation at any time before the taking of such a vote. Any Class T director, including the Specified Class T Director, may be removed for cause, which will be determined in accordance with Delaware law,

 
99 without the concurrence of our NGC or the approval of the holders of our Class E common stock; provided, however, that each of the LTBT and the Founder LLC has agreed to provide 30 calendar days’ notice to the other stockholder and our NGC prior to effecting a removal of any director for cause. 4.1.1.2.2 Changes to the LTBT and Class T Common Stock The terms of the LTBT and the rights of our Class T common stock may be amended as follows (any of which, the “Trust Amendment Threshold”): • if the Trustees are voting in favor of such amendments, upon approval of 80% of the authorized members of our board of directors and 80% of the Trustees then in office (in each case, rounded up or down to the nearest whole number (any exact 0.5 rounding up)); • if our Class F common stock remains outstanding and the Trustees are not voting in favor of such amendments: o until the third anniversary of the completion of the global offering, upon approval by (i) our Class F common stock acting pursuant to the unanimous approval of the Continuing Founders, (ii) a majority of the votes cast by our Class E common stock (subject to a quorum of 40% of our outstanding Class E common stock), and (iii) a majority of the votes cast by our outstanding Class A common stock (subject to a quorum of a majority of outstanding Class A common stock); or o at any time, upon approval by (i) our Class F common stock acting by decision of 66 2/3% of the Continuing Founders (rounded up to the nearest whole number), (ii) 75% of the votes cast by our Class E common stock (subject to a quorum of a majority of outstanding Class E common stock), and (iii) a majority of the votes cast by our Class A common stock (subject to a quorum of a majority of outstanding Class A common stock); or • if no Class F common stock remains outstanding and the Trustees are not voting in favor of such amendments, upon approval of 85% of our outstanding shares of Class A common stock. In addition, our Class T common stock may be redeemed by us for no consideration upon approval of persons comprising the above thresholds for amendments of the terms of the LTBT or the rights of our Class T common stock. 4.1.1.2.3 Trustees of the LTBT The LTBT is governed by five Trustees. The Trustees have the authority to appoint the Trustees by majority vote of the Trustees then in office and to remove the Trustees by majority vote of the total number of authorized Trustees or by the unanimous approval of the other Trustees then in office and the approval of our NGC, provided that the LTBT must provide at least 30 days’ prior written notice to our NGC before effecting any such appointment or removal. The notice period is waivable by our NGC in its discretion. Trustees may also be removed by order of the Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware upon petition by a person designated by the Trust Agreement as having the power to enforce the agreement if a Trustee has engaged in disqualifying conduct and removal would best serve the purpose of the LTBT. Trustees will serve annual terms, and there is no limit to the number of terms a Trustee may serve. Trustees are selected based on their expertise in areas relevant to the LTBT’s purpose, including AI safety, national security, public policy, social enterprise, and related fields. In practice to date, the Trustees and company executives have collaborated closely on sourcing, interviewing, and selecting Trustees. Of the five authorized seats for Trustees, one is currently vacant. Dr. Neil “Buddy” Shah has served as a Trustee and Chair of the LTBT since June 2023. Dr. Shah will also serve as an initial manager of the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund. Dr. Shah has served as Chief Executive Officer of the Clinton Health Access Initiative (“CHAI”), a global health organization focused on improving access to health services in low- and middle-income countries, since June 2022. Prior to joining CHAI, Dr. Shah served as Managing Director of GiveWell, a nonprofit organization focused on directing charitable capital to cost-effective global health and development programs, and, before that, as co-founder and Chief Executive Officer of IDinsight, a global advisory, data analytics, and research organization. He holds an A.B. in Economics from Harvard University, an M.D. with an emphasis in global health policy from Albert Einstein College of Medicine, and an M.P.A. in International Development from Harvard Kennedy School of Government. Dr. Shah was selected to serve as a Trustee because of his expertise in global health, impact measurement, and social enterprise, and his experience evaluating the long-term societal effects of large-scale programs. Richard Fontaine has served as a Trustee since April 2025. Mr. Fontaine has served as Chief Executive Officer of the Center for a New American Security (“CNAS”), a bipartisan national security research institution, since February 2019, having previously served as President of CNAS from 2012 to 2019 and as Senior Fellow from 2009 to 2012. Mr. Fontaine serves concurrently as Executive Director of the Trilateral Commission’s North America group, a position he has held

 
100 since July 2019. Prior to joining CNAS and the Trilateral Commission, Mr. Fontaine served as foreign policy advisor to Senator John McCain, including as advisor to the McCain 2008 presidential campaign and subsequently as Minority Deputy Staff Director of the Senate Armed Services Committee. He has also served as Associate Director for Near Eastern Affairs at the National Security Council, and he has held positions at the U.S. Department of State and on the staff of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. Mr. Fontaine was selected to serve as a Trustee because of his extensive background in foreign policy and national security, and he will address the growing intersection between AI capabilities and geopolitical risks. Dr. Ben S. Bernanke has served as a Trustee since June 2026. Since 2014, Dr. Bernanke has been a Distinguished Fellow in Economic Studies at the Brookings Institution, a public policy research organization. Dr. Bernanke served as Chairman of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System from February 2006 to January 2014, having been appointed to that position by Presidents George W. Bush and Barack Obama. Prior to serving as Federal Reserve Chairman, Dr. Bernanke served as chairman of the President’s Council of Economic Advisers and as a member of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. Moncher Professor of Physics and of Astronomy at Harvard University, where he has been a member of the faculty since 2003. Dr. Stubbs was selected to serve as a Trustee because of his expertise in experimental physics and the application of AI to science and education, and his experience leading scientific projects across academia, government, and the national laboratories. 4.1.1.2.4 Certain Relationships and Transactions with the LTBT and its Trustees We provide funding to the LTBT, which holds all of our Class T common stock, to support its operations and the compensation of its Trustees. In the years ended December 31, 2023, 2024, and 2025, we paid $2,716,750, $0, and $906,089 to the LTBT, respectively. During the nine months ended September 30, 2026, we paid $8,425,213 to the LTBT. In addition, Dr. Shah receives annual cash compensation of $25,000 for his service as the Chair of the LTBT. Trustee compensation will not vary with or be conditioned upon the profits or any action or inaction of our company. The donation will be used to support CNAS research examining how AI is reshaping global competition, national security, international security, democratic governance, and other issues related to emerging technology and security.

 
101 4.1.1.3 Founder Voting Structure We believe that our seven co-founders, Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Christopher Olah, as a group, are distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission. Our co-founders have been instrumental in building our leadership position and establishing the mission-driven values that define our company. In addition, Dr. Amodei serves as our Chief Executive Officer and a member of our board of directors and Ms. Amodei serves as our President and Chairperson of our board of directors. Their long-term strategic vision has been critical to our success and will continue to guide our future. In our highly competitive industry, success requires visionary leadership, strong direction, and the kind of decisiveness necessary to make bold investments, pursue transformative opportunities, and compete effectively against formidable competitors, while also balancing the pecuniary interests of our stockholders with the Company Purpose and the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct. We believe that our success depends in part on establishing a capital structure that enables our co-founders, management, and board of directors to focus on strategic initiatives that create lasting value for our stakeholders, rather than facing pressure to prioritize short-term results or purely pecuniary objectives at the expense of our long-term vision and mission. Immediately prior to the completion of the global offering, we will issue a single share of Class F common stock, a special class of our common stock, to the Founder LLC, a limited liability company of which our seven co- founders will initially be the sole members and that will be managed by its members. Our Class F common stock will be entitled to an aggregate number of votes that equals 50.1% of the total voting power of our outstanding shares of capital stock as of the applicable record date with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally, including the election of our directors other than the Class T directors. Our Class F common stock will be voted by the Founder LLC in a manner determined in accordance with the Founder LLC Agreement. Generally, the Founder LLC will vote as determined by a majority of the members of the Founder LLC entitled to vote thereunder. Our seven co-founders will initially be the sole members. Upon the incapacity or death of any of our co-founders, a successor member may be admitted to the Founder LLC until the tenth anniversary of the completion of the global offering. We refer to our seven co-founders and any successors in the Founder LLC as “Continuing Founders.” When there have been fewer than three Continuing Founders (not including any successor member who is a “Non- Qualifying Member” as defined in the Founder LLC Agreement) for 90 consecutive calendar days, a 450-day transition period will commence (the “Class F Transition Period”). Upon completion of the Class F Transition Period, all of our Class F common stock and Class E common stock then issued and outstanding will be redeemed by us for no consideration and certain other governance changes will take effect. Regardless of the length of time that has elapsed since the completion of the global offering or the circumstances that resulted in the removal of a Continuing Founder, one or more successor members may be admitted to the Founder LLC during the Class F Transition Period as needed to ensure that there are three Continuing Founders serving until completion of the Class F Transition Period. The admission of any successor member during the Class F Transition Period will not cure the event that commenced the Class F Transition Period or extend the Class F Transition Period. For additional information, see the section titled “11.2.1.3 Our Capital Stock Following Completion of the Global Offering.” A Continuing Founder will be removed from the Founder LLC upon the earliest to occur of (i) such Continuing Founder’s resignation as a member of the Founder LLC; (ii) such Continuing Founder’s death or incapacity; (iii) with respect to each of our seven original co-founders, such original co-founder’s ceasing to hold (together with such original co- founder’s related holders) on any record date for a vote of our stockholders a number of shares of Class A common stock (including shares subject to options, RSUs, and other convertible securities) equal to at least 2% of the shares of Class A common stock held by such original co-founder and their related holders as of the completion of the global offering; (iv) such Continuing Founder’s removal for “cause” (as defined in the Founder LLC Agreement), which includes specified competitive activities described in the Founder LLC Agreement; (v) with respect to any successor member admitted to the Founder LLC prior to the commencement of the Class F Transition Period, other than a successor member who is a member during the Class F Transition Period, the tenth anniversary of the completion of the global offering; or (vi) with respect to each of our seven original co-founders, the commencement of a leave of absence approved by a Supermajority of the other Continuing Founders, which may not be approved during the Class F Transition Period or if the grant of the leave of absence would itself cause the Class F Transition Period to commence. Each Continuing Founder will be entitled to one vote when determining how our Class F common stock will be voted. If a majority of the Continuing Founders cannot agree on how our Class F common stock will be voted, then our Class

 
102 F common stock will generally be voted proportionately with the votes of our Class A common stock cast on the matter (subject to a quorum of a majority of outstanding Class A common stock). With respect to certain matters, our Class F common stock will be voted “for” the proposal only if a greater threshold of Continuing Founders agree, and if the greater threshold is not met, our Class F common stock will be voted “against” the proposal. See the section titled “11.5 Class F Common Stock Voting Mechanics.” The Founder LLC Agreement will not govern the voting of any shares of our Class A common stock held by the co- founders or their related holders. Each co-founder (or their related holders) will be able to vote shares of our Class A common stock held by them in their discretion, regardless of the manner in which the Founder LLC will vote our Class F common stock. The voting power of our Class F common stock will not be impacted by future issuances of our capital stock that may cause economic or voting dilution to stockholders, such as issuances for capital raising purposes, acquisitions, or employee compensation. This structure will allow the Founder LLC to determine the outcome of matters submitted to a vote of our stockholders generally, including the election of those directors not elected by the LTBT, certain amendments to our organizational documents, and the approval by our stockholders of any merger, consolidation, sale of substantially all our assets, or other major corporate transaction requiring stockholder approval. 4.1.1.4 Our Co-Founders Our seven co-founders co-founded Anthropic in January 2021. Each co-founder will initially be a member of the Founder LLC and a Continuing Founder for purposes of the Class F common stock structure described above. Brief biographical information about each co-founder is set forth below.5 Dario Amodei has served as our Chief Executive Officer and a member of our board of directors since co-founding Anthropic in January 2021. See the section titled “9.1.2 Executive Officers” for Dr. Amodei’s full biographical information. Daniela Amodei has served as our President and a member of our board of directors since co-founding Anthropic in January 2021. Tom Brown co-founded Anthropic in January 2021 and serves as our Chief Compute Officer, leading the technical organization responsible for securing, scaling, and effectively using our compute resources. Prior to co-founding Anthropic, Mr. Brown led the engineering of GPT-3 at OpenAI and, along with Dario Amodei, co-invented deep reinforcement learning from human feedback, a specific form of reinforcement learning in which human evaluators rate the model’s responses, and those ratings are used as the reward signal to guide training (“RLHF”), which was central to converting base large language models (AI models trained primarily on large datasets to understand and generate natural language and computer code, “LLMs”) into modern conversational assistants such as Claude. He holds an M.Eng. in Computer Science from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Before joining OpenAI, Mr. Clark was a technology journalist covering supercomputers, neural networks, and advanced technology, writing for publications including The Register and BusinessWeek. Prior to co-founding Anthropic, Dr. Kaplan was a researcher at OpenAI and an associate professor of physics at Johns Hopkins University, where he taught courses on the foundations of deep learning. Except as set forth in this paragraph, references to our “co-founders” elsewhere in this prospectus do not include Mr. Mann.

 
103 Sam McCandlish co-founded Anthropic in January 2021 and serves as our Chief Architect. Dr. McCandlish is a theoretical physicist and machine learning researcher specializing in large-scale model training and AI systems architecture. Prior to co-founding Anthropic, Dr. McCandlish made significant contributions to AI safety research at OpenAI, where he built and led a team focused on the science and scaling of machine learning; his work on Scaling Laws helped pave the way for large-scale advancements in AI, including the development of GPT-3.
