153 In addition, the majority of our compute is contracted under multi-year commitments that we typically procure 12 to 18 months in advance of availability. When customer demand or research needs exceed this long-term capacity, we procure short-term compute that currently costs significantly more than comparable compute procured under our multi-year commitments. We expect our use of short-term compute to continue to increase in the near term and to in turn compress our operating margin and Adjusted Operating Margin as a result. 5.2.1 Adoption of Claude Each successive version of a Claude model is designed to advance the frontier with capabilities that customers value most, including coding, agentic workflows, computer use, and complex reasoning, which unlock new categories of use and drive compounding demand from new and existing customers. Claude’s intelligence is a primary driver of its diffusion and our revenue growth: because Claude leads at the AI frontier, customers rapidly adopt it, quickly see real value, and organically expand their use. We complement this intelligence-led growth with direct go-to-market and Applied AI teams and extend our reach through native availability across all three major cloud platforms—AWS, GCP, and Azure—and through partnerships with systems integrators, consultants, and data platforms. We deliver this intelligence through an integrated approach. Our Claude model family is the foundation, with model classes optimized for different points along the capability-cost-speed curve. On top of our models, Claude Platform gives developers access to the primitives we use ourselves, which they can use to build their own AI solutions. We have also built first-party applications on Claude Platform for customers that prefer a ready-to-deploy option. We believe the value of this integrated approach is reflected in the increasing number of customers that use both Claude Platform and our first-party applications. For the three months ended September 30, 2026, over 50% of our customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis used Claude Platform and at least one of our first-party applications, up from approximately 30% for the three months ended December 31, 2025. As more customers adopt Claude and expand their usage, we have rapidly grown our base of customers that generate meaningful revenue. We had more than 11,900 customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis as of September 30, 2026, up from more than 950 as of September 30, 2025. In addition, as customers further embed Claude into their most critical workflows and growth initiatives, many rapidly expand their deployments into higher revenue tiers. As of September 30, 2026, we had more than 1,900 customers with $1 million or more of revenue on a TTM basis and approximately 250 customers with $10 million or more of revenue on a TTM basis. This customer momentum is driven by significant usage expansion as customers realize the value of deploying Claude across their organizations. The value that Claude delivers to customers has helped drive our Net Revenue Retention of approximately 900% as of September 30, 2026 (unaudited). The growth in our business reflects the degree to which enterprises are embedding Claude directly into their business- critical workflows. Despite these trends, adoption across the global economy remains nascent. As Claude’s capabilities continue to advance, we believe the addressable opportunity will expand, and Claude will continue its rapid diffusion across more enterprises. 5.2.2 Compute Efficiency Compute is the most significant operating cost in our business, and compute efficiency is a critical determinant of our operating efficiency and revenue. Our research-driven algorithmic improvements in training and inference optimization and multi-chip compute architecture have combined to dramatically increase our compute efficiency as our revenue has scaled. The result is that we are able to continue increasing the intelligence our research can produce and the revenue our business can generate per dollar of compute investment. We define compute efficiency as maximizing the intelligence produced and revenue generated per dollar of compute invested. Three pillars drive our compute efficiency: • Training Efficiency. Our researchers regularly innovate compute multipliers. Increasingly, Claude itself assists in the research and engineering that produce each successive version of our models, which is a recursive dynamic we refer to as “closing the loop,” with successive versions of our models accelerating the development of the next and compounding these gains across model generations. • Inference Efficiency. Our researchers have delivered meaningful compute multipliers for inference— reducing the compute required to serve a given level of model performance—while our engineering teams have driven significant optimizations in how efficiently that compute is utilized in production. This allows us to provide greater value for customers and generate greater revenue from our compute base over time, which is

 
154 critical as we have consistently operated in a compute-constrained environment where customer demand exceeds available compute. • Multi-Chip Compute Approach. We train and serve Claude natively across four major chip families (AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs and AMD GPUs) using a proprietary orchestration layer that enables us to optimize workloads for price and performance. This flexibility, which took years and significant investment to build and we believe is difficult to replicate at scale, expands our available compute, reduces dependence on any single vendor, and enables us to continuously route workloads to the most optimal hardware for those workloads. This foundation, paired with Claude’s increasing understanding of chip and model architectures, allows us to onboard new chip platforms in a fraction of the time this once required. Revenue per dollar of compute (compute efficiency, measured as revenue divided by compute and infrastructure expenses) has expanded meaningfully, even as we have accelerated research and product velocity and expanded our internal Claude usage. For example, our revenue grew 1,127% year-over-year for the three months ended September 30, 2026 (unaudited), compared to our compute and infrastructure expenses that grew 382% during the same period (unaudited). Compute efficiency increased by a factor of 4.3x from 0.40x in the three months ended March 31, 2025 to 1.72x in the three months ended September 30, 2026 (each unaudited). While serving our growing customer demand, we also advanced the frontier with new leading models, including Mythos 5, Fable 5, and Opus 5, and launched new products, including Claude Cowork, Claude Security, and Claude Design. In the three months ended September 30, 2026, our underlying compute efficiency improvements were partially offset by the delivery of additional compute, including $5.0 billion of compute under short-term commitments (unaudited), which currently costs significantly more than comparable compute procured under our multi-year commitments. This reduced revenue per dollar of compute compared to the preceding quarter. 5.2.3 Operating Efficiency Our operating efficiency is derived from our high talent density, our efficient go-to-market, and how extensively our teams leverage Claude in their work. Claude is the common thread, amplifying the output of our employees. For example, over 90% of the contributions to our codebase in September 2026 were written by Claude. Additionally, the average daily volume of code contributed to our codebase per engineer in the three months ended September 30, 2026 was over 45 times the average daily volume in the year ended December 31, 2024. From September 30, 2025 to September 30, 2026, TTM revenue increased approximately 1,200% while headcount increased approximately 170%, driving TTM revenue per employee from $1.4 million to over $6.6 million (each unaudited), a reflection of extraordinary talent density and a culture built to compound it. Our go-to-market model reflects this as well—intelligence-led growth and broad distribution partnerships enable us to rapidly expand customer adoption and revenue without being limited by the rate at which we can grow our sales and marketing organization, resulting in greater sales efficiency as compared to typical enterprise technology companies. Our revenue was $33.2 billion for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, up from $2.5 billion for the nine months ended September 30, 2025 (each unaudited). Our operating loss was $1.3 billion for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, down from $5.2 billion for the nine months ended September 30, 2025 (each unaudited). The result of our revenue growth, compute efficiency, and operating efficiency has been a significant improvement in Adjusted Operating Income, which was $4.1 billion for the nine months ended September 30, 2026 (unaudited), up from an Adjusted Operating Loss of $3.1 billion for the nine months ended September 30, 2025 (unaudited). Driven by our operating efficiency, our Adjusted Operating Margin increased by 236 percentage points to 15% in the three months ended September 30, 2026 from (221)% in the three months ended March 31, 2025 (each unaudited). We expect operating margin and Adjusted Operating Margin to fluctuate over time, particularly in periods when substantial incremental compute is delivered to us and we incur the associated expenses. See the section titled “5.9 Supplemental Financial Information” for a description of and information about Adjusted Operating Income (Loss) and Adjusted Operating Margin, as well as a reconciliation of these financial measures to the most directly comparable financial measures calculated in accordance with U.S. GAAP. Our operating loss was $567 million for the three months ended September 30, 2026, compared to an operating income of $974 million for the three months ended June 30, 2026, primarily driven by $5.0 billion of compute under short- term commitments, which currently costs significantly more than comparable compute procured under our multi-year commitments, and $2.0 billion of non-cash charges related to our donation matching program (each unaudited). Adjusted Operating Income increased for the three months ended September 30, 2026 to $2.5 billion compared to $2.2 billion for the three months ended June 30, 2026, while Adjusted Operating Margin decreased from 19% for the three

 
155 months ended June 30, 2026 to 15% for the three months ended September 30, 2026, primarily driven by the $5.0 billion of short-term compute noted above (all unaudited). 5.2.4 Compute Investments Investing in compute is a prerequisite for long-term growth. We invest in compute for research, model development, serving customers, and internal usage of Claude. Our commercial traction, research progress, and the scale of the opportunity ahead give us the conviction to continue investing aggressively in compute. An increasing portion of these investments relates to building out our own compute and infrastructure and vertically integrating across the compute supply chain to secure long-term compute at the scale required for frontier model development. These investments take the form of capital expenditures and other commitments, including lease obligations, that we incur well in advance of the related compute becoming operational and generating revenue. As a result, we expect this build-out to change the cash flow profile of our business and to be a significant use of net cash in operating and investing activities for the foreseeable future. See the section titled “5.12 Liquidity and Capital Resources” for more information. In addition, as our compute needs have grown substantially, we are shifting from sourcing compute solely through fixed- term cloud agreements to a hybrid model that also includes leasing chips directly and hosting them in dedicated facilities operated on our behalf. We refer to this additional source of compute as Anthropic Direct, which helps to address our scaling compute requirements and we believe will provide long-term economic advantages. Anthropic Direct represents a more flexible use of capital by allowing us to separate our commitments for data center capacity from our commitments for the compute infrastructure deployed inside them. Because data centers require longer lead times but represent a smaller fraction of total compute costs, this approach enables us to secure data center capacity early while deferring larger accelerator investments until our specific compute needs are more certain. As of and subsequent to September 30, 2026, we have entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements, including short-term commitments, as well as leases not yet commenced, with an aggregate committed spend of approximately $900.9 billion (unaudited). These commitments include approximately $451.6 billion (unaudited) expected to be incurred before December 31, 2030, and substantially all of the remainder is expected to be incurred between 2031 and 2045. Approximately $70.7 billion (unaudited) of these commitments are due in the 12 months following September 30, 2026. A significant portion of this total committed spend relates to Anthropic Direct, and we expect it to represent a growing share of our compute investments over time. The flexibility from Anthropic Direct allows us to backfill the short-term compute we procure during periods of high demand with more cost-effective, long-term compute as our dedicated infrastructure comes online. We intend to fund these investments through the revenue we generate and the capital that we raise. As of September 30, 2026, and prior to taking into account the net proceeds to us from the global offering and the concurrent private placement, we had $146.6 billion of liquidity, consisting of $95.6 billion of cash and cash equivalents, $36.3 billion of short-term investments, and $14.8 billion of availability under our A&R Credit Facility (as defined below) (all unaudited). We also maintain significant funding support from our strategic partners, including up to $77.0 billion in available financing capacity under our NPAs and up to $5.0 billion in equity commitments (of which $10.0 billion and $2.5 billion, respectively, will be reduced upon the closing of the concurrent private placement, the proceeds of which are included in the net proceeds described below) (all unaudited). In addition, we estimate that the net proceeds to us from the global offering and the concurrent private placement will be approximately $84.6 billion, based upon the assumed initial public offering price of $74.00 per share, which is the midpoint of the estimated offering price range set for the U.S. offering, and after deducting estimated underwriting discounts and commissions and estimated offering expenses payable by us, or approximately $93.7 billion if the underwriters’ option to purchase additional shares of our Class A common stock from us is exercised in full. 5.2.5 How We Generate Revenue At the foundation of our business is our family of four Claude model classes—Mythos (including Fable), Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku—each optimized for a different point on the capability-cost-speed curve. Our frontier models allow customers to match the right model to each use case. Customers typically use higher-capability models for complex reasoning, coding, and agentic workflows where greater model intelligence is required. Customers also frequently adopt our full range of models, routing individual tasks to the models that are most optimized to meet their needs along the capability- cost-speed curve. The model a customer uses and the volume of usage are the primary drivers of customer spend. We establish a direct contractual relationship with the customer and offer customers the flexibility to purchase directly from us or through CSP marketplaces, and many customers utilize both channels.

 
156 Pay-for-intelligence, our consumption-based revenue model, is our primary revenue model and currently represents the substantial majority of our total revenue. Under this model, customers pay for usage, which is metered in tokens and priced according to the model selected. Our pay-for-intelligence revenue is primarily generated from customers building applications incorporating Claude or utilizing our first-party applications. In addition, we offer certain of our applications on a subscription basis, serving both enterprises and prosumers. Under this model, customers pay a subscription fee for a specified level of usage and capabilities during the subscription term, which is generally 12 months or less. Depending on the model, platform, or applications chosen by our customers, they enter into pay-for-intelligence pricing, subscription-based pricing, or both. For example, when subscribers approach or exhaust the usage capacity included in their tier, they may utilize a higher subscription tier or purchase more intelligence directly, creating a seamless bridge from subscription to incremental pay-for-intelligence revenue. A growing number of enterprise customers agree to non-cancelable annual or multi-year contracts with minimum spend commitments in exchange for a committed price list. These contracts result primarily in consumption-based revenue. Consumption-based revenue increased from $288 million, or 75% of total revenue, for the year ended December 31, 2024, to $3.8 billion, or 83% of total revenue, for the year ended December 31, 2025, to $26.3 billion, or 79% of total revenue, for the nine months ended September 30, 2026 (each unaudited). Subscription-based revenue increased from $98 million, or 25% of total revenue, to $789 million, or 17% of total revenue, to $6.9 billion, or 21% of total revenue over the same periods (each unaudited). The larger dollar increase in consumption-based revenue reflects the growth in customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis. For 2023, our revenue of $41 million was substantially all consumption-based, reflecting our early operations. We expect consumption-based revenue to continue to represent the substantial majority of total revenue for the foreseeable future. Our recent growth may reflect early-stage adoption dynamics, the nascency of the AI market, and rapid initial customer expansion that may not be sustainable over time. We expect our revenue growth rate to decline over time, and it may decline significantly and more rapidly than we anticipate as our revenue base increases and as the market matures. 5.2.6 Our Customers and Approach to Claude Diffusion 5.2.6.1 Our Customers We serve enterprises of all sizes and across industries, in nearly every region of the world. Organizations that use Claude range from the world’s largest enterprises to AI-native startups, research institutions, and mission-driven organizations working on some of the world’s most consequential problems. Customers realize value from Claude in three primary ways: more productive employees, faster processes, and embedded intelligence in their products. As enterprise customers push Claude into increasingly complex workflows, we engage with them to understand their evolving requirements, which helps shape our product roadmap. This feedback loop deepens customer relationships with each release and makes Claude more capable for all customers. Software developers have been core to our strategy: they are simultaneously the architects of applications built on our platform, and they encode their workflows and institutional knowledge into Claude-powered agents. Developers have been our earliest adopters and often most discerning users: they apply models to unanticipated use cases quickly and surface the edge cases that sharpen each successive version of a Claude model. Claude Code is now embedded in software development workflows across major organizations, with these relationships often beginning with individual engineers who recognized the value of autonomous coding agents and accelerated adoption across their enterprises. The same intelligence and capabilities we deliver to enterprises are also valuable to prosumers in their personal endeavors. These users provide strategic value as a top-of-funnel engine for our enterprise business—individuals who utilize Claude for their personal work and then champion it inside their organizations. We are seeing broad-based growth across customer use cases, from software development to financial analysis, content creation, and complex knowledge work. Claude is extensible: regardless of entry point, enterprises quickly discover that frontier intelligence applies to a wide and expanding range of tasks across their organizations. As a result, what sometimes begins as a single use case frequently expands into broader adoption spanning coding, legal analysis, financial modeling, customer operations, and other knowledge-intensive work. 5.2.6.2 Our Approach to Claude Diffusion A core driver of Claude’s diffusion is its intelligence—as Claude’s capabilities advance, value to customers expands, and that value drives greater adoption. Ensuring the accessibility of such intelligence is also critical, and we do that in the

 
157 following ways: through our composable platform and applications that meet customers where they are, through our go-to-market and Applied AI teams directly, and through partnerships that extend our reach at scale. Intelligence-Led Growth. Our platform and applications are the primary mechanism through which Claude’s intelligence can reach users. As users begin building, brainstorming, and problem-solving with Claude, they quickly come to rely on it as a trusted partner in their work. As Claude becomes part of how people work, they experience firsthand what frontier intelligence makes possible, and such individual adoption reshapes how entire organizations operate. This pattern repeats across organizations: prosumers become internal champions, teams expand their use of Claude, and what begins as a single workflow grows into something that impacts how an entire organization operates. This pattern has been core to our revenue growth. Direct Teams. This organic adoption is complemented and enhanced through our direct go-to-market teams who help scale Claude to organizations with complex workflows and business processes. By the time our direct teams engage a customer, Claude is often already in use. Our go-to-market teams use this organic momentum to build executive sponsorship and drive enterprise-wide adoption. Applied AI Teams. Our Applied AI teams embed more deeply with select customers, building solutions that make it easier for organizations to benefit from Claude’s intelligence. They work with enterprises to design and deploy custom solutions, specialized workflows, and domain-specific implementations tailored to the customer’s own requirements. This work drives deeper adoption within individual customers and generates the feedback and information from users that help to shape our platform and product roadmap. Cloud Partnerships. Claude is accessible on all three major cloud platforms, AWS, GCP, and Azure, allowing enterprises to deploy Claude within the infrastructure, security perimeters, and commitment structures they already operate. These CSPs extend our reach through their large combined field teams that are empowered to sell our platform and applications, accelerating market adoption at a scale we believe would be difficult for any single organization to directly replicate. We have a joint go-to-market approach with these CSPs through which we establish direct contractual relationships with our customers while paying a fee to each CSP. This structure allows us to foster stronger commercial alignment with these CSPs, avoid channel conflict, set pricing, and realize the financial benefits of ongoing compute efficiency improvements. Ecosystem Partnerships. Major global systems integrators have built dedicated Claude practices with teams trained to deploy our platform and applications. Go-to-market alliances with leading data platforms embed Claude into data infrastructure that enterprises already operate, facilitating adoption of Claude within existing workflows and making it easier for enterprises to realize value from Claude. Ode with Anthropic. We recently launched an AI services company in partnership with leading private equity firms to bring Claude’s capabilities to mid-sized companies across sectors, building solutions on the Claude Platform and supporting customers over the long term. Ode with Anthropic will partner closely with our Applied AI and go-to-market teams. Together, these approaches have led to a structurally efficient approach to facilitating the diffusion of Claude in the economy, with our sales, marketing, and partnerships expenses representing 17% of revenue for the nine months ended September 30, 2026. 5.3 Key Factors Affecting Our Performance 5.3.1 Remaining at the Frontier of AI We believe enterprises consistently choose the most capable and trustworthy AI systems, making our position at the frontier an important driver of our success. Our ability to rapidly grow our revenue is partially dependent on our continued delivery of more intelligent and capable models. Our experience is that as we deliver models with meaningfully improved capabilities that deliver higher intelligence per dollar spent, customers find new applications for AI across their businesses, accelerating adoption and revenue growth. This can be seen in the trajectory of our model family adoption. Successive versions of our most intelligent generally available model have delivered meaningfully greater intelligence and capabilities. With each release, we have seen most customers utilize the latest version of our models, reinforcing the direct relationship between frontier model quality and revenue generation. As we deliver more capable models, customers have expanded their usage into new use cases and increased their spending accordingly.

 
158 We expect our ability to deliver innovation in intelligence and capability at the frontier to remain a key driver of revenue growth in future periods, and maintaining a leading position requires continued investment in research and compute, top technical talent, and access to capital sufficient to support our growth trajectory. 5.3.2 Securing Sufficient Compute and Optimizing Its Utilization Our ability to continue advancing intelligence at the frontier depends on securing sufficient compute for research, model development, serving customers, and internal usage of Claude. Our ability to leverage heterogeneous compute helps us to secure compute at sufficient scale and optimal price-performance. If any of our chip partners are unable to deliver committed compute or experience delays, or if we need to procure incremental compute, we benefit from having a range of partners as opposed to being overly reliant on any one partner. The availability, timing, and cost of compute are subject to factors largely outside our control, including the concentration of chip and memory manufacturing among a limited number of suppliers and geographies, constraints on the availability of power and data center capacity, and evolving export controls. We have historically operated in a compute-constrained environment in which demand for compute has exceeded the supply available to us. In addition, certain of the CSPs on which we rely for compute are also strategic investors in us, are our customers, and offer AI models and services that compete with ours. These multifaceted relationships could give rise to conflicts of interest or competitive dynamics that adversely affect our access to compute, its cost, or the prioritization of our workloads. As our compute needs have grown substantially, we are shifting from sourcing compute solely through fixed-term cloud agreements to a hybrid model that also includes leasing chips directly and hosting them in dedicated facilities operated on our behalf. We refer to this additional source of compute as Anthropic Direct, which helps to address our scaling compute requirements and provides potential long-term economic advantages of direct hosting. Anthropic Direct provides us with a more flexible use of capital by allowing us to separate our commitments for data center capacity from our commitments for the accelerators deployed inside them. Because data centers require longer lead times but represent a smaller fraction of total compute costs, this approach enables us to secure data center capacity early while deferring larger accelerator investments until our specific compute needs are more certain. Optimizing the utilization of our compute is equally important to our success in satisfying customer demand. We continuously direct compute to its highest-value use case, balancing the need to advance research and model development with the need to serve our customers and support internal usage of Claude. We rely on compute efficiencies, such as the discovery of compute multipliers, to get the most out of the compute that we procure. Our ability to effectively direct compute and drive compute efficiencies will be an important determinant of both our pace of innovation and our financial results over time. 5.3.3 Attracting and Retaining Technical Talent Advancing the frontier and maximizing the return on our compute investment require that we attract, hire, and retain top technical talent. Talent attraction and retention start with our seven co-founders, all of whom have remained with the company. We believe our culture and mission alignment enable us to hire and retain the talent required to continuously push the frontier of AI forward in a safe and responsible way. We expect our ability to continue attracting and retaining top technical talent to remain a key determinant of our pace of innovation and our financial results in future periods. 5.3.4 Our Continued Access to Capital We must make significant investments in compute for research, model development, serving customers, and internal usage of Claude. Our compute requires substantial upfront commitments and ongoing payments as the compute becomes available to us. Our compute commitments will continue to grow as we scale our business. Our ability to secure sufficient compute is directly linked to our ability to access capital on favorable terms, such as through equity or debt financing or cash flow from operations. In order to maintain our access to capital, we must continue to demonstrate that we are able to invest that capital in a highly productive way. The best measures of our progress are Claude’s intelligence and capability, and customer adoption of Claude. Our ability to convert compute investment into frontier model performance, and then increase customer adoption, will be a key determinant of our access to capital. Our ability to sustain access to capital depends in part on demonstrating a credible trajectory toward profitability. Our revenue growth, compute efficiency, and operating efficiency have significantly improved our operating margin and Adjusted Operating Margin, but we plan to keep investing heavily, which will adversely impact our results of operations. Our compute commitments are substantial and generally must be satisfied regardless of our revenue or utilization, while our access to additional capital depends on a number of conditions, many of which are outside our control, including

 
159 market conditions and investor demand. In addition, a portion of our compute and infrastructure build-out has been funded or supported by capital or credit support provided or facilitated by certain of our CSPs and chip partners. Our ability to reduce this reliance over time depends in part on our ability to obtain financing from independent sources on our own credit. 5.3.5 Our Ability to Diffuse Claude in the Enterprise Our financial performance depends on the pace and breadth at which AI, and in particular Claude, is adopted across the global economy. While Claude’s capabilities already address a wide range of enterprise use cases, we believe that enterprise adoption remains nascent. We believe that our ability to capture this opportunity and drive revenue growth in future periods will depend on three dynamics: First, our ability to translate model improvements into accessible products and platform capabilities. In the nine months ended September 30, 2026, we launched an aggregate of 250 new model versions, platform features and applications, including new capabilities in Claude Code, Claude Cowork, and vertical solutions for key industries. Our growth depends on continuing this pace of product innovation and reducing the friction between Claude’s capabilities and customer workflows. Our growth also depends on how quickly new capabilities reach customers, which in turn depends on the steps we take to assess and mitigate the risks of each model during development and before and after release. In the past, these steps have included delaying the release of new models and limiting their initial availability, such as our initial release of Mythos through Project Glasswing and our later release of Fable 5 as a generally-available model with safety restrictions, and in the future, as we learn more about model capabilities and behavior, could include additional measures that affect whether, how, and when we develop or release new models or capabilities. We evaluate whether to delay or restrict a release based on the results of our pre-release capability and safety evaluations and our assessment of whether available safeguards adequately mitigate the identified risks, and we may also take such steps where those evaluations are inconclusive. For more information, see the section titled “4.14.6 Safeguards” specifically subsection “Our Approach to Model Releases.” These measures, and any laws, regulations, or standards governing frontier model development that may be adopted, could cause new use cases to emerge more slowly and slow the enterprise adoption and expansion on which our revenue growth depends. We believe that enterprises prefer models that are safe and aligned, and that our continued investment in safety strengthens customer trust and supports long- term adoption. Second, our ability to expand and diversify distribution. A large portion of our growth to date has been self-service and organic. As AI adoption extends further into enterprises and more regulated industries, we are investing in direct go- to-market, Applied AI teams, and partnerships across all three major cloud platforms, systems integrators, consultants, and data platforms. We are also expanding our ability to serve international customers through the growth of regional offices and partnerships in key markets, and we expect international expansion to be a meaningful driver of revenue growth as global demand for AI accelerates. The effectiveness of these investments, and our ability to hire and retain go-to-market talent, will be a meaningful determinant of growth. Third, our ability to land new customers and expand within existing accounts. The number of customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis grew from approximately 20 as of December 31, 2023, to approximately 200 as of December 31, 2024, to approximately 1,500 as of December 31, 2025, and to more than 11,900 as of September 30, 2026. Total revenue from these customers grew from approximately $37 million to $220 million to $3.5 billion to $26.1 billion and represented 90%, 57%, 76%, and 74% of total revenue for the years ended December 31, 2023, 2024, and 2025, and the TTM period ended September 30, 2026, respectively (each unaudited). The remaining 26% of total revenue for the TTM period ended September 30, 2026 (unaudited) was generated by approximately 40 million customers, each with less than $100,000 of revenue on a TTM basis. In addition, as of September 30, 2026, we had more than 1,900 customers with $1 million or more of revenue on a TTM basis and approximately 250 customers with $10 million or more of revenue on a TTM basis. Despite this growth, our penetration into the largest enterprises remains early. Over 50% of the Fortune 500 and over 30% of the Global 2000 were customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis as of September 30, 2026. We believe we are in the early stages of our expansion within these customers, with our revenue from these Fortune 500 customers representing, on average, less than 0.1% of their total expenses for the three months ended September 30, 2026. We compare this measure against our largest Fortune 500 customers, who are further along in their adoption of AI. For the three months ended September 30, 2026, revenue from our top 10 Fortune 500 customers represented, on average, less than 1% of their total expenses—still a small fraction of their overall spend, but over eight times the average of our Fortune 500 customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis. We believe the difference reflects the

 
160 substantial runway we have to deepen adoption, both within our largest customers and within customers earlier in their adoption of Claude.23 Claude adoption is broad-based. No single customer represented more than 10% of our revenue for the nine months ended September 30, 2026. Approximately 79% of our revenue came from customers outside of our top five customers for the three months ended September 30, 2026, up from approximately 64% for the three months ended March 31, 2026 (each unaudited). At the same time, our largest customers continue to expand. For the three months ended September 30, 2026, our revenue from each of our top five customers reached a record high. 5.3.6 Customer Usage Patterns Our revenue is influenced by customer usage patterns, which are impacted by the frequency and capability of new model version releases, as well as seasonal trends, each of which can create variability in our results from period to period. The continuous and overlapping cadence of new model version releases is inherent to remaining at the frontier of AI development. For example, model versions released in the six months ended September 30, 2026 accounted for over 80% of our revenue for the three months ended September 30, 2026 (unaudited). As we have released successive versions of Claude models, we have continued to see revenue growth as new capabilities unlock additional use cases, prompting new customers to adopt Claude and existing customers to expand their usage. Our customer usage patterns have also typically exhibited seasonality, particularly around holiday and vacation periods in the summer and winter, when certain workflows slow down and overall customer activity declines. For example, developer commits and feature launches are typically slower during the code freezes that many companies schedule over holidays. Consistent with this pattern, for the two weeks ended January 2, 2026, total customer spend declined by approximately 20% compared to the prior two weeks ended December 19, 2025. However, our historical growth rates may mask the impact of seasonal trends on our results. These dynamics are inherent aspects of a pay-for-intelligence revenue model and may be important determinants of our financial results in future periods. Because of these seasonal patterns, our results of operations have varied, and are expected to continue to vary, from period to period, and our results for any one period may not be indicative of our results for any future period. As our revenue growth rate declines over time, we expect seasonal effects to become more apparent in, and to have a greater effect on, our period-to-period results, and to make it more difficult to forecast our results of operations. 5.3.7 Our Commitment to Public Benefit Our commitment to public benefit extends to how we deploy our resources. We intend to direct a meaningful portion of our resources toward ensuring that frontier intelligence is safe and its benefits are broadly distributed, which we refer to as our public benefit initiatives. This may include significant contributions to nonprofit organizations, research institutions, and other third parties working on problems where AI can have the greatest positive impact, as well as programs designed to make Claude accessible to underserved communities, educators, and public institutions. As part of these initiatives, we contributed 846,840,960 shares of our Class N common stock, representing 5% of our fully diluted shares as of June 30, 2026 (assuming full conversion of the Amazon Notes), to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, our wholly owned subsidiary dedicated to the Company Purpose, which we refer to as the Initial Public Benefit Issuance. As the value we create grows, we intend for the public benefit to share meaningfully in that growth as well. To that end, our board of directors has approved a framework for additional contributions tied to future increases in our share price. Following the global offering and the concurrent private placement, our board of directors, in its discretion, may issue shares of our Class N common stock to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund (or other designee) representing up to an additional 2% of our then-outstanding shares (plus any shares subject to options, RSUs, and other convertible securities and any shares held by the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund) each time our share price appreciates 50% above the prior share price milestone, beginning with our initial public offering price. A share price milestone is reached only when our closing share price has exceeded the applicable threshold on at least 90 of the trailing 120 consecutive trading days, and our average closing share price over the 10 trading days prior to such issuance also exceeds that threshold. Although our board of directors has approved this framework, any future contributions will be made at the discretion of our board of directors. The shares that are contributed to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, including the Initial Public Benefit Issuance, may be transferred or donated to a third party, or otherwise sold in a registered public offering or private placement transaction in furtherance of our public benefit initiatives. Our board of directors will determine the allocations and distributions from the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund until it approves a specific governance structure for the entity, at which point decision-making authority is expected to transition to designated managers of 23 For purposes of this measure, we include only Fortune 500 customers that are publicly traded and calculate the measure using total expenses as reported in their publicly available financial statements.

 
161 the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund operating under that structure. The initial managers are Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Jack Clark, and Dr. Neil “Buddy” Shah. The Initial Public Benefit Issuance and the additional share contribution framework represent one of the ways in which we intend to pursue the Company Purpose, but they are not the exclusive means of doing so. We expect to dedicate additional resources, and to make other business and operational decisions, in furtherance of the Company Purpose outside of, and in addition to, these equity contributions. In addition, we maintain a donation matching program through which employees can pledge a meaningful portion of their equity awards or equivalent cash proceeds to a donor-advised fund or other nonprofit organization, and we match those donations with shares of our Class N common stock. In the same way the Company Purpose defines how we direct our work as an organization, our donation matching program reflects a parallel commitment by our employees to direct the personal financial value created by that work toward the public good. We view our donation matching program as a meaningful expression of the Company Purpose and a reflection of the values that define our culture. In addition, our co-founders have each pledged to dedicate 80% of their personal equity in Anthropic to philanthropic causes, separate from and not eligible for our donation matching program. Decisions we make to advance our public benefit initiatives may, in any given period, reduce our revenue, increase our expenses, lower our Adjusted Operating Margin, contribute to dilution, and reduce our profitability on a per share basis relative to what we would otherwise report. Our public benefit-related expenses, which currently consist primarily of charitable donations under our donation matching program, were not significant before the three months ended September 30, 2026. For the nine months ended September 30, 2026, expenses related to our donation matching program were $2.1 billion, representing approximately 6% of our total operating expenses for that period (unaudited). However, we expect the cadence and magnitude of resources directed toward our public benefit initiatives to increase in future periods and remain a factor affecting our results of operations. 5.4 Components of Results of Operations 5.4.1 Revenue We generate revenue as customers use Claude through our platform and applications, including Claude Code, Claude Cowork, and vertical solutions for key industries. Claude is powered by our proprietary Claude model family, a set of frontier models, each with varying levels of capability, cost, and speed. Enterprise customers access our intelligence service directly from us or through CSP marketplaces, where we maintain direct contractual relationships with our customers. Depending on the model, platform, or applications chosen by our customers, they enter into pay-for-intelligence pricing, subscription-based pricing, or both. A growing number of enterprise customers agree to annual or multi-year contracts with minimum spend commitments. Revenue is recognized when customers use our intelligence service, based on the quantity of tokens consumed. Subscriptions are generally prepaid on a monthly or annual basis, and are subject to usage limits that reset over short periods, which results in revenue being recognized on a ratable basis over the subscription period, which is generally 12 months or less. We expect our revenue growth rate to decline over time and to fluctuate from period to period. Revenue growth in any period may be affected by customer usage patterns, customer adoption, the deployment of our models, platform, and applications, the pricing of our offerings, the timing and success of new model and product releases, measures we decide to implement to safely deploy new capabilities, our ability to continue meeting customer requirements, and other factors affecting demand for our models, platform, and applications, including those described in the section titled “1.1.24 We are at an early stage of our revenue growth, we have experienced rapid growth in recent periods, and our historical growth rates are not indicative of future performance or our ability to sustain or forecast future revenue growth.” In addition, our revenue has included, and we expect will continue to include, amounts from customers that we subsequently determine are using our models, platform, and applications in violation of our usage policy or commercial terms. We believe this dynamic is common in our industry. Because detection, investigation, and enforcement take time, we recognize revenue from such customers when the related services are provided, before restricting or terminating their access. Based on our detection and review process, we estimate that revenue from such customers represented approximately 5% to 7% of our revenue for the nine months ended September 30, 2026. This estimate requires judgment and may change as our detection methodologies evolve and we identify previously undetected usage. We expect the percentage of revenue from customers using our models, platform, and applications in violation of our usage policy or commercial terms to decline in future periods as we have enhanced our detection and enforcement efforts, in

 
162 particular in August and September 2026; however, the timing and magnitude of any resulting adverse effect on our revenue and revenue growth are uncertain. 5.4.2 Operating Expenses 5.4.2.1 Compute and Infrastructure Compute and infrastructure expenses primarily consist of costs attributable to operating our technology infrastructure, which supports the full range of workloads for our models, including research, model development, serving customers, and internal usage of Claude. These costs primarily consist of compute fees paid to CSPs under committed and on- demand arrangements, including storage, networking, and connectivity, and related support costs, infrastructure costs associated with serving customer workloads through partner channels, colocation facility costs, equipment leases and committed power costs associated with our data center operations, and third-party application infrastructure software costs directly related to our compute operations. Beginning in 2026, as our obligations commence under compute and infrastructure leases, these expenses also include operating lease costs, amortization of finance lease assets, variable lease costs, and depreciation and amortization on owned servers, networking equipment, and related data center assets. See Note 8 to our consolidated financial statements, which are incorporated in, and form part of, this prospectus (see “10.1 Consolidated Financial Statements”) for a functional presentation of our operating expenses, including cost of revenue, and a description of the workloads underlying the compute and infrastructure expenses within each functional caption. Within that functional presentation, substantially all of the cost of revenue consists of compute and infrastructure expenses associated with customer-serving workloads. Additionally, cost of revenue includes certain personnel-related costs, and allocated overhead costs. Customers adopt and retain our technology based on whether our models are at the frontier of AI capability and maintaining that frontier position is essential to revenue generation. Each model release represents continuous intelligence improvements, making ongoing model development a critical factor in revenue generation. We operate an iterative cycle in which compute deployed to model development yields more capable and efficient models. Those efficiency gains free compute to serve additional customer workloads. In turn, serving our customers at scale generates feedback that informs research and model development. In this cycle, customer-serving activity and model development are each a direct input that informs the other, and we therefore view compute and infrastructure costs as critical to our ability to generate revenue within a short time of incurring such costs. We expect compute and infrastructure expenses to increase in absolute dollars and remain our largest operating expense for the foreseeable future as additional committed compute becomes available to us under multi-year arrangements with CSPs, and as we continue to invest in additional compute. These expenses are paid and recognized as compute becomes available to us, rather than when committed, and are generally fixed in the near term given the majority of our compute is contracted under multi-year commitments that we typically procure 12 to 18 months in advance of availability. When customer demand or research needs exceed this long-term capacity, we procure short-term compute that currently costs significantly more than comparable compute procured under our multi-year commitments. We deploy this committed compute as a single, shared resource across all workloads, and thus plan, incur, and assess it on a total basis rather than by individual workload. As a result, compute and infrastructure expenses as a percentage of revenue will depend primarily on how our revenue scales relative to our total committed compute cost base. In addition, as part of our public benefit initiatives, we intend to direct a meaningful portion of our resources, which may include compute, toward ensuring that the benefits of frontier intelligence are broadly accessible, and we expect to significantly scale these efforts over time. 5.4.2.2 Personnel Personnel expenses primarily consist of stock-based compensation, including expense related to stock options, RSUs, and restricted stock awards (“RSAs”), cash compensation, including base salaries and bonuses, employee benefits, including health and welfare benefits, and employer payroll taxes. We expect personnel expenses to increase in absolute dollars as we continue to expand our headcount to support the growth of our business. We also expect to incur additional stock-based compensation expense in connection with the global offering, including for certain RSUs for which the performance condition will be satisfied upon the effectiveness of the registration statement with respect to the U.S. offering. We expect that personnel expenses may fluctuate as a percentage of revenue depending on the timing and magnitude of stock-based compensation expense, and the pace of hiring across our organization.

 
163 5.4.2.3 Bartz Settlement Bartz settlement consists of the charge we recorded in 2025 to settle the Bartz litigation. See Note 13 to our consolidated financial statements, which are incorporated in, and form part of, this prospectus (see “10.1 Consolidated Financial Statements”) for additional information. 5.4.2.4 Sales, Marketing, and Partnerships Sales, marketing, and partnerships expenses primarily consist of fees paid to channel partners and marketing and advertising costs, including media and public relations spend. We expect sales, marketing, and partnerships expenses to increase in absolute dollars as we continue to invest in activities to drive continued adoption and expanded usage of our models. We expect that sales, marketing, and partnerships expenses may fluctuate as a percentage of revenue depending on the timing of and spend on marketing campaigns and changes in the terms of our channel partner distribution arrangements and the cost to deliver our intelligence service. 5.4.2.5 Other Operating and Administrative Other operating and administrative expenses primarily consist of charitable donations expense related to our donation matching program, vendor costs related to data quality and performance evaluation services, information technology and cloud software costs, payment processing and platform fees, facility and occupancy costs, non-income taxes, professional services costs, bad debt expense, and depreciation and amortization related to non-data center assets. We expect that other operating and administrative expenses will increase in absolute dollars as our business grows and as a result of operating as a public company, including expenses related to compliance with SEC rules and regulations, the listing standards of the Nasdaq Global Select Market, additional costs for directors’ and officers’ liability insurance, and professional services. We also expect other operating and administrative expenses to fluctuate as a percentage of our revenue over time as our business grows, in part as we significantly scale our public benefit initiatives, including expanded programs to make Claude accessible to underserved communities, increased charitable donation matching, contributions to philanthropic vehicles or foundations we may establish or support in the future, and other efforts aligned with our mission. 5.4.3 Interest Income Interest income consists of interest earned on our cash and cash equivalents and short-term investments which primarily consist of debt securities, including U.S. Treasury and agency securities, corporate debt, and commercial paper. 5.4.4 Change in Fair Value of Convertible Notes, Derivative Liabilities, and SAFEs Change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs consists of gains and losses as a result of recording our convertible promissory notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFE liabilities at fair value at the end of each reporting period. Because these instruments are marked to market, increases in our enterprise valuation drive increases in this expense. We will continue to recognize changes in the fair value of our convertible notes until they are converted into equity, repaid, or otherwise settled. For more information, see Note 4 to our consolidated financial statements, which are incorporated in, and form part of, this prospectus (see “10.1 Consolidated Financial Statements”). 5.4.5 Other Income (Expense), Net Other income (expense), net consists primarily of the change in fair value of strategic investments and financial instruments, the change in fair value of certain derivative instruments in connection with an acquisition of a privately- held company in December 2025, interest expense from finance leases, and foreign currency exchange gains and losses. For more information on the acquisition, see Note 15 to our consolidated financial statements, which are incorporated in, and form part of, this prospectus (see “10.1 Consolidated Financial Statements”). 5.4.6 Provision for Income Taxes The provision for income taxes primarily consists of income taxes in certain federal, state, local, and foreign jurisdictions in which we conduct business. Our effective tax rates will vary depending on the impact of the valuation allowance and nondeductible fair value adjustments to derivatives, as well as the relative proportion of foreign income to domestic income, generation of tax credits, changes in the valuation of our deferred tax assets and liabilities, and changes in tax laws.

Provision for income taxes was not material for the periods presented. 5.9 Supplemental Financial Information 5.9.1 Non-U.S. GAAP Financial Measures / Alternative Performance Measures To supplement our consolidated financial statements prepared and presented in accordance with U.S. GAAP, we use certain non-U.S. GAAP financial measures, which qualify as Alternative Performance Measures, as described below, to facilitate analysis of our operating performance and for internal planning and forecasting purposes. In accordance with the European Securities and Markets Authority’s (“ESMA”) “Guidelines on alternative performance measures” of October 5, 2015, as amended, the following sections set out information related to certain financial measures the Group uses to measure its performance that are not required by or presented in accordance with U.S. GAAP and which it regards as alternative performance measures (“Alternative Performance Measures” or “APMs”) within the meaning of the aforementioned guidelines issued by ESMA. We use Adjusted Operating Income (Loss), Adjusted Operating Margin, and Adjusted Net Income (Loss) to evaluate our operating performance, formulate business plans, prepare budgets and forecasts, and make strategic decisions, including those relating to operating expenses and the allocation of internal resources. By excluding certain items that management believes are not directly reflective of the ongoing operating performance of our business, we believe these non-U.S. GAAP financial measures or Alternative Performance Measures provide investors, analysts, and others with meaningful insight and enhance their overall understanding of our business and financial performance by providing a more consistent and comparable overview of our financial performance across periods. Other companies in our industry, including those with similar business models, may define or calculate similarly titled measures in different ways, which may limit the usefulness of these measures for direct comparison. In addition, other companies may not publish these or similar metrics. Further, these metrics have certain limitations in that they do not include the impact of certain expenses that are reflected on our consolidated statements of operations. Thus, our non- U.S. GAAP financial measures or Alternative Performance Measures should not be viewed in isolation or as a replacement for the most directly comparable financial measures prepared in accordance with U.S. GAAP. We encourage investors and others to review our business, financial condition, and results of operations in their entirety, not to rely on any single financial measure, and to view our non-U.S. GAAP financial measures or Alternative Performance Measures in conjunction with their respective most directly comparable financial measures calculated in accordance with U.S. GAAP, as well as our consolidated financial statements and accompanying notes, which are incorporated in, and form part of, this prospectus (see “10.1 Consolidated Financial Statements”).

 
173 5.9.1.1 Adjusted Operating Income (Loss) and Adjusted Operating Margin We define Adjusted Operating Income (Loss) as operating loss excluding (i) stock-based compensation expense, (ii) non-cash charitable contributions, and (iii) the Bartz settlement. Similarly, an increase (decrease) of 1.0 million in the number of shares offered by us, as set for the U.S. offering, would increase (decrease) Working Capital by $73 million, assuming the assumed initial public offering price of $74.00 per share (the midpoint of the estimated price range set for the purposes of the U.S. offering) remains the same, and after deducting the estimated underwriting discounts and commissions and estimated offering expenses payable by us. The increases in each quarter were driven by successive model and product releases that drove higher usage, expansion, and broader adoption across our offerings, with both consumption-based and subscription-based revenue contributing. The number of customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis grew from approximately 400 as of March 31, 2025 to more than 11,900 as of September 30, 2026. For the three months ended September 30, 2025 to the three months ended December 31, 2025, the increase in revenue due to higher usage was partially offset by a decrease of approximately $70 million from price reductions introduced as part of new model versions and contractual discounts. For the three months ended June 30, 2026 to the three months ended September 30, 2026, the increase in revenue due to higher usage was partially offset by a decrease of approximately $600 million from price reductions introduced as part of new model versions and contractual discounts. Price changes did not have a material impact on the other quarterly revenue trends presented. 5.11.2 Operating Expenses 5.11.2.1 Compute and Infrastructure Compute and infrastructure expenses increased sequentially in each of the quarters presented, from $944 million for the three months ended March 31, 2025 to $9.9 billion for the three months ended September 30, 2026, driven by the delivery of committed compute under our multi-year arrangements. Because we typically procure compute 12 to 18 months in advance of availability, these expenses are generally fixed in the near term and increase as committed compute becomes available to us. Compute and infrastructure expenses as a percentage of revenue decreased from 251% for the three months ended March 31, 2025 to 48% for the three months ended June 30, 2026, as revenue growth outpaced the growth of our committed compute cost base, and increased to 58% for the three months ended September 30, 2026, reflecting the delivery of additional compute. This includes $5.0 billion of compute under short-term commitments, which currently costs significantly more than comparable compute procured under our multi-year commitments. 5.11.2.2 Personnel Personnel expenses increased sequentially in each of the quarters presented through the three months ended June 30, 2026, driven by headcount growth and the associated increases in compensation, including stock-based compensation. Personnel expenses decreased in the three months ended September 30, 2026, primarily driven by lower stock-based compensation expense due to certain option awards becoming fully vested, partially offset by higher cash compensation resulting from headcount growth. 5.11.2.3 Bartz settlement In the three months ended September 30, 2025, we recorded a $1.5 billion charge to settle the Bartz litigation. See Note 13 to our consolidated financial statements, which are incorporated in, and form part of, this prospectus (see “10.1 Consolidated Financial Statements”).

 
177 5.11.2.4 Sales, Marketing, and Partnerships Sales, marketing, and partnerships expenses increased sequentially in each of the quarters presented, with the most significant increases observed in the three months ended March 31, 2026 and June 30, 2026. The increases were primarily driven by fees paid to channel partners, reflecting the growth of our business, and increased marketing and advertising expenses, driven by higher media spend to support product launches. Sales, marketing, and partnerships expenses as a percentage of revenue decreased from 22% for the three months ended March 31, 2026 to 14% for the three months ended September 30, 2026, primarily driven by a decrease in revenue generated from sales through channel partners as a percentage of total revenue and changes in the terms of our channel partner distribution arrangements. 5.11.2.5 Other Operating and Administrative Other operating and administrative expenses increased over the quarters presented, other than in the three months ended March 31, 2026, which reflected lower donation matching program charges than in the three months ended December 31, 2025. The overall increase reflected vendor costs related to data quality and performance evaluation services, information technology and cloud software costs, payment processing and platform fees, and professional services costs as our business scaled. The increases in the three months ended December 31, 2025 and September 30, 2026 were primarily driven by non-cash charges related to our donation matching program. 5.11.3 Operating Income (Loss) Our operating loss widened in the three months ended June 30, 2025, primarily driven by the delivery of additional committed compute under our CSP arrangements, the associated expenses of which increased by more in dollars than our revenue in the period, and in the three months ended September 30, 2025, which included the Bartz settlement. Our operating loss narrowed in the three months ended December 31, 2025 and March 31, 2026, and we generated operating income of $1.0 billion for the three months ended June 30, 2026, as revenue growth outpaced the growth in total operating expenses. We incurred an operating loss of $567 million for the three months ended September 30, 2026, primarily driven by $5.0 billion of compute under short-term commitments and $2.0 billion of non-cash charges related to our donation matching program. We expect our operating results to continue to fluctuate from quarter to quarter, particularly as the amount of incremental compute we receive, and the associated expenses we incur, may vary from period to period. 5.11.4 Interest Income Interest income increased sequentially in each of the quarters presented, from $51 million for the three months ended March 31, 2025 to $1.2 billion for the three months ended September 30, 2026, primarily driven by higher average cash and cash equivalents and short-term investments balances. 5.11.5 Change in Fair Value of Convertible Notes, Derivative Liabilities, and SAFEs Changes in the fair value of our convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs resulted in expense in each of the quarters presented, primarily driven by increases in the fair value of our outstanding convertible promissory notes resulting from increases in our enterprise valuation during each period. The expense was largest in the three months ended June 30, 2026, reflecting the increase in our enterprise valuation in connection with our Series H financing. We will continue to recognize changes in fair value until these instruments are converted into equity, repaid, or otherwise settled. See Note 4 and Note 9 to our consolidated financial statements, which are incorporated in, and form part of, this prospectus (see “10.1 Consolidated Financial Statements”). 5.11.6 Other Income (Expense), Net Other income (expense), net was not material for the quarters presented prior to 2026. Other income (expense), net of $(309) million, $(8.4) billion, and $(1.6) billion for the three months ended March 31, 2026, June 30, 2026, and September 30, 2026, respectively, was primarily driven by the initial fair value recognition and subsequent change in fair value of the assets and liabilities recognized under the partner financing arrangements. See Note 4 to our consolidated financial statements, which are incorporated in, and form part of, this prospectus (see “10.1 Consolidated Financial Statements”). 5.11.7 Provision for Income Taxes Provision for income taxes was not material for the quarters presented prior to the three months ended September 30, 2026. Provision for income taxes increased to $396 million for the three months ended September 30, 2026, primarily
