To date, we have financed our compute and infrastructure primarily under arrangements with

 
179 our CSPs, as well as through proceeds from the financing activities described above and cash generated from operations. As of September 30, 2026, we had cash and cash equivalents of $95.6 billion, $36.3 billion of short-term investments, and $14.8 billion available under the A&R Credit Facility, as described below. Cash and cash equivalents consist of cash held in checking and interest-bearing accounts, money market funds, and other highly liquid investments with original maturities of three months or less from the date of purchase. We have generated losses from our operations, as reflected in our accumulated deficit of $156.2 billion, which includes $135.1 billion related to changes in the fair value of our convertible notes driven by increases in our enterprise valuation and derivative liabilities since 2023, including $94.3 billion during the nine months ended September 30, 2026. Additionally, we have generated negative cash flows from operating and investing activities in 2023, 2024, and 2025, driven by ongoing expenditures to support business growth including investments to secure access to more compute and infrastructure capacity. We generated positive cash flows from operating activities of $6.6 billion for the nine months ended September 30, 2026. We continue to invest in our own data center infrastructure and enter into compute and infrastructure capacity arrangements to support anticipated demand for our intelligence service. Given the long lead times between contracting for, purchasing, or leasing compute and that compute becoming available to serve workloads, we secure these arrangements well in advance of anticipated demand. To secure certain data center development projects, which require significant capital commitments in advance of deployment, we have in some cases relied, and expect to continue to rely, on arrangements with financing sources or partners who guarantee the lease obligations to support the development of data center capacity that is expected to host such partners’ chips or computing infrastructure. Our ability to expand compute and infrastructure capacity through these arrangements in the future may depend on the continued willingness and ability of a limited number of CSPs, partners, and financing sources to enter into and perform under such arrangements. In some cases, we may also make payments in advance of the delivery of the equipment or infrastructure. We anticipate making significant and increased investments for the foreseeable future, including for owned or leased compute and infrastructure in advance of delivery. These investments help ensure we have the technological resources to maintain and expand our position at the frontier of AI. Our increasing efforts to build out our compute and infrastructure require substantial capital expenditures and are changing the cash flow profile of our business. Whereas the compute purchased through our CSP arrangements is generally paid for as the compute becomes available to us, we expect an increasing portion of our compute and infrastructure investment to take the form of capital expenditures and other commitments, including lease obligations, that require significant upfront payments well in advance of the related compute becoming operational. We expect our capital expenditures to increase significantly as we expand our build-out, and we expect these investments to result in significant net cash used in operating and investing activities for the foreseeable future. Our net cash used in these activities may increase regardless of whether our financial performance improves. The magnitude and timing of these investments are inherently uncertain and may change materially over short periods, including as a result of decisions to accelerate or expand our build-out, and such changes could rapidly and significantly affect our cash flows for a given period. In addition, these investments are subject to known trends and uncertainties that could adversely affect our results of operations. The compute and chips necessary for frontier model development are available from a limited number of suppliers and geographies and are subject to intense competition, supply constraints, and evolving export controls, and we have historically operated in a compute-constrained environment in which demand for compute has exceeded the supply available to us. In addition, certain of the CSPs and chip partners on which we rely provide us capital or credit support, serve as our infrastructure vendors, and develop and offer AI models and services that compete with ours. These relationships could give rise to conflicts of interest that affect our access to compute, its cost, the prioritization of our workloads, or the terms on which such capital or credit support is provided. For a discussion of these and other risks, see the section titled “1 Risk Factors.” We also intend to use a portion of the net proceeds we receive from the global offering and the concurrent private placement to satisfy our anticipated tax withholding and remittance obligations of $3.8 billion related to the RSU Settlement. This amount is based upon the assumed initial public offering price of $74.00 per share, which is the midpoint of the estimated offering price range set for the U.S. offering, and an assumed 50.90% tax withholding rate. Each $1.00 increase or decrease in the assumed initial public offering price of $74.00 per share would increase or decrease, as applicable, the amount we would be required to pay to satisfy our tax withholding and remittance obligations related to the RSU Settlement by $52 million. Our future capital requirements will depend on many factors, including our revenue growth, the timing and extent of our investments in compute and infrastructure capacity, including additional or expanded CSP, equipment lease and data center arrangements, the success and expansion of our sales, marketing, and business development strategies, any potential future investment in complementary businesses, products, technologies, assets, and talent, risks associated with the AI industry, and other factors described under “5.3 Key Factors Affecting Our Performance.” As a result of

 
180 these and other factors, we may be required to seek additional financing sooner than we currently anticipate. If we determine that additional financing is required, we may not be able to raise it on terms acceptable to us or at all. Any such financing, if completed, may be costly, dilutive, or lead to restrictions on how we operate our business. If we are unable to raise additional capital when required, or if we cannot expand our operations or otherwise capitalize on our business opportunities because we lack sufficient capital, our business, financial condition, results of operations, and cash flows would be adversely affected. Over the longer term, we expect to have significant cash requirements as we continue to invest in our business, primarily for compute and infrastructure, including our data center infrastructure build-out, as well as for general operating needs. We expect to fund these long-term cash requirements through a combination of cash flows from operations, proceeds from equity financings, including the net proceeds from the global offering and the concurrent private placement, proceeds from debt financings and potential future indebtedness, and financing arrangements with our partners, including under our note purchase agreements and our equipment lease and data center arrangements. Our ability to meet these requirements over the long term depends on our ability to grow our revenue and generate cash flows from operations and to access additional capital on acceptable terms. If sufficient funds are not available, we may be required to reduce, defer, or forgo planned investments, which could adversely affect our business, competitive position, and results of operations. 5.12.1 Revolving Credit Agreement On May 14, 2025, we entered into a credit agreement with Morgan Stanley Senior Funding, Inc., Barclays Bank PLC, Citibank, N.A., Goldman Sachs Lending Partners LLC, JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., Royal Bank of Canada and MUFG Bank, Ltd. acting as lenders (as amended from time to time prior to the A&R Credit Agreement, the “Credit Agreement”) and Morgan Stanley Senior Funding, Inc., as administrative agent and collateral agent for the lenders, which initially provided for a $2.5 billion senior secured revolving credit facility with a $400 million letter of credit sublimit (the “Initial Credit Facility”). In September 2025, we amended the Initial Credit Facility to increase the aggregate revolving commitments to $2.75 billion, and in November 2025, we further amended the Initial Credit Facility to increase the aggregate revolving commitments to $3.25 billion. On September 4, 2026, we entered into the A&R Credit Agreement, which amended and restated the Credit Agreement to provide for a $15.0 billion senior secured revolving credit facility with the full amount thereof available for letters of credit with Morgan Stanley Bank, N.A., Barclays Bank PLC, Citibank, N.A., Goldman Sachs Lending Partners LLC, JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., Wells Fargo Bank, National Association, Bank of America, N.A., Deutsche Bank AG New York Branch, Royal Bank of Canada, UBS AG, Stamford Branch, Bank of Montreal, BNP Paribas, Crédit Agricole Corporate and Investment Bank, Mizuho Bank, LTD., MUFG Bank, Ltd., Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation, The Toronto-Dominion Bank, New York Branch, Capital One, National Association and U.S. Bank National Association acting as lenders and Morgan Stanley Senior Funding, Inc., as administrative agent and collateral agent for the lenders (the “A&R Credit Facility”). The A&R Credit Facility will mature on September 4, 2031, subject to earlier springing maturity if more than $500 million in aggregate scheduled cash principal payments on certain of our indebtedness are required within the 91-day period preceding the date on which any such scheduled principal payment is due, and we do not have sufficient liquidity to make all such payments then due and remain in pro forma compliance with our financial covenant, subject to certain other exceptions and conditions set forth in the A&R Credit Agreement. The proceeds of the A&R Credit Facility may be used for working capital, general corporate purposes, and other lawful purposes. We may request borrowings in U.S. dollars or certain other agreed currencies, subject to the terms of the A&R Credit Agreement. As of September 30, 2026, we had no borrowings drawn under the A&R Credit Facility and $205 million of standby letters of credit outstanding. As of September 30, 2026, we were in compliance with all covenants under the A&R Credit Agreement. We may borrow, repay, and reborrow amounts under the A&R Credit Facility from time to time. We are required to pay commitment fees on the unused portion of the A&R Credit Facility and fees in connection with letters of credit. On and after the Guarantee and Collateral Release Date (as defined below), such commitment fees will vary depending on our credit ratings, as set forth in the A&R Credit Agreement. Our obligations under the A&R Credit Facility are required to be guaranteed by certain of our material subsidiaries and secured by substantially all of our assets and the assets of such subsidiary guarantors, subject to certain exceptions and exclusions set forth in the A&R Credit Agreement. The A&R Credit Agreement further provides that, on and after the date we have obtained an Investment Grade Rating (as defined in the A&R Credit Agreement) from at least two out of three of Moody’s, S&P, and Fitch, at our election, all guarantees and security interests securing the obligations under the A&R Credit Facility will be released, discharged, and terminated, subject to certain conditions set forth in the A&R Credit Agreement (such date, the “Guarantee and Collateral Release Date”).

 
181 Borrowings under the A&R Credit Facility bear interest at rates based on the Alternate Base Rate (as defined in the A&R Credit Agreement), Term SOFR Rate (as defined in the A&R Credit Agreement), or other applicable benchmark rates in the case of foreign currencies, plus an applicable margin. From and after the Guarantee and Collateral Release Date, such applicable margin will vary depending on our credit ratings, as more fully set forth in the A&R Credit Agreement. In addition, the A&R Credit Agreement includes customary affirmative and negative covenants, including, but not limited to, restrictions on additional indebtedness, liens, asset sales, investments, mergers, and restricted payments. On and after the Guarantee and Collateral Release Date, the negative covenants limiting asset sales, investments, restricted payments, and affiliate transactions will cease to apply and the negative covenants restricting additional indebtedness and liens will be modified in certain respects, including to permit additional indebtedness, subject to a cap on certain indebtedness that is secured by assets that do not secure the A&R Credit Facility or that is incurred or guaranteed by restricted subsidiaries that are not guarantors under the A&R Credit Facility. The A&R Credit Agreement includes a financial covenant requiring that we maintain liquidity of at least $5.0 billion as of the last day of each fiscal quarter, beginning with the fiscal quarter ending December 31, 2026. The A&R Credit Agreement also includes customary events of default, which, if triggered, could result in the acceleration of amounts due under the A&R Credit Facility and termination of the commitments thereunder. 5.12.2 AMD Agreement On July 20, 2026, we entered into a hardware supply framework agreement (the “Hardware Supply Agreement”) with AMD to purchase, lease, or access AMD-based Helios rack-scale systems featuring AMD Instinct™ MI450 series GPUs. Pursuant to the terms of the Hardware Supply Agreement, AMD has provided a commitment to purchase up to $5.0 billion of our Class N common stock (the “AMD Equity Commitment”), which becomes available for us to draw on in increments following the achievement of specified AMD GPU delivery and deployment milestones. In connection with the concurrent private placement, we entered into a letter agreement with AMD under which, upon the closing of the concurrent private placement, the $2.5 billion purchase price paid by AMD for shares of our Class N common stock in the concurrent private placement will satisfy a portion of the AMD Equity Commitment by reducing, on a dollar-for- dollar basis, the amount available for us to draw. As a result, following the closing of the concurrent private placement, up to $2.5 billion of the AMD Equity Commitment will remain, which will become available for us to draw only to the extent that the cumulative amount accrued based on AMD GPU delivery and deployment milestones exceeds the aggregate purchase price paid by AMD in the concurrent private placement. Based on the deployment schedule contemplated by the Hardware Supply Agreement, we expect the first of the AMD GPU delivery and deployment milestones to be achieved in 2027. Following the completion of the global offering, any subsequent purchases of our Class N common stock by AMD pursuant to the Hardware Supply Agreement will be made at a price per share equal to the volume-weighted average price of our Class A common stock over the 30 trading days immediately preceding the applicable closing date of such purchase, and we must make any draw request within 12 months following the final delivery and deployment of AMD GPU capacity under the Hardware Supply Agreement. 5.12.3 Convertible Notes 5.12.3.1 Overview We have entered into NPAs with each of Google (through Google LLC), Amazon (through Amazon Web Services, Inc.), and Broadcom that provide for the issuance of convertible promissory notes and, in certain cases, shares of our non- voting capital stock. Our NPAs with Google consist of agreements entered into in September 2023 and August 2024, pursuant to which all convertible promissory notes previously issued thereunder have been fully converted into non- voting redeemable convertible preferred stock and under which no additional notes may be issued, and an agreement entered into in March 2026 (“Google 2026 NPA”), which provides for potential future financing capacity, subject to certain conditions described below. Our NPAs with Amazon consist of the Amazon 2023 NPA and the Amazon 2024 NPA, pursuant to which we previously issued convertible promissory notes, approximately $6.2 billion aggregate principal amount of which remains outstanding as described below under “5.12.3.2 Outstanding Notes” and under which no additional notes may be issued, and the 2026 Stock Purchase and Convertible Note Facility Agreement, dated as of April 20, 2026, by and between us and Amazon (“Amazon 2026 NPA”), which provides for potential future financing capacity, subject to certain conditions described below. The Infrastructure Partner 2026 NPA provides for potential future financing capacity, if needed, subject to certain conditions described below. The principal economic terms of the NPAs that relate to our outstanding notes and potential future financing capacity are summarized in the tables below. To the extent an NPA creates an obligation to issue notes in the future, that obligation is accounted for as a derivative liability on our consolidated balance sheets until the related note is issued. For additional information, including the historical issuance and conversion of notes under these agreements, see Notes 9 and 16 to our consolidated

 
182 financial statements, which are incorporated in, and form part of, this prospectus (see “10.1 Consolidated Financial Statements”). 5.12.3.2 Outstanding Notes The following table summarizes the notes outstanding under our NPAs as of September 30, 2026 which consist entirely of non-interest-bearing rollover notes issued to Amazon under the Amazon 2023 NPA and the Amazon 2024 NPA, neither of which provides for the issuance of additional notes. Under the terms of the applicable notes, no portion of a note converts to the extent that, immediately following the conversion, Amazon would hold more than 12% of our capitalization, calculated for this purpose to include all of our outstanding capital stock on an as-converted basis together with shares underlying our outstanding equity awards and other outstanding convertible securities. Amazon may waive this limitation in its sole discretion but has elected not to do so in connection with the global offering. Prior to the global offering, the portion of each note that could not convert without exceeding this ownership cap was reissued as a rollover note in lieu of the shares of our non-voting redeemable convertible preferred stock that would otherwise have been issued to Amazon. The decrease was primarily driven by a decrease in prepaid hosting services reflecting the consumption during 2025 of hosting capacity that had been prepaid in prior periods and an increase in accounts payable, accrued expenses, and other current liabilities due to increased CSP costs and the timing of related payments. The decrease was partially offset by higher cash payments, including a payment related to the Bartz settlement, higher cash compensation costs from headcount growth, and an increase in accounts receivable.

 
189 Net cash used in operating activities for the year ended December 31, 2024 increased by $4.1 billion compared to the year ended December 31, 2023. The increase was primarily driven by an increase in prepaid hosting services due to business expansion requiring additional hosting capacity. Net cash provided by operating activities was $6.6 billion for the nine months ended September 30, 2026 as compared to cash used in operating activities of $2.0 billion for the nine months ended September 30, 2025. Our operating cash flows result primarily from cash received from our customers, offset by cash payments we make for products and services, employee compensation, operating leases, and interest. The increase in operating cash flow was primarily driven by an improvement in net loss adjusted for non-cash items, partially offset by a lower benefit from changes in working capital, primarily reflecting the timing of payments to vendors and cash receipts from customers. Working capital at any point in time is subject to many variables, including the timing of billings and cash collections, vendor payment terms, and the timing of invoice receipt and payment. 5.12.5.2 Investing Activities Net cash used in investing activities for the year ended December 31, 2025 increased by $3.1 billion compared to the year ended December 31, 2024. The increase was primarily driven by increased purchases of new short-term investments, including U.S. Treasury and agency securities, and corporate debt securities, as well as higher capital expenditures related to servers, networking, and infrastructure equipment, and purchases of intangible assets. These increases were partially offset by proceeds from sales and maturities of short-term investments. Net cash used in investing activities for the year ended December 31, 2024 increased by $20 million compared to the year ended December 31, 2023. The increase was primarily driven by increased capital investments in leasehold improvements and purchases of intangible assets. Net cash used in investing activities was $36.5 billion for the nine months ended September 30, 2026 as compared to cash used in investing activities of $2.0 billion for the nine months ended September 30, 2025, which primarily reflects the increased purchases of short-term investments, including commercial paper, U.S. Treasury and agency securities and corporate debt securities, in addition to prepayments for leased assets and equipment, and higher capital expenditures related to servers, networking, and infrastructure equipment. This was partially offset by proceeds from sales and maturities of short-term investments. 5.12.5.3 Financing Activities Net cash provided by financing activities for the year ended December 31, 2025 increased by $12.7 billion compared to the year ended December 31, 2024. The increase was primarily driven by increased proceeds from the issuance of redeemable convertible preferred stock, net of issuance costs. Net cash provided by financing activities for the year ended December 31, 2024 increased by $4.9 billion compared to the year ended December 31, 2023. The increase was primarily driven by increased proceeds from the issuance of convertible notes for cash and increased proceeds from the issuance of redeemable convertible preferred stock, net of issuance costs. Net cash provided by financing activities was $110.7 billion for the nine months ended September 30, 2026 as compared to cash provided by financing activities of $18.5 billion for the nine months ended September 30, 2025. Additionally, this amount excludes payments under certain other compute and infrastructure arrangements that do not specify a fixed dollar commitment. We estimate these payments to be in the range of $150 billion to $175 billion (each unaudited). In general, to the extent counterparties do not fulfill obligations, such as meeting agreed upon delivery dates, we have the ability to terminate all or a portion of our obligations under such arrangements, or, under certain agreements, to obtain other specified remedies, such as service credits or adjustments to the timing of our commitments, rather than terminate. Market risk represents the risk of loss that may impact our financial position due to adverse changes in financial market prices and rates. Our market risk exposure is primarily the result of fluctuations in interest rates and foreign currency exchange rates. 5.13.1 Interest Rate Risk As of September 30, 2026, we had $95.6 billion of cash and cash equivalents and $36.3 billion of short-term investments in a variety of securities, including money market funds, U.S. Treasury and agency securities, corporate debt securities, and commercial paper. In addition, we had $2.6 billion of restricted cash primarily due to amounts held as collateral for our lease and other obligations. Our cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments are held for working capital purposes, and we do not enter into investments for trading or speculative purposes. A hypothetical 100 basis point increase or decrease in interest rates would have resulted in a decrease or increase, respectively, of $310 million in the market value of our cash equivalents and short-term investments as of September 30, 2026. 5.13.2 Foreign Currency Exchange Risk We transact business globally in multiple currencies, with the vast majority of our revenue denominated in U.S. dollars and, to a lesser extent, other currencies such as euros and British pounds. Our international revenue, as well as costs and expenses denominated in foreign currencies, and intercompany transactions with our foreign subsidiaries, expose us to the risk of fluctuations in foreign currency exchange rates against the U.S. dollar. A hypothetical 10% change in foreign currency exchange rates applicable to our business would not have had a material impact on our consolidated financial statements as of September 30, 2026. We have not entered into derivative or hedging transactions, but we may enter into such arrangements in the future if our exposure to foreign currency becomes more significant. 5.14 Critical Accounting Estimates Our discussion and analysis of our financial condition and results of operations are based upon our financial statements, which have been prepared in accordance with U.S. GAAP. U.S. GAAP requires us to make certain estimates and judgments that affect the amounts reported in our financial statements. We base our estimates on historical experience, anticipated future trends, and other assumptions we believe to be reasonable under the circumstances. Because these accounting estimates require significant judgment, our actual results may differ materially from our estimates. We believe that of our significant accounting policies, which are described in Note 1 to our consolidated financial statements, which are incorporated in, and form part of, this prospectus (see “10.1 Consolidated Financial Statements”), the following accounting policies involve a greater degree of judgment and complexity. Accordingly, these are the policies we believe are the most critical to aid in fully understanding and evaluating our consolidated financial condition, results of operations, and cash flows. 5.14.1 Stock-Based Compensation We measure compensation expense for all stock-based payment awards, including stock options and RSUs, granted to employees, directors, and other service providers, based on the estimated fair value of the awards on the date of grant. The most significant input in determining the fair value of a stock option is the estimated fair value of our common stock. The estimated fair value of our common stock is also used to measure the grant-date fair value of RSUs and RSAs, including those subject to performance-based vesting conditions. 5.14.1.1 Stock Options We estimate the fair value of stock options granted to employees, consultants, officers, and directors using the Black- Scholes-Merton option pricing model on the date of grant. The fair value of stock options that are expected to vest is recognized as compensation expense on a straight-line basis over the requisite service period. Forfeitures are accounted for when they occur. The Black-Scholes-Merton model considers several variables and assumptions in estimating the fair value of stock- based awards. These variables include:

 
194 • Fair Value of Common Stock. Because our common stock is not yet publicly traded, we must estimate the fair value of our common stock. Our board of directors considers numerous objective and subjective factors to determine the fair value of our common stock as discussed in the section titled “5.14.2 Common Stock Valuations” below. • Expected Volatility. Since we have no trading history of our common stock, the expected volatility of our underlying common stock is estimated by taking the weighted-average historical volatility of a group of comparable publicly traded companies over a period equal to the expected life of the options. • Expected Term. Expected term represents the period over which we anticipate stock-based awards to be outstanding. We estimate the expected term based on the options’ vesting term and contractual terms, such that the expected life is equal to the average of the stock-based award’s weighted-average vesting period and its contractual term. • Risk-Free Rate. The expected risk-free rate assumption is based on the U.S. Treasury instruments whose term is consistent with the expected term of the stock options. • Expected Dividend Yield. The expected dividend yield is zero, as we have never declared or paid any dividends and have no current plans to do so. As of September 30, 2026, there was approximately $1.8 billion of total unrecognized compensation cost related to unvested stock options (unaudited), which is expected to be recognized over a weighted-average period of 1.2 years. 5.14.1.2 Restricted Stock Units and Restricted Stock Awards We have granted RSUs to our employees and non-employee service providers under our 2021 Plan. RSUs outstanding as of September 30, 2026 have both service-based and performance-based vesting conditions. The service-based vesting period for these awards is typically four years. Upon satisfaction of the performance-based condition, RSUs for which the service-based vesting condition has also been satisfied will vest immediately, and any remaining unvested RSUs will vest ratably over the remaining service period. The performance-based condition is generally satisfied upon the occurrence of a change in control event or the effective date of the registration statement in respect of the U.S. offering. As of September 30, 2026, no stock-based compensation expense had been recognized for such RSUs because the performance-based condition was not satisfied. In connection with the global offering, we will begin recording stock- based compensation expense based on the grant-date fair value of the RSUs (or, for RSUs modified as part of the RSU Modification (as defined in “9.12.2.12 Post-Fiscal Year End Compensation Changes and Equity Awards”), their modification-date fair value) using the accelerated attribution method. As of September 30, 2026, there was approximately $32.3 billion of total unrecognized stock-based compensation expense related to RSUs (unaudited). Of that amount, $8.2 billion relates to RSUs for which the service-based vesting condition had been satisfied or partially satisfied (unaudited). Following the completion of the global offering, stock-based compensation expense related to our RSUs will result in increases in our expenses in future periods, in particular the quarter in which the global offering is completed, as the performance-based vesting condition applicable to a significant portion of our outstanding RSUs will be satisfied upon the effectiveness of the registration statement with respect to the U.S. offering. Upon the completion of the global offering, we will record cumulative stock-based compensation expense of approximately $14.2 billion related to RSUs outstanding as of September 30, 2026, reflecting modifications of such RSUs subsequent to September 30, 2026 at interpolated modification-date fair values based on the midpoint of the estimated offering price range set for the U.S. offering, for which (i) the service-based vesting condition will be fully or partially satisfied as of November 19, 2026 and (ii) the performance-based vesting condition will be satisfied upon the effectiveness of the registration statement in respect of the U.S. offering. We have granted RSAs to founders, early employees, advisors, and in connection with acquisitions. The RSAs consist of awards with a service-based vesting condition. RSAs are measured at fair value of the underlying common stock on the date of grant. We record compensation cost for these awards using the straight-line method over the requisite service period. 5.14.2 Common Stock Valuations Prior to our initial public offering, given the absence of a public trading market of our Class A common stock, and in accordance with the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants Accounting and Valuation Guide, Valuation of Privately-Held-Company Equity Securities Issued as Compensation, our board of directors exercised reasonable judgment and considered numerous objective and subjective factors to determine the best estimate of the fair value of our common stock, including:

 
195 • contemporaneous third-party valuations of our common stock; • the prices paid for common or redeemable convertible preferred stock sold to third-party investors by us and prices paid in secondary transactions, including any tender offers; • the rights, preferences, and privileges of our redeemable convertible preferred stock relative to those of our common stock; • actual and forecasted operating and financial performance; • our stage of development; • the industry outlook; • the lack of marketability of our common stock; • the likelihood of achieving a liquidity event, such as an initial public offering or a sale of the Company, given prevailing market conditions; • the history and nature of our business, industry trends, and competitive environment; and • general economic outlook, including economic growth, inflation and unemployment, interest rate environment, and global economic trends. Our board of directors determined the fair value of our common stock by first determining the enterprise value of our business and then allocating the value among the various classes of our securities to derive a per share value of our common stock. The enterprise value of our business was primarily estimated by reference to the closest round of equity financing to the date of the valuation. In allocating the enterprise value of our business among the various classes of stock prior to the global offering, we used a hybrid method based on a contingent claims analysis (“CCA”) and a common stock equivalent (“CSE”) method. The CCA is based on the Black-Scholes-Merton option pricing model, which models each class of stock as a call option with a unique claim on our assets. The CSE method presumes that all shares of redeemable convertible preferred stock convert into common stock based upon their conversion terms and other differences in the rights and preferences of the shares of redeemable convertible preferred stock are ignored. After the allocation of enterprise value to the various classes of stock, a discount for lack of marketability (“DLOM”) is applied to arrive at a fair value of the common stock. A DLOM is meant to account for the lack of opportunity to sell private company stock that is not traded on public exchanges. In making the final determination of common stock value, consideration is also given to the recent sales and/or expected sales of common stock. Application of these approaches involves the use of estimates, judgment, and assumptions that are complex and subjective, such as those regarding our expected future revenue, expenses, and future cash flows, discount rates, market multiples, the selection of comparable companies, and the probability of possible future events. Changes in any or all of these estimates and assumptions or the relationships between those assumptions impact our valuations as of each valuation date and may have a material impact on the valuation of our common stock. Following the global offering, it will not be necessary to determine the fair value of our common stock, as the shares of our common stock will be traded in the public market. 5.14.3 Fair Value of Convertible Notes, Derivative Liabilities, and SAFEs We elected to account for our convertible notes at fair value pursuant to Accounting Standards Codification (“ASC”) Topic 825, Financial Instruments. The convertible notes are recognized at their estimated fair value on our consolidated balance sheet, and changes in fair value are recorded in change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs in our consolidated statement of operations. We elected the fair value option to eliminate the accounting complexity that would otherwise result from separately accounting for the liability and equity components of the convertible notes under the traditional bifurcation model. In connection with the 2023 and 2024 note purchase agreements with both Amazon and Google, we recognized derivative liabilities representing obligations to issue future convertible notes pursuant to the terms of those agreements. The derivative liabilities were measured at estimated fair value, with changes in fair value recorded in change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs in the consolidated statement of operations. The estimated fair value of the convertible promissory notes is determined using a hybrid approach comprising a CCA and a CSE method. The analysis estimates the fair value of the convertible promissory notes using a scenario-based

 
196 analysis that considers the probability-weighted present value of the instruments across the range of possible outcomes available to the note holders, including conversion into redeemable convertible preferred stock or Class N common stock, cash repayment at maturity, and cash settlement at a premium upon a change of control. The scenarios included consider the probability-weighted value of the instruments in the CCA and CSE framework. The application of this methodology involves the use of complex and subjective estimates, judgments, and assumptions, including the probability and timing of each settlement scenario such as a qualified equity financing, initial public offering, direct listing, or change of control; the estimated fair value of our equity securities into which the notes may convert; the applicable conversion prices, which vary by note series and are contingent on factors such as elapsed time since issuance and contractual caps and percentage discounts; and the ownership thresholds and rollover provisions that determine the extent to which principal balances convert into equity versus being reissued as rollover notes. In particular, the ownership cap and rollover mechanism—whereby conversion is capped at specified ownership thresholds and any unconverted principal balance is re-issued as a non-interest bearing rollover note that remains subject to fair value measurement—requires significant judgment in estimating what proportion of each note financing will convert versus roll over, because this determination depends on the size and structure of future equity financings that are inherently uncertain. Changes in any or all of these estimates and assumptions, or the relationships between those assumptions, impact our valuations as of each measurement date and may have a material impact on the amounts recognized in our consolidated statement of operations. The fair value option election described above also applied to the SAFEs that we issued during the year ended December 31, 2023. The SAFEs were measured at estimated fair value using the same scenario-based framework, with the monetary settlement amount fixed at inception and the number of equity shares received upon conversion being variable; consistent with the convertible notes, changes in fair value were recorded in change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs in the consolidated statement of operations. All SAFEs were converted into redeemable convertible preferred stock during the years ended December 31, 2023 and 2024, and no SAFEs remained outstanding as of December 31, 2024 or 2025. No SAFEs were outstanding at any point during the nine months ended September 30, 2026. Accordingly, the primary ongoing estimation exposure under the fair value option relates to the convertible notes and rollover notes described above. For additional information regarding our convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs, including descriptions of the individual instruments, their key terms, conversion activity, and balances during the periods presented, see Note 9 to our consolidated financial statements, which are incorporated in, and form part of, this prospectus (see “10.1 Consolidated Financial Statements”). 5.14.4 Leases We lease facilities and equipment, including compute and infrastructure capacity, under operating and finance leases. We determine whether an arrangement is or contains a lease at inception and evaluate the classification of our leases at lease commencement and, as necessary, upon modification. Accounting for leases requires significant judgment, including determining whether an arrangement is or contains a lease, and significant estimates, including the expected lease term, the fair value of the leased property, and our incremental borrowing rate. Given the size and duration of our lease portfolio, changes in our estimate of the fair value of the underlying leased asset, the expected lease term, or the determination of our incremental borrowing rate could result in a different lease classification or a materially different measurement of our right-of-use assets and lease liabilities. 5.14.5 Income Taxes We account for income taxes using the asset and liability method, recognizing deferred tax assets and liabilities for temporary differences between the financial reporting and tax bases of assets and liabilities, as well as for net operating loss and credit carryforwards, measured at enacted tax rates applicable in the years of expected reversals. We establish valuation allowances when necessary to reduce deferred tax assets to amounts more-likely-than-not expected to be realized, based on the weighting of positive and negative evidence. Assessing the realizability of our deferred tax assets is an area of significant management judgment. We evaluate our deferred tax assets for recoverability based on historical taxable income, projected future taxable income, reversal patterns of existing temporary differences, and available tax planning strategies. As an AI company operating in a rapidly evolving market with significant ongoing investment in compute and infrastructure, our projections of future taxable income are inherently uncertain. Should our assessment of the recoverability of deferred tax assets change, our income tax provision would be adjusted in that period, which could materially impact our results of operations.

 
197 We account for uncertain tax positions in accordance with ASC Topic 740, Income Taxes. Tax benefits from uncertain positions are recognized when it is more likely than not that the position will be sustained on examination based on its technical merits, measured at the amount that is more likely than not to be realized upon settlement. These assessments require judgment, particularly with respect to the qualification and documentation of research and development tax credits, where supporting evidence may be subject to differing interpretations. The actual outcome of these matters may differ materially from our current estimates. We recognize interest and penalties related to unrecognized tax benefits within our provision for income taxes. 5.14.6 Loss Contingencies We are involved in legal claims, proceedings, and other regulatory and administrative matters that arise in the ordinary course of business, certain of which may include speculative claims for substantial or indeterminate amounts of damages. We routinely assess each significant matter and its potential financial exposure. We record a liability when we believe it is both probable that a loss has been incurred and the amount can be reasonably estimated, and we disclose matters for which a loss is reasonably possible and the loss or range of loss can be estimated. These assessments require significant judgment in determining both the likelihood and estimated amount of potential losses. We base our accruals on the best information available at the time, taking into account the specific facts and circumstances of each matter, the merits of our defenses, and the impact of negotiations, settlements, regulatory proceedings, rulings, and advice of legal counsel. Our estimates are subject to change as additional information becomes available and as matters develop, and we have in prior periods revised our assessments based on updated information. 5.15 Recent Accounting Pronouncements See Note 1 to our consolidated financial statements, which are incorporated in, and form part of, this prospectus (see “10.1 Consolidated Financial Statements”), for a description of recently adopted accounting pronouncements and recently issued accounting pronouncements not yet adopted.

Working Capital Statement The Company is of the opinion that the Group has sufficient working capital for its present requirements, that is for at least the next twelve months from the date of this prospectus (without taking into account the net proceeds from the sale of any of the Company’s shares in the global offering).

 
199 7. Terms and Conditions of the Securities The shares offered in the global offering, including the European retail shares, are shares of Class A common stock of the Company. Prospective investors should note that in connection with the global offering, we will reorganize our capital stock. The Company’s amended and restated certificate of incorporation that will become effective immediately prior to the completion of the global offering will provide for five classes of authorized capital stock: a class designated as participating common stock, a class designated as Class T common stock (referred to as Class T common stock), a class designated as Class F common stock (referred to as Class F common stock), a class designated as Class E common stock (referred to as Class E common stock), and a class designated as preferred stock. • The class of capital stock designated as participating common stock will be divided into two series, designated Class A common stock and Class N common stock (referred to as Class N common stock). The rights of the holders of Class A common stock and Class N common stock will be identical, except with respect to voting and conversion, with each share of Class A common stock being entitled to one vote per share, overall limited to 49.9% with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally by the voting rights attached to our Class F common stock as described below, and shares of Class N common stock having no voting rights, except as otherwise required by law. • Our Class T common stock is, and will continue to be, a special class of stock that is issued to the Long-Term Benefit Trust (which is intended to operate as an independent body of five financially disinterested trustees). Through our Class T common stock, the Long-Term Benefit Trust generally has the authority to elect and remove the Class T directors, who together will constitute a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. Our Class T common stock does not otherwise have voting rights with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally and has no economic rights. • Our Class F common stock is a special class of our common stock, consisting of a single share, that will be issued to the Founder LLC (a limited liability company of which our seven co-founders will initially be the sole members), and will be entitled to an aggregate number of votes that equals 50.1% of the total voting power of our outstanding shares of capital stock as of the applicable record date with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally, including the election of our directors other than the Class T directors. Our Class F common stock will not have any economic rights. • Our Class E common stock is a special class of our common stock that will be issued to our employees, excluding our co-founders. Our Class E common stock will be entitled to vote only on certain matters and will not have any economic rights. Our preferred stock will be issuable by our board of directors, subject to limitations set forth in our amended and restated certificate of incorporation, which will become effective immediately prior to the completion of the global offering, and as prescribed by Delaware law, in one or more series, and our board of directors will be empowered to establish from time to time the number of shares to be included in each series and, subject to such limitations, fix the designation, powers, preferences and rights of the shares of each series and any of its qualifications, limitations, or restrictions, in each case without further vote or action by our stockholders. Initially, no shares of preferred stock will be outstanding. For a description of our capital stock as it will be authorized, issued and outstanding following completion of the offering, see “11.2.1.3 Our Capital Stock Following Completion of the Global Offering.” 7.1 Information Concerning the Shares 7.1.1 Type and Class of Shares The European retail shares are newly issued shares of Class A common stock of the Company. Our shares of Class A common stock have been and will be created under the laws of Delaware, United States. For further information on our common stock and the authorization to issue preferred stock, see the section titled “11.2.1.3 Our Capital Stock Following Completion of the Global Offering.”

 
200 7.1.2 Form and Certification of the Shares Our shares of Class A common stock are registered uncertificated shares. Shares of Class A common stock can be held directly with our transfer agent and registrar. Upon the completion of the global offering, the transfer agent and registrar for our Class A common stock will be Computershare Trust Company, N.A. The transfer agent’s address is 150 Royall Street, Canton, Massachusetts 02021. Our shares of Class A common stock can also be held in book-entry form through The Depository Trust Company, 140 58th Street, Brooklyn, New York 11220, United States, as clearing system, and its direct and indirect participants. 7.1.3 Trading Symbol, ISIN We have applied to list our Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market having the trading symbol “ANT” and the ISIN US03703U1079. 7.1.4 Denomination Our shares of Class A common stock are denominated in U.S. dollars, par value $0.00001 per share. 7.1.5 Rights Attached to the Shares 7.1.5.1 Voting Rights Holders of our Class A common stock are entitled to one vote for each share held on all matters submitted to a vote of stockholders generally, including the election of our directors other than the Class T directors. The Founder LLC as holder of our single share of Class F common stock will be entitled to an aggregate number of votes that equals 50.1% of the total voting power of our outstanding shares as of the applicable record date on matters submitted to a vote of stockholders generally. Our Class F common stock will be voted in the manner provided by the Founder LLC Agreement. Consequently, if the Founder LLC as holder of our single share of Class F common stock exercises its voting rights, the voting power of the holders of our Class A common stock will be limited to 49.9%. For information on the Founder LLC Agreement and the voting mechanics of our Class F common stock, see the sections titled “11.4 Founder LLC Agreement” and “11.5 Class F Common Stock Voting Mechanics.” We have not provided for cumulative voting for the election of directors in our amended and restated certificate of incorporation. For information on the voting rights of our other share classes, see “11.2.1.3 Our Capital Stock Following Completion of the Global Offering.” 7.1.5.2 Dividend Rights Subject to preferences that may apply to any shares of preferred stock outstanding at the time, the holders of our Class A common stock and Class N common stock are entitled to receive dividends out of funds legally available if our board of directors, in its discretion, determines to issue dividends and then only at the times and in the amounts that our board of directors may determine. Our Class T common stock, Class F common stock, and Class E common stock are not entitled to receive dividends. See the section titled “12 Dividend Policy” for more information. 7.1.5.3 No Preemptive or Similar Rights Our Class A common stock is not entitled to preemptive rights, and is not subject to redemption or sinking fund provisions. 7.1.5.4 Right to Receive Liquidation Distributions If we become subject to a liquidation, dissolution, or winding-up, including in bankruptcy, the assets legally available for distribution to our stockholders would be distributable ratably among the holders of our Class A common stock and Class N common stock and any participating preferred stock outstanding at that time, subject to prior satisfaction of all outstanding debt and liabilities and the preferential rights of and the payment of liquidation preferences, if any, on any outstanding shares of our capital stock. In the event of our liquidation, dissolution, or winding-up, including bankruptcy, holders of our Class T common stock, Class F common stock, and Class E common stock shall be entitled to receive par value ($0.00001) per share but shall not otherwise participate in such distributions. 7.1.6 Creation of the Offered Shares On October 23, 2026, in connection with the global offering, the board of directors of the Company authorized a pricing committee of the board of directors of the Company to approve the offering and issuance of the shares in the initial public offering and a pricing committee to determine the final pricing and related terms of the offering.

 
201 7.2 Transferability of the Shares Except for those shares held by “affiliates” (as defined in Rule 144 under the U.S. Securities Act) and for the restrictions set forth in “8.6 Lock-Up and Market Standoff Agreements,” all shares of our Class A common stock, including the European retail shares, will be freely transferable without restriction or further registration under the U.S. Securities Act. 7.3 Offerors of the Shares The offering of the European retail shares in the European retail offering is made by the Company together with each of the European underwriters whose identities, contact details and LEIs are set out in section “2.1 Persons Responsible for the Contents of the Prospectus.” 7.4 U.S. Takeover Regulation As the shares of Class A common stock will be registered with the SEC under the U.S. Exchange Act, any offer which relates to our Class A common stock will have to comply with the United States’ provisions relating to tender offers, which are set forth in Section 14(d) and Section 14(e) of the U.S. Exchange Act as well as in Regulation 14D and Regulation 14E. The main provisions applicable to tender offers are: (1) the original offer period allows for acceptance of a tender offer within an acceptance period of at least 20 U.S. business days (10 U.S. business days in the case of certain negotiated, all-cash tender offers), subject to mandatory extension in certain conditions; (2) the extension of withdrawal rights for the holders of our Class A common stock; (3) application of all holder and best price provisions (which require that all holders of our Class A common stock receive the same offer price for their Class A common stock); (4) prompt payment of the offer consideration (i.e., settlement within three days), and (5) restrictions on the option of the bidder to acquire our Class A common stock by other means than pursuant to a tender offer. Under U.S. securities laws, there are no mandatory tender offer rules. In addition, certain provisions of Delaware law, our amended and restated certificate of incorporation and our amended and restated bylaws, which will become effective immediately prior to the completion of the global offering, which are summarized below, may have the effect of delaying, deferring, or discouraging another person from acquiring control of us, and are also designed, in part, to encourage persons seeking to acquire control of us to negotiate first with our board of directors. See “11.3 Anti-Takeover Provisions” for additional information. For private tender offers we facilitated in respect of our Class A common stock, see “11.6.4 Tender Offers.” 7.5 Taxation Warning Prospective investors should be warned that the tax legislation of their country of citizenship, domicile or residency and the tax legislation of the Company’s country of incorporation (i.e., the United States) may have an impact on the income received from the shares. Prospective investors are strongly recommended to consult their own tax advisers.

 
202 8. Details of the Offer 8.1 Terms and Conditions of the Offer The global offering of our Class A common stock consists of (i) a public offer in the United States, registered under the U.S. Securities Act pursuant to a registration statement on Form S-1 filed with the SEC, referred to as the U.S. offering, (ii) the public offer to retail investors in Germany, Denmark, Finland, France, Ireland, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain and Sweden contemplated by, and on the basis of, this prospectus, referred to as the European retail offering, (iii) the public offer to retail investors in Switzerland contemplated by, and on the basis of, this prospectus, referred to as the Swiss retail offering, (iv) a public offer in Australia, (v) a public offer in certain provinces and territories of Canada, (vi) a public offer in Japan, (vii) a public offer in the United Kingdom, and (viii) private placements (the offerings contemplated under (ii) through (viii) are collectively referred to as the international offering, and together with the U.S. offering are referred to as the global offering). In the European retail offering, a maximum of 80,135,135 newly issued shares of Class A common stock are offered, referred to as the European retail shares. The global offering initially comprises: (i) 801,351,354 newly issued shares of Class A common stock sold by the Company, including the European retail shares, (ii) up to 23,648,646 existing shares of Class A common stock sold by the selling stockholders identified in section “8.5 Selling Stockholders in the Global Offering” (together referred to as the base shares) and (iii) up to 123,750,000 newly issued shares of Class A common stock which may be sold by the Company to cover potential over-allotments (referred to as the additional shares). The European retail shares form a tranche within the global offering and comprise newly issued shares of Class A common stock of the Company. Any shares offered in the global offering which do not form part of the European retail tranche are offered in any Member State of the EEA solely in circumstances falling within the scope of application of Article 1(4) of the Prospectus Regulation and in Switzerland solely in circumstances falling within the scope of application of Article 36(1) of the FinSA. The European retail offering contemplated by this prospectus is solely made by the Company together with Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, Citigroup, J.P. Morgan, Deutsche Bank, BNP PARIBAS and Crédit Agricole CIB referred to as the European underwriters. The European retail shares are at the same time offered to retail investors in Switzerland on the basis of this prospectus as filed with a Swiss prospectus office for automatic acceptance in accordance with Article 54(2) of the FinSA. The simultaneous public offering of the European retail shares in the Swiss retail offering is solely made by the Company together with UBS AG, Bahnhofstrasse 45, 8001 Zurich, Switzerland (“UBS Investment Bank” or the “Swiss underwriter”) and is made on the terms applicable to the European retail offering as set forth in this prospectus. 8.1.1 Eligible Retail Investors The European retail offering is solely addressed to individual persons or legal entities which do not qualify as qualified investors within the meaning of Article 2 point (e) of the Prospectus Regulation (referred to as retail investors) and which are resident or located in one of the Covered EEA Countries. The Prospectus Regulation defines qualified investors as persons or entities that are listed in points (1) to (4) of Section I of Annex II to Directive 2014/65/EU, as amended (“MiFID II”), and persons or entities who are, on request, treated as professional clients in accordance with Section II of that Annex, or recognized as eligible counterparties in accordance with Article 30 of MiFID II unless they have entered into an agreement with their bank or financial intermediary to be treated as non-professional clients in accordance with the fourth paragraph of Section I of that Annex. The Swiss retail offering is solely addressed to individual persons or legal entities which do not qualify as professional clients within the meaning of the FinSA. The FinSA defines “professional clients” as those persons or entities that either (i) are listed in Article 4(3) FinSA and which have not declared an opting-in pursuant to Article 5(5) FinSA or (ii) have requested to be treated as professional client (opting-out) pursuant to Article 5(1) FinSA. In each case, orders may also be placed by financial intermediaries which act on behalf of retail investors and by financial intermediaries otherwise acting as a fiduciary or agent for one or more investor accounts, where (a) each such account is a retail investor and (b) the financial intermediary has investment discretion with respect to each such account. Investors who have doubts as to whether they meet the eligibility criteria should contact their bank or financial intermediary to verify their client classification with that bank or financial intermediary.

In such case, the increased offering price would be reflected in a final prospectus filed with the SEC pursuant to Rule 424(b) under the U.S. Securities Act. Any decision on the listing of the Company’s Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market will be made solely by Nasdaq, Inc. at its discretion. We do not currently intend to list our Class A common stock on any exchange in any other jurisdiction in which the global offering is made. The Company has not engaged any entities which give a firm commitment to act as intermediaries in secondary trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market. 8.4.2 Stabilization, Over-Allotment, and Green Shoe 8.4.2.1 Stabilization Transactions In order to facilitate the offering of our Class A common stock, Morgan Stanley & Co. LLC, acting as stabilization agent on behalf of the underwriters, may engage in transactions that stabilize, maintain, or otherwise affect the price of our Class A common stock. Specifically, the underwriter may sell more shares of Class A common stock than the underwriters are obligated to purchase under the underwriting agreement, creating a short position. A short sale is covered if the short position is no greater than the number of shares available for purchase under the underwriters’

 
215 option to purchase additional shares set forth in section “8.4.2.2 Option to Purchase Additional Shares.” The underwriter can close out a covered short sale by exercising the underwriters’ option to purchase additional shares or purchasing shares in the open market. In determining the source of shares to close out a covered short sale, the underwriter will consider, among other things, the open market price of our Class A common stock compared to the price available under the underwriters’ option to purchase additional shares. The underwriter may also sell shares of Class A common stock in excess of the underwriters’ option to purchase additional shares, creating a naked short position. The underwriter must close out any naked short position by purchasing shares of Class A common stock in the open market. A naked short position is more likely to be created if the underwriter is concerned that there may be downward pressure on the price of our Class A common stock in the open market after pricing that could adversely affect investors who purchase shares of Class A common stock in the global offering. As an additional means of facilitating the global offering, the underwriter may bid for, and purchase, shares of Class A common stock in the open market to stabilize the price of our Class A common stock. These activities may raise or maintain the market price of our Class A common stock above independent market levels or prevent or slow a decline in the market price of our Class A common stock. The underwriter is not required to engage in these activities and may end any of these activities at any time. The underwriters may offer and sell the shares of common stock through certain of their affiliates or other registered broker-dealers or selling agents. Stabilization transactions may be undertaken on the Nasdaq Global Select Market. Under securities laws of the United States, there is no prescribed maximum period in which stabilization transactions may be carried out. 8.4.2.2 Option to Purchase Additional Shares We will grant to the underwriters an option, exercisable for 30 days from the date of the underwriting agreement, to purchase up to an additional 123,750,000 newly issued shares of Class A common stock at the final public offering price, less underwriting discounts and commissions. The underwriters may exercise this option solely for the purpose of covering over-allotments, if any, made in connection with the offering of the shares of common stock offered in the global offering. Net tangible book value dilution per share to new investors represents the difference between the amount per share paid by purchasers of shares of our Class A common stock in the global

 
225 offering and the as further adjusted net tangible book value per share of our Class A common stock and Class N common stock immediately after completion of the global offering and the concurrent private placement. Net tangible book value per share is determined by dividing our total tangible assets less our total liabilities and redeemable convertible preferred stock by the number of shares of our Class A common stock and Class N common stock outstanding; because our Class T common stock, Class F common stock and Class E common stock have no economic rights, they are excluded from the per share calculation. Our historical net tangible book value as of September 30, 2026 was $(150.6) billion, or $(68.47) per share (unaudited). Our as adjusted net tangible book value as of September 30, 2026 was $22.7 billion, or $1.90 per share, based on the total number of shares of our Class A common stock and Class N common stock outstanding as of September 30, 2026, after giving effect to the Preferred Stock Conversion, Convertible Notes Conversion, Initial Public Benefit Issuance, and RSU Settlement (unaudited). After giving effect to (i) the adjustments set forth above, (ii) the sale by us of 801,351,354 shares of our Class A common stock in the global offering at the assumed initial public offering price of $74.00 per share, which is the midpoint of the estimated offering price range set for the U.S. offering, after deducting estimated underwriting discounts and commissions and estimated offering expenses payable by us, (iii) the sale by us of 351,351,348 shares of our Class N common stock in the concurrent private placement at the assumed initial public offering price of $74.00 per share, which is the midpoint of the estimated offering price range set for the U.S. offering, and (iv) the use of net proceeds from the global offering and the concurrent private placement, together with existing cash and cash equivalents, if necessary, to satisfy the estimated tax withholding and remittance obligations related to the RSU Settlement, our as further adjusted net tangible book value as of September 30, 2026 would have been $107.4 billion, or $8.21 per share (unaudited). This represents an immediate increase in as further adjusted net tangible book value of $6.31 per share to our existing stockholders and an immediate dilution in as further adjusted net tangible book value of $65.79 per share to investors purchasing shares of our Class A common stock in the global offering at the assumed initial public offering price. Dr. Amodei has served as our Chief Executive Officer and a member of our board of directors since co- founding Anthropic in January 2021. Prior to co-founding Anthropic, Dr. Amodei served as Vice President of Research, among other positions, at OpenAI, an AI research lab, from July 2016 to December 2020. Before joining OpenAI, Dr. Amodei served as a Senior Research Scientist at Google Brain, an AI research team at Google, from October 2015 to June 2016. Dr. Amodei completed a postdoctoral fellowship at Stanford University School of Medicine. Dr. Amodei holds a Ph.D. in Biophysics from Princeton University and a B.S. in Physics from Stanford University. We believe that Dr. Amodei is qualified to serve on our board of directors because of the perspective and experience he brings from his deep expertise in the AI industry and as our Chief Executive Officer and as a co-founder. Daniela Amodei. Ms. Amodei has served as our President and a member of our board of directors since co-founding Anthropic in January 2021. Ms. Amodei also currently serves as the Chairperson of our board of directors. Prior to co- founding Anthropic, Ms. Amodei held several positions at OpenAI, an AI research lab, including Vice President of Safety and Policy, Vice President of People, and Engineering Manager, between October 2018 and December 2020. Before joining OpenAI, Ms. Amodei was a Risk Manager, among other positions, at Stripe, a financial technology and payment processing company, from May 2013 to July 2018. Ms. Amodei holds a B.A. in English Literature from the University of California, Santa Cruz. We believe that Ms. Amodei is qualified to serve on our board of directors because of the perspective and experience she brings through her deep expertise in the AI industry and as our President and as a co- founder. Krishna Rao. Mr. Rao has served as our Chief Financial Officer since April 2024. Prior to joining Anthropic, Mr. Rao served as Chief Financial Officer at Fanatics Commerce, an online sports merchandise and retail platform, from May 2023 to April 2024. Before that, he served as the Chief Financial Officer of Cedar, a healthcare technology company, from July 2021 to May 2023. Prior to Airbnb, Mr. Rao was a Principal in the Private Equity Group at Blackstone, a global investment firm, from September 2011 to September 2015. Mr. Rao began his career as a strategy consultant at Bain, a global management consulting firm, from September 2005 to July 2008. Mr. Rao holds a J.D. from Yale Law School and an A.B. in Economics from Harvard College. 9.1.3 Non-Employee Directors Reed Hastings. Mr. Hastings has served as a member of our board of directors since May 2025. Mr. Hastings co- founded Netflix, a global streaming service, and served as Netflix’s Chief Executive Officer and President from 1999 to January 2023, Executive Chairman from January 2023 to April 2025, and Chairman of the board from April 2025 to June 2026. Prior to Netflix, Mr. Hastings founded Pure Software, a software development tools company, in 1991 and served as its Chief Executive Officer until its acquisition by Rational Software in 1997. Mr. Hastings currently serves on the board of Bloomberg, a financial data and media company. Mr. Hastings holds an M.S.C.S. in Artificial Intelligence from Stanford University and a B.A. in Mathematics from Bowdoin College. We believe that Mr. Hastings is qualified to serve as a member of our board of directors because of his extensive board experience at major technology companies, his demonstrated commitment to responsible innovation and its societal impact, his deep understanding of technology’s transformative potential, and his philanthropic focus on education and AI’s impact on humanity. Christopher Liddell. Mr. Liddell has served as a member of our board of directors since February 2026. In the private sector, Mr. Liddell has served as the Chief Financial Officer of several public companies, including Microsoft and International Paper, and served as Vice Chairman and Chief Financial Officer at General Motors. Mr. Liddell has served as a Director of Commonwealth Fusion Systems, a fusion power company, since March 2025, and as a Director of the Council on Foreign Relations, a nonpartisan U.S. think tank focused on foreign policy and international affairs, since July 2025. He also held positions with the U.S. government from January 2017 to January 2021, including serving at the White House as the Deputy Chief of Staff, Director of Strategic Initiatives, and as a member of the American Technology Council. Mr. Liddell holds a Master of Philosophy from the University of Oxford and a Bachelor of Engineering from the University of Auckland. We believe that Mr. Liddell is qualified to serve as a member of our board of directors because of his wide range of experience from his corporate and public service career and his deep expertise in the financial management of publicly listed companies. Vasant “Vas” Narasimhan. Dr. Narasimhan has served as a member of our board of directors since April 2026. Dr. Narasimhan has served as the Chief Executive Officer of Novartis AG, a global medicine company, since February 2018. He joined Novartis in April 2005 and has held numerous leadership roles across the organization, including Global Head of Drug Development and Chief Medical Officer from February 2016 to January 2018 and Global Head of Development from September 2014 to February 2016. Dr. Narasimhan holds an M.D. from Harvard Medical School, an M.P.P. from the Harvard Kennedy School, and a B.A. in Biology from the University of Chicago. We believe that Dr. Narasimhan is qualified to serve as a member of our board of directors because of his extensive experience leading a large global public company in a highly regulated industry and his track record of responsibly stewarding breakthrough science at scale. Yasmin Razavi. Ms. Razavi has served as a member of our board of directors since March 2023. Ms. Razavi joined Spark Capital, a venture capital firm, in July 2017 and has served as a General Partner since March 2020. Prior to joining Spark Capital, Ms. Razavi served as an investor at Index Ventures, a venture capital firm, from August 2014 to August 2015, and as a consultant at McKinsey & Company, a business management consulting firm, from August 2012 to August 2014. Ms. Razavi holds an M.B.A. from Harvard Business School and a Bachelor of Applied Science and Engineering from the University of Toronto. We believe that Ms. Razavi is qualified to serve as a member of our board of directors because of her experience in venture capital and growth-stage investing, her deep expertise in enterprise go-to-market strategies, and her understanding of the technology sector and scaling high-growth companies. 9.2 Family Relationships Dario Amodei, our Chief Executive Officer and a member of our board of directors, and Daniela Amodei, our President and Chairperson of our board of directors, are siblings. There are no other family relationships among any of our executive officers or directors. 9.3 Code of Conduct Our board of directors has adopted a code of conduct that applies to all of our employees, officers, and directors, including our Chief Executive Officer, President, Chief Financial Officer, and other executive and senior financial

 
230 officers. The full text of our code of conduct will be posted on the investor relations page of our website. We intend to disclose any amendments to our code of conduct, or waivers of its requirements, on our website or in filings under the U.S. Exchange Act. 9.4 Board of Directors Our business and affairs are managed under the direction of our board of directors. Our board of directors currently consists of six directors. Pursuant to our current certificate of incorporation and amended and restated voting agreement, our current directors were elected as follows: • Dr. Amodei, as our Chief Executive Officer, was elected by holders of our Class A common stock (excluding shares of Class A common stock issued or issuable upon conversion of the shares of our redeemable convertible preferred stock); • Mr. Liddell was elected as the designee nominated by holders of our Class A common stock (excluding shares of Class A common stock issued or issuable upon conversion of the shares of our redeemable convertible preferred stock); • Ms. Razavi was elected by holders of our Senior Voting Preferred Stock (as defined in our current certificate of incorporation); and • Ms. Amodei, Mr. Hastings, and Dr. Narasimhan were elected as the designees nominated by the LTBT as the holder of our Class T common stock. Our amended and restated voting agreement will terminate and the provisions of our current certificate of incorporation by which our directors were elected will be amended and restated in connection with the global offering.
