Upon the completion of the global offering, our board of directors will consist of seven authorized directors, with one seat vacant, elected as follows: • The holder of our Class T common stock, the LTBT, will generally have the authority to elect and remove the four Class T directors, subject to the following procedures: o As the sole holder of Class T common stock, the LTBT generally has the authority to elect and remove the Class T directors, who together will constitute a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. The Class T common stock will not vote on the election or removal of directors elected by the holders of our Class A common stock and Class F common stock, who will be elected or removed solely by the holders of Class A common stock and Class F common stock, voting together. o Prior to nominating or removing a Class T director, the LTBT must provide at least 30 days’ notice to our NGC, which notice period is waivable by our NGC in its discretion. Following the completion of the global offering, our NGC will be composed of one Class T director and two directors who are not Class T directors and will act by majority vote. o With respect to the Specified Class T Director, the LTBT’s ability to nominate that director, to remove that director without cause, or to change the director designated as the Specified Class T Director is subject to the concurrence of the NGC. If the NGC does not concur with such nomination, removal, or change in designation within 15 days of receiving notice, the matter may be submitted to a vote of the holders of our Class E common stock. If submitted to a vote of the holders of Class E common stock, approval of the LTBT’s proposal will require a majority of the votes cast by the Class E common stock (subject to a quorum of a majority of the outstanding Class E common stock). The LTBT may withdraw any notice of nomination, removal, or change in designation at any time before the taking of such a vote. o The initial Class T directors will be Mr. Hastings, Dr. Narasimhan, Mr. Liddell, and one vacancy. Mr. Liddell will serve as the Specified Class T Director. • The holders of our Class A common stock and Class F common stock, voting together as a single class, will have the authority to elect and remove the remaining three directors, who will initially be Dr. Amodei, Ms. Amodei, and Ms. Razavi. With respect to tie votes, in general the affirmative vote of a majority of the directors present at a meeting (at which a quorum is present) is required for an act of our board of directors. If the directors present at a meeting are evenly divided

 
231 on a matter, the matter will not receive the affirmative vote of a majority of the directors present and will not be approved. However, certain matters require supermajority approval as specifically provided by Delaware law, our amended and restated certificate of incorporation, or our amended and restated bylaws. For example, any change in the number of authorized directors (prior to the Class T Sunset Time), and the designation or issuance of any series of preferred stock, will require, among other approvals, the approval of 80% of the authorized members of the board of directors. For additional information, see the sections titled “11.2.1.3 Our Capital Stock Following Completion of the Global Offering” and “4.1.1.2.1 Election and Removal of Directors.” 9.5 Director Terms Our amended and restated certificate of incorporation that will become effective immediately prior to the completion of the global offering will provide that prior to the Class F Sunset Time, we will not have a classified board of directors, and all directors will be elected for annual terms. Each director’s term will continue until the next annual meeting and until the election and qualification of their successor, or their earlier death, resignation, or removal. Following the Class F Sunset Time, our board of directors will shift to having a classified board of directors consisting of three classes of approximately equal size, each serving staggered three-year terms. At such time, each of our directors would be assigned by the then-current board of directors to a class. If our Class T common stock remains outstanding, the Class T directors and the remaining directors shall be allocated among the classes so that each class includes a proportionate number of Class T directors and other directors. Upon expiration of the term of a class of directors, directors for that class would each be elected for a three-year term at the annual meeting of stockholders in the year in which that term expires. As a result, only one class of directors would be elected at each annual meeting of our stockholders, with the other classes continuing for the remainder of their respective three-year terms. Each director’s term would continue until the third annual meeting of stockholders following their election and until their successor has been elected and qualified, or until their earlier death, resignation, or removal. Any increase or decrease in the number of directors would be distributed among the three classes so that, as nearly as practicable, each class would consist of one-third of our directors. Regardless of the class or classes of stock by which a director is elected, there is no limit to the number of terms a director may serve. 9.6 Stockholder Meetings and Actions by Written Consent Our amended and restated certificate of incorporation that will become effective immediately prior to the completion of the global offering will provide that for so long as our Class F common stock or Class T common stock remains outstanding, our stockholders may act by written consent with respect to certain actions, including any action to elect or remove directors. Although stockholders will have the ability to take these actions by written consent, we value the perspectives of all of our stockholders and, in accordance with the listing standards of the Nasdaq Global Select Market, we expect to hold an annual meeting of stockholders and to solicit the votes of holders of our Class A common stock in respect of relevant matters to be considered at such meeting, including the election of our directors who are not Class T directors. 9.7 Board Leadership Our board of directors has appointed Daniela Amodei to serve as Chairperson of our board of directors. As Chairperson, Ms. Amodei will preside over meetings of our board of directors and stockholders, advise the Chief Executive Officer, and perform such other duties as specified in our amended and restated bylaws or as determined by our board of directors from time to time. Our board of directors has appointed Reed Hastings to serve as Lead Independent Director. As Lead Independent Director, Mr. Hastings will, among other things, preside over meetings of our independent directors, advise the Chairperson on the scheduling and agenda for board meetings and any other matters of concern to the independent directors, serve as a liaison between the Chairperson and the independent directors, and perform such other duties as specified in our amended and restated bylaws or as determined by the independent directors from time to time. Our board of directors believes that having a Lead Independent Director is an important component of sound corporate governance and provides an effective check and balance to ensure that our board of directors can operate independently of management where appropriate, including with respect to performance evaluation and compensation matters.

 
232 9.8 Director Independence Our board of directors has undertaken a review of the independence of each director. Based on information provided by each director concerning their background, employment, and affiliations, our board of directors has determined that Mr. Hastings, Mr. Liddell, Dr. Narasimhan, and Ms. Razavi do not have a relationship that would interfere with the exercise of independent judgment in carrying out the responsibilities of a director and that each of these directors is “independent” as that term is defined under the listing standards of the Nasdaq Global Select Market. In making these determinations, our board of directors considered the current and prior relationships that each non-employee director has with our company and all other facts and circumstances our board of directors deemed relevant in determining their independence, including the beneficial ownership of our capital stock by each non-employee director, and the transactions involving them described in the section titled “11.6 Certain Relationships and Related Person Transactions.” 9.9 Corporate Governance Regime We will be required to comply with the Nasdaq Global Select Market listing standards and corporate governance requirements, under which we are considered a “controlled company” within the meaning of the Nasdaq Global Select Market corporate governance requirements because the LTBT, as the sole holder of our Class T common stock, generally has the power to elect a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. As a result, we may elect not to comply with certain corporate governance requirements, including: • the requirement that a majority of our board of directors consist of independent directors; • the requirement that our board of directors have a nominating and corporate governance committee that is comprised entirely of independent directors with a written charter addressing the committee’s purpose and responsibilities; and • the requirement that our board of directors have a compensation committee that is comprised entirely of independent directors with a written charter addressing the committee’s purpose and responsibilities. If we elect not to comply with certain requirements, you will not have the same protections afforded to stockholders of companies that are subject to all of the Nasdaq Global Select Market corporate governance requirements. Although we qualify as a “controlled company,” we do not expect to rely on this exemption except with respect to our NGC, which will not consist entirely of independent directors. Our board of directors currently consists of a majority of independent directors and our audit and compensation committees currently consist entirely of independent directors. In the event that we cease to be a “controlled company” and our Class A common stock continues to be listed on the Nasdaq Global Select Market, we will be required to comply with the provision that our NGC be comprised entirely of independent directors within the applicable transition period. 9.10 Committees of the Board of Directors Our board of directors has established an audit committee, a compensation committee, an NGC, and a safety and risk committee. The composition and responsibilities of each of the committees of our board of directors are described below. Members will serve on these committees until their resignation or as otherwise determined by our board of directors. 9.10.1 Audit Committee Our audit committee consists of Mr. Liddell, Mr. Hastings, and one vacancy, with Mr. Liddell serving as Chairperson. We expect to take advantage of a phase-in period under the Nasdaq Global Select Market corporate governance requirements that allows us to have at least one member on the audit committee upon the listing date, of our Class A common stock, at least two members within 90 days of the listing date and at least three members within one year of the listing date. Our audit committee will consist of three members within one year of the listing date. In addition, each member of the audit committee will meet the requirements for independence under the listing standards of the Nasdaq Global Select Market and Rule 10A-3 under the U.S. Exchange Act. Each member of our audit committee will also meet the financial literacy and sophistication requirements of the listing standards of the Nasdaq Global Select Market. Following the completion of the global offering, our audit committee will, among other things: • select a qualified firm to serve as the independent registered public accounting firm to audit our financial statements; • help to ensure the independence and performance of the independent registered public accounting firm; • discuss the scope and results of the audit with the independent registered public accounting firm, and review, with management and the independent registered public accounting firm, our interim and year-end results of operations; • prepare the report of the audit committee for inclusion in our proxy statements to be filed with the SEC; • develop procedures for employees to submit concerns anonymously about questionable accounting or audit matters; • review our policies on risk assessment and risk management; • review related person transactions; and • approve or, as required, pre-approve, all audit and all permissible non-audit services, other than de minimis non-audit services, to be performed by the independent registered public accounting firm. Prior to the global offering, we did not have a formal policy with respect to compensation payable to our non-employee directors for service as directors. 9.12.1.1 Non-Employee Director Compensation Policy In September 2026, our board of directors adopted, and our stockholders approved, a formal compensation policy for our non-employee directors (the “Director Compensation Policy”), which will become effective the day immediately prior to the date of effectiveness of the registration statement with respect to the U.S. offering. In November 2026, our compensation committee recommended, and our board of directors approved, an amendment and restatement of the Director Compensation Policy to include cash compensation for our safety and risk committee. The summary set forth below describes our Director Compensation Policy, as amended and restated. Following the effectiveness of our Director Compensation Policy, each non-employee director will receive cash and equity compensation for board services as described below. We also will reimburse our non-employee directors for reasonable, customary, and properly documented expenses for travel to board and committee meetings. 9.12.1.1.1 Cash Compensation Non-employee directors will be entitled to receive the following cash compensation for their services: (i) $100,000 per year for service as a board member; (ii) $75,000 per year for service as non-executive chair of the board of directors (if applicable); (iii) $60,000 per year for service as lead independent director (if applicable); (iv) $40,000 per year for service as chair of the audit committee; (v) $20,000 per year for service as a member of the audit committee; (vi) $30,000 per year for service as chair of the compensation committee; (vii) $15,000 per year for service as a member of the compensation committee; (viii) $30,000 per year for service as chair of the NGC; (ix) $15,000 per year for service as a member of the NGC; (x) $40,000 per year for service as chair of the safety and risk committee; and (xi) $20,000 per year for service as a member of the safety and risk committee. Each non-employee director who serves as the chair of a committee will receive only the additional annual fee as the chair of the committee and not also the additional annual fee as a member of the committee. All cash payments to non- employee directors will be paid quarterly in arrears on a prorated basis. 9.12.1.1.2 Equity Compensation Annual Award. Each non-employee director automatically will be granted, on the date of each annual meeting of stockholders beginning in 2027, an award of RSUs (the “Annual Award”) with a value of $325,000 (the “Annual Award Grant Value”), which value will be converted to a number of shares of our Class A common stock in accordance

 
236 with then-current standard company practices using the same methodology applied to employee equity awards pursuant to the company’s equity grant policy, as most recently approved by our board of directors or a board committee that has been designated appropriate authority (the “Conversion Methodology”). An Annual Award will vest in four equal quarterly installments on each Quarterly Vesting Date (as defined below) that occurs following the grant date of the Annual Award, provided that, in any event, the Annual Award will vest in full on the day immediately before the date of our next annual meeting of stockholders that follows the grant date of the Annual Award, subject to the non- employee director continuing to be a service provider to us through the applicable vesting date. “Quarterly Vesting Date” means February 20, May 20, August 20, and November 20 of a given year. Initial Award and Pro-Rated Annual Award. Each person who first becomes a non-employee director following the effective date of the Director Compensation Policy will be automatically granted: • an award of RSUs with a value of $400,000, which value will be converted to a number of shares of our Class A common stock subject to such award using the Conversion Methodology (an “Initial Award”); and • an award of RSUs with a value equal to the Annual Award Grant Value multiplied by the fraction obtained by dividing (A) the number of full months during the period beginning on the date the individual first becomes a non-employee director and ending on the one-year anniversary of the date of our then-most recent annual meeting of stockholders by (B) 12, which will be converted to a number of shares of our Class A common stock subject to such award using the Conversion Methodology (a “Pro-Rated Annual Award”). The grant of each Initial Award and Pro-Rated Annual Award will be made effective on the first trading date on or after the date on which such individual first becomes a non-employee director (such date, the “Initial Start Date”). If an individual is a member of our board of directors and also an employee, becoming a non-employee director due to termination of employment will not entitle the non-employee director to an Initial Award or a Pro-Rated Annual Award. The Initial Award will vest as follows: 12.5% of the RSUs will vest on the six-month anniversary of the Vesting Commencement Date (as defined below) and the balance of the RSUs will vest in 14 successive equal quarterly installments on each Quarterly Vesting Date thereafter, subject to the non-employee director remaining a service provider to us through the applicable vesting date. “Vesting Commencement Date” means the first Quarterly Vesting Date that occurs on or following the Initial Start Date. The Pro-Rated Annual Award will vest in equal installments on each Quarterly Vesting Date that occurs between the Initial Start Date and the earlier of (i) our next annual meeting of stockholders that occurs after the Pro-Rated Annual Award’s grant date or (ii) the one-year anniversary of our most recent annual meeting of stockholders, provided that, in any event, the Pro-Rated Annual Award will vest in full on the day immediately before the date of our next annual meeting of stockholders that occurs after the Pro-Rated Annual Award’s grant date (for purposes of clarity, each such Quarterly Vesting Date and the final vest date that occurs on the date immediately before our next annual meeting of stockholders or one-year anniversary of our most recent annual meeting of stockholders, as applicable, will be counted as one installment such that, if there are two such Quarterly Vesting Dates, the Pro-Rated Annual Award shall vest in three equal installments), subject to the non- employee director remaining a service provider to us through the applicable vesting date. 9.12.1.1.3 Change in Control In the event of a “change in control” (as defined in our 2026 Plan), each non-employee director will fully vest in their outstanding equity awards granted pursuant to the Director Compensation Policy under our 2026 Plan, including any Initial Award and Pro-Rated Annual Award or Annual Award, provided that the non-employee director continues to be a non-employee director through such date. 9.12.2 Executive Compensation 9.12.2.1 Compensation Discussion and Analysis The purpose of this Compensation Discussion and Analysis (“CD&A”) section is to discuss our compensation philosophy, our executive compensation program, and the compensation for our named executive officers (“NEOs”). Our NEOs for the year ended December 31, 2025 were: • Dario Amodei, our Chief Executive Officer, Co-Founder, and Director; • Daniela Amodei, our President, Co-Founder, and Director; and • Krishna Rao, our Chief Financial Officer.

 
237 This discussion contains forward-looking statements that are based on our current plans, considerations, expectations, and determinations regarding future compensation programs. See also the section titled “2.7 Note Regarding Forward- looking Statements.” Actual compensation programs that we adopt in the future may differ materially from the currently planned programs summarized in this discussion. For additional information regarding the compensation programs for, and compensation provided to, our NEOs, see the section titled “9.12.2.12 Post-Fiscal Year End Compensation Changes and Equity Awards.” 9.12.2.2 Executive Summary At Anthropic, we strive to build a team that is aligned with our mission and values. Executive compensation reflects our overall compensation philosophy, which prioritizes competitive pay that targets the 90th percentile of the super intelligence24 development market, consistent pay for the same role, level, and location, and simplicity of plan design. In 2025, we offered a competitive mix of base salary, long-term equity incentive awards (including stock options and RSUs), and other benefits to attract and retain top talent in a competitive market environment. 9.12.2.3 Compensation Philosophy and Objectives Our executive compensation philosophy is to provide our executive officers with consistent cash and equity compensation for the same role, level, and location. When determining executive compensation, we review each executive’s current compensation against role- and level-specific market data. We do this bi-annually as part of our performance and compensation cycle where we review proposed market-based and promotion-based cash and equity increases for executives. We plan to continue to regularly review, and potentially adjust, our executive compensation programs to ensure they are consistent with our compensation philosophy as a public company. In determining compensation for our senior leaders, we distinguish between our seven co-founders (among whom only Dr. Amodei and Ms. Amodei are executive officers) and our other senior leaders who are not co-founders (among whom only Mr. Rao is an executive officer). Each co-founder is paid equal compensation. As a non-co-founder senior leader, Mr. Rao received base salary and equity compensation based on market data for his role and level. Our executive compensation program is structured to achieve the objectives described below. We regularly review our executive compensation program to assess whether it meets these objectives and adapts to evolving economic conditions. • Competitive Pay to Attract and Retain Top Talent. We provide our executives with competitive cash and equity pay for each role, location, and level to attract mission-aligned, top executive talent. • Internal Parity. We take internal parity into account when determining executive compensation. As co- founders, Dr. Amodei and Ms. Amodei are awarded equal compensation, including any annual cash or equity increases. As a non-co-founder senior leader, Mr. Rao is compensated based on the market data from our peer group for his role, level, and location. We review market data twice a year and make adjustments to our compensation benchmarks as needed. • Aligning Executive Interests with Our Stockholders. We provide incentives that seek to align our executives’ interests with those of our stockholders through long-term equity awards, which vest over time. 9.12.2.4 Compensation Governance Highlights What We Do: What We Do Not Do: ☑ Maintain a competitive, consistent, and simple compensation philosophy to attract, retain, and motivate top executive talent. ☒ Enter into employment agreements that provide for fixed terms, automatic compensation increases, or guaranteed equity grants. ☑ Focus our executive compensation program on at-risk compensation, which aligns stockholder and executive interests. ☒ Provide single-trigger change of control benefits or excessive cash severance. ☑ Deliver a majority of our NEOs’ compensation opportunities in the form of long-term equity awards. ☒ Provide our NEOs with golden parachute excise tax reimbursement or “gross-ups.” ☑ Conduct regular compensation reviews to ensure alignment with competitive market practices. ☒ Provide perquisites as a meaningful component of our executive compensation. 24 For purposes of this prospectus, we use the terms “super intelligence,” “SI,” “artificial intelligence,” and “AI” interchangeably.

 
238 What We Do: What We Do Not Do: ☑ Provide for double-trigger change of control severance provisions for only our Chief Financial Officer, and none of our other NEOs. ☒ Maintain any executive pension plans, or any retirement programs that are not generally available to all employees. ☒ Award option grants at discounted stock prices. 9.12.2.5 Executive Compensation Process 9.12.2.5.1 Role of the Board of Directors and Compensation Committee Our executive compensation program has historically been overseen by the non-employee members of our board of directors, which, as a group, has made decisions regarding the compensation for our NEOs after considering recommendations from management, as further discussed below. Following the completion of the global offering, the compensation committee of our board of directors will oversee our executive compensation program and provide recommendations to our board of directors on compensation decisions for our executive officers. The compensation committee will work closely with its independent compensation consultant (engaged in connection with the global offering, as described below) and meet regularly to make decisions on our executive compensation program. We expect that our compensation committee will review a variety of market data and information, including survey data, and consider the recommendations of its independent compensation consultant when making compensation decisions. Following the completion of the global offering, the compensation committee’s responsibilities will include, among other things, reviewing and approving (or making recommendations to our board of directors, as applicable): overall compensation strategy; amounts and form of executive compensation; goals and objectives to be considered in determining the compensation of our Chief Executive Officer and other executive officers; annual and long-term incentive plans and benefit plans; board of directors compensation; whether such compensation policies and practices create risks that are reasonably likely to have a material adverse effect on the company; annual say-on-pay vote results; annual proxy and CD&A disclosure; and compensation peer group. 9.12.2.5.2 Role of Management Our Chief Executive Officer and our other executive officers do not set their own compensation, nor are they present when our board of directors sets their individual compensation. Our President reviews and advises on compensation for the seven co-founders but does not make specific recommendations on, or participate in decisions related to her compensation or our Chief Executive Officer’s compensation. Our President also provides her evaluation and makes recommendations with respect to base salary and equity awards for each other executive officer, which are considered by our board of directors as it ultimately makes its determinations. Our people team provides further analysis and feedback as requested by our board of directors with regard to the compensation of our executives. 9.12.2.5.3 Role of Independent Compensation Consultant In connection with the global offering, we have engaged Semler Brossy Consulting Group LLC as an independent compensation consultant to formalize our post-offering compensation programs and implement compensation arrangements that reflect our compensation philosophy described above. 9.12.2.6 Elements of Executive Compensation The key elements of our 2025 executive compensation program are summarized in the table below. Compensation Element Form of Compensation Guaranteed vs. At-Risk Philosophy Base Salary Cash Guaranteed Provide market-competitive fixed compensation to attract and retain key executives. Long-Term Equity Incentive Program Service-Based Options; RSUs with Service- Based and Performance- Based Vesting Conditions At-Risk The value of option and RSU awards is correlated to our stock price, promoting sustainable long-term value creation. Multi-year service vesting schedule promotes retention, long-term ownership, and continuity of leadership. Other Benefits Other N/A Aligned with market practices and serve to attract, motivate, and retain key talent. Intended to ensure the safety of our NEOs, enhance productivity, and minimize distractions.

 
239 9.12.2.6.1 Base Salary Our board of directors generally reviews the base salaries of our NEOs twice a year. The factors used to determine base salary for our executives include market data for the role, level, and location, as well as internal parity (which, for our co-founder NEOs, includes considerations related to parity with our technical leadership). From January 1, 2025 to June 15, 2025, the annual base salary for each of Dr. Amodei and Ms. Amodei was $600,000. Effective June 16, 2025, the annual base salary for each of Dr. Amodei and Ms. Amodei was increased to $700,000. The increase in the executives’ cash compensation was intended to ensure competitive and equitable compensation for our leaders. In particular, the salary increases recognized their ongoing leadership roles, while considering relative parity across executives, including our technical leadership. From January 1, 2025 to December 15, 2025, the annual base salary for Mr. Rao was $700,000, which was increased to $850,000 effective December 16, 2025. The salary increase was based on market data for Mr. Rao’s role and level, as well as internal parity for non-co-founder senior leaders who are not executive officers. 9.12.2.6.2 Long-Term Equity Incentive Program Each year, our NEOs are eligible to receive equity awards under our 2021 Plan. By structuring the majority of our NEOs’ target total direct compensation payable in the form of equity that vests over a number of years, we create incentives for our NEOs to remain employed with Anthropic and pursue actions that will benefit our company and stockholders over the long term. On June 12, 2025, our board of directors granted 992,500 options (“2025 Options”) and 1,717,000 RSUs (“2025 RSUs”) to each of Dr. Amodei and Ms. Amodei, after carefully considering several factors, including each executive’s experience, skills, responsibilities, and impact to the company; individual and company performance; and internal parity. The 2025 Options vested in equal monthly installments over a one-year period beginning on January 1, 2025, subject to the executive’s continuous service with the company through each vest date. The 2025 Options were granted with an exercise price equal to $2.38 per share. The 2025 RSUs vest on the first date upon which both a service-based condition and a performance-based condition are satisfied. The service-based condition is satisfied as to 1/12th of the total 2025 RSUs on February 20, 2026, and on each quarterly anniversary thereafter, subject to the executive’s continuous service with the company through each service-based vest date. The performance-based vesting condition of the 2025 RSUs will be satisfied upon the effectiveness of the registration statement with respect to the U.S. offering. 9.12.2.6.3 Perquisites and Other Executive Benefits We generally provide the same benefits to all of our employees, including our NEOs, and generally do not maintain benefit plans that cover only executive officers or provide perquisites or personal benefits to our NEOs. However, we do provide certain travel and security benefits to some of our NEOs. These benefits are described in more detail below. Our board of directors believes these benefits are reasonable and necessary, and for the benefit of our company. These benefits are intended to promote the productivity of our executives, in addition to ensuring their personal health, safety, and security. The aggregate incremental cost of providing these benefits to our NEOs is disclosed in the “All Other Compensation” column of the summary compensation table in section “9.12.2.11 Summary Compensation Table.” 9.12.2.6.3.1 Travel We maintain a Travel and Expense Policy (the “Travel Policy”), which outlines guidelines and allowances for executive travel and expenses, recognizing the needs and responsibilities of our senior leadership team. The Travel Policy governs all business-related travel and expenses for our executives, except to the extent benefits are provided through a security program authorized and/or approved by our board of directors. Dr. Amodei and Ms. Amodei are entitled to certain enhanced travel benefits recommended by the security studies on which their security program is based (discussed in the section below titled “9.12.2.6.3.2 Security Services”). The Travel Policy is reviewed annually by our management team to ensure it remains appropriate and aligned with company objectives and industry standards. To the extent required by the relevant tax laws, the value of any personal use, including any personal elements of business trips, will be treated as taxable compensation to the executive, and we do not cover, reimburse, or otherwise “gross-up” any income tax due from any applicable executive on such compensation. Except as noted in the subsection below titled “9.12.2.6.3.2 Security Services,” none of our NEOs were provided with private aviation services for personal travel in 2025.

 
240 9.12.2.6.3.2 Security Services The protection of our senior leadership is a critical priority for our company and our stockholders. In connection with our security program and our evaluation of security threats, we offer security services to certain of our NEOs and may provide security services to other NEOs in the future. Such security services may include: (i) individual protection services (including the protection of family members) and home security systems and monitoring, (ii) private aviation, and (iii) private car and driver services. These safeguards are implemented due to the variety of business-related security concerns faced by our senior leaders, and they are comparable to those provided to senior leaders of comparable high- profile companies in the technology industry. In 2025, a leading security consulting firm conducted independent, third-party security studies regarding the personal and security risks of our Chief Executive Officer and our President. Based on these security studies, increased media attention for Anthropic, and the identification of bona fide business-related, heightened security concerns arising as a result of the respective positions of Dr. Amodei and Ms. Amodei within the company, our board of directors determined that enhanced personal security services were necessary to increase the safety and protection of Dr. Amodei and Ms. Amodei, and to avoid an impact to our business continuity if a security incident occurred. Our board of directors regularly assesses security concerns and reviews the security services provided to Dr. Amodei and Ms. Amodei and the cost of such services in light of such concerns, and other benefits to our company. The security measures for Dr. Amodei and Ms. Amodei in 2025 included (i) individual protection services (including during personal travel), which included the protection of family members, as well as enhanced home security systems and surveillance, (ii) private car and driver services for ground transportation, and (iii) in the case of Dr. Amodei, the use of private aircraft for both business and personal travel. Given the importance of the roles of Dr. Amodei and Ms. Amodei at Anthropic, our board of directors required the security measures described above for the benefit of our company, and we view the costs of these services as necessary and appropriate. In the “All Other Compensation” column of the summary compensation table in section “9.12.2.11 Summary Compensation Table,” we have disclosed the aggregate incremental cost of the security benefits that may be deemed to be perquisites under current relevant disclosure rules. We did not pay expenses for personal security for any other NEOs in 2025, except in connection with business-related travel. 9.12.2.6.3.3 Health and Welfare Benefits During 2025, we provided the following benefits to our NEOs on the same basis as our other eligible employees: medical; dental; vision; flexible spending account; health savings account; life insurance; short-term and long-term disability insurance; fertility benefits; mental well-being benefits; health and wellness timesaver stipend; work from home stipend; education assistance program; commuting allowance; and a 401(k) retirement plan with employer match. 9.12.2.7 Executive Employment Agreements We entered into an offer letter with Mr. Rao dated March 2, 2024 (“Rao Offer Letter”), which offer letter was in effect during 2025 and was terminated in October 2026. The Rao Offer Letter provided for “at-will” employment and set forth Mr. Rao’s initial annual base salary, his eligibility to participate in our benefit plans generally, and a new hire stock option grant to purchase 14,000,000 shares of our Class A common stock under our 2021 Plan (“Rao Options”). The Rao Options vested with respect to 1/4th of the shares on the 12-month anniversary of Mr. Rao’s first day of employment with the company and 1/48th of the shares in equal monthly installments thereafter, subject to Mr. Rao’s continuous service with the company through each vest date. The Rao Offer Letter also provided for certain severance and change of control benefits. For information regarding the severance and change of control benefits for Mr. Rao during 2025, please refer to the sections below titled “9.12.2.8 Termination and Change of Control Benefits” and “9.12.2.17 Potential Payments upon Termination or Change of Control.” Upon the termination of the Rao Offer Letter, we entered into a letter agreement with Mr. Rao as described below. In addition, each NEO is subject to our standard confidential information and invention assignment agreement which provides for restrictions on employee non-solicitation (during employment and for 12 months post-termination), customer non-solicitation (during employment), confidentiality (perpetual), and assignment of intellectual property rights. 9.12.2.8 Termination and Change of Control Benefits The employment of our NEOs is “at-will,” meaning we can terminate them at any time, and they can terminate their employment with us at any time. Other than Mr. Rao, our NEOs were not entitled to any severance or change of control benefits during 2025.

 
241 During 2025, the Rao Offer Letter provided that if, at any time, his employment was terminated by the company without “cause” or he resigned for “good reason” (as such terms were defined in the Rao Offer Letter), then, subject to his execution of a release of claims in favor of the company and other conditions, he would be entitled to the following severance payments and benefits: (i) an amount equal to six months of his then-current base salary, (ii) payment of monthly premiums for coverage under the Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act (“COBRA”) for up to six months, and (iii) accelerated vesting as to 1/8th of the Rao Options. The Rao Offer Letter further provided that if, within 30 days prior to, upon, or at any time following a “change of control” (as defined in our 2021 Plan), his employment was terminated by the company without cause or he resigned for good reason, then, subject to his execution of a release of claims in favor of the company and other conditions, 100% of any then-unvested shares subject to his then-outstanding equity awards, including the Rao Options, would accelerate and vest. If, in the change of control, his then-outstanding equity awards would otherwise have been terminated for no consideration at the closing of the change of control event, then those awards would instead have become fully vested as of immediately prior to such closing. Upon the termination of the Rao Offer Letter in October 2026, we entered into a letter agreement with Mr. Rao continuing the change of control vesting acceleration benefit described herein on the same terms, without alteration. For additional information regarding the severance and change of control benefits for our NEOs, see the sections titled “9.12.2.12 Post-Fiscal Year End Compensation Changes and Equity Awards” and “9.12.2.17 Potential Payments upon Termination or Change of Control.” 9.12.2.9 Other Compensation Governance Practices 9.12.2.9.1 Compensation Recovery Policy We have adopted an executive compensation recoupment policy intended to comply with the requirements of Rule 10D- 1 under the U.S. Exchange Act and the rules of the stock exchange on which our securities are listed (“Clawback Policy”) that will be effective upon the effectiveness of the registration statement with respect to the U.S. offering. The Clawback Policy will generally require us to recover erroneously awarded incentive-based compensation that was received by covered executive officers in the event we are required to prepare an accounting restatement due to any material non-compliance with any financial reporting requirement under the securities laws (including any required accounting restatement to correct an error in previously issued financial statements that is material to the previously issued financial statements), or that would result in a material misstatement if the error were corrected in the current period or left uncorrected in the current period. The Clawback Policy generally covers incentive-based compensation received on or after the effective date of the Clawback Policy and during the three-year period prior to the date we are required to prepare the financial restatement. The amount required to be recovered is the excess of the amount of incentive-based compensation received over the amount that otherwise would have been received based on the restated financial measure. 9.12.2.9.2 Hedging, Pledging, and Insider Trading We are dedicated to fostering high standards of ethical business conduct and adherence to applicable laws, rules, and regulations. Accordingly, we maintain our Insider Trading Policy, which we believe is appropriately designed to foster compliance with insider trading laws, rules, and regulations, and the listing standards of the Nasdaq Global Select Market that will be applicable to us. Our Insider Trading Policy applies to all of our officers, directors, and employees, as well as designated consultants, and specifically prohibits ownership of financial instruments or participation in investment strategies that hedge the economic risk of owning our equity securities, such as prepaid variable forwards, equity swaps, and collars. Directors, officers, and other employees are prohibited from maintaining company securities in a margin account or otherwise pledging company securities as collateral for a loan, provided that certain limited exceptions may be permitted. In addition, we prohibit our executive officers, directors, and employees from purchasing or selling our securities while in possession of material, non-public information or otherwise utilizing such information for their personal benefit. We maintain a quarterly blackout window where applicable individuals may not trade. 9.12.2.9.3 Policies and Practices Related to the Grant of Certain Equity Awards Close in Time to the Release of Material Nonpublic Information We periodically grant stock options to our NEOs, employees, and other service providers. We have historically granted options on or shortly after a newly hired employee’s start date. We have historically granted refresh, promotion, or market adjustment options when and as determined by our board of directors. We have no specific policy or practice regarding the timing of options or other equity grants in relation to the public disclosure of material nonpublic information by the company.

 
242 9.12.2.10 Tax and Accounting Considerations 9.12.2.10.1 Tax Considerations Section 162(m) of the U.S. Code imposes a $1 million limit on the amount of compensation that we may deduct as a business expense in any year with regard to certain of our most highly paid executive officers. While our board of directors considers the deductibility of compensation as one factor in determining executive compensation, our board of directors retains the discretion to award compensation that is not deductible as it believes that it is in our best interests to maintain flexibility in our approach to executive compensation in order to design a program that we deem to be the most effective in attracting, motivating, and retaining key executives and aligning pay with performance. 9.12.2.10.2 Accounting Considerations Our board of directors takes accounting considerations into account in designing compensation plans and arrangements for our NEOs and other employees. We follow the Financial Accounting Standards Board’s Accounting Standards Codification Topic 718 (“FASB ASC Topic 718”) for our stock-based compensation awards. FASB ASC Topic 718 requires us to measure the compensation expense for all share-based payment awards based on the grant date “fair value” of these awards. 9.12.2.11 Summary Compensation Table The following table shows the compensation awarded, paid to, or earned by each of our NEOs for the year ended December 31, 2025: Name and Principal Position Year Salary ($) Stock Awards ($)(1)(2) Option Awards ($)(1) All Other Compensa- tion ($) Total ($) Dario Amodei Chief Executive Officer, Co- Founder, and Director 2025 654,167 9,264,932 4,028,558 4,010,641 (3) 17,958,298 Daniela Amodei President, Co-Founder, and Director 2025 654,167 9,264,932 4,028,558 2,461,341 (4) 16,408,998 Krishna Rao Chief Financial Officer 2025 706,250 — — 14,000 (5) 720,250 __________________ (1) The amounts reported represent the aggregate grant-date fair value of the RSUs or options awarded to the NEOs calculated in accordance with FASB ASC Topic 718. The performance-based condition will be satisfied upon the effectiveness of the registration statement with respect to the U.S. offering.

If, in the change of control, his then-outstanding equity awards would otherwise have been terminated for no consideration at the closing of the change of control event, then those awards would instead become fully vested as of immediately prior to such closing. Upon the termination of the Rao Offer Letter in October 2026, we entered into a letter agreement with Mr. Rao continuing the change of control vesting acceleration benefit described herein on the same terms, without alteration.
