Consequently, our directors and certain officers will not be personally liable to us or our stockholders for monetary damages for any breach of fiduciary duties as directors and officers, except liability for the following: • any breach of the director’s or officer’s duty of loyalty to our company or our stockholders; • any act or omission not in good faith or that involves intentional misconduct or a knowing violation of law; • for our directors, unlawful payments of dividends or unlawful stock repurchases or redemptions as provided in Section 174 of the DGCL; • any transaction from which the director or officer derived an improper personal benefit; or • for our officers, any action by or in the right of the corporation. Any amendment to, or repeal of, these provisions will not eliminate or reduce the effect of these provisions in respect of any act, omission, or claim that occurred or arose prior to that amendment or repeal. If the DGCL is amended to provide for further limitations on the personal liability of directors and officers of corporations, then the personal liability of our directors and officers will be further limited to the greatest extent permitted by the DGCL. In addition, we expect to adopt amended and restated bylaws, which will become effective immediately prior to the completion of the global offering, and which will provide that we will indemnify, to the fullest extent permitted by law, any person who is or was a party or is threatened to be made a party to any action, suit, or proceeding by reason of the fact that they are or were one of our directors or officers or are or were serving at our request as a director or officer of another corporation, partnership, joint venture, trust, or other enterprise. Our amended and restated bylaws are expected to provide that we may indemnify to the fullest extent permitted by law any person who is or was a party or is threatened to be made a party to any action, suit, or proceeding by reason of the fact that they are or were one of our employees or agents or are or were serving at our request as an employee or agent of another corporation, partnership, joint venture, trust, or other enterprise. Our amended and restated bylaws will also provide that we must advance expenses incurred by or on behalf of a director or officer in advance of the final disposition of any action or proceeding, subject to limited exceptions. Further, we have entered into or will enter into indemnification agreements with each of our directors and executive officers that may be broader than the specific indemnification provisions contained in the DGCL. These indemnification agreements require us, among other things, to indemnify our directors and executive officers against liabilities that may arise by reason of their status or service. These indemnification agreements also require us to advance all expenses incurred by the directors and executive officers in investigating or defending any such action, suit, or proceeding. We believe that these agreements are necessary to attract and retain qualified individuals to serve as directors and executive officers. The limitation of liability and indemnification provisions that are expected to be included in our amended and restated certificate of incorporation, amended and restated bylaws, and indemnification agreements that we have entered into or will enter into with our directors and executive officers may discourage stockholders from bringing a lawsuit against our directors and executive officers for breach of their fiduciary duties. They may also reduce the likelihood of derivative litigation against our directors and executive officers, even though an action, if successful, might benefit us and other stockholders. Further, a stockholder’s investment may be adversely affected to the extent that we pay the costs of

 
288 settlement and damage awards against directors and executive officers as required by these indemnification provisions. We cannot predict whether, when, or the amount of any future claims for indemnification in connection with any settlement or judgment. Under Delaware law and our amended and restated certificate of incorporation, in the absence of a conflict of interest, no failure to satisfy the balancing obligations associated with our status as a PBC shall, for purposes of the exculpation, advancement, and indemnification rights of our directors and officers, constitute an act or omission not in good faith, or a breach of the duty of loyalty. We have obtained insurance policies under which, subject to the limitations of the policies, coverage is provided to our directors and executive officers against loss arising from claims made by reason of breach of fiduciary duty or other wrongful acts as a director or executive officer, including claims relating to public company securities matters, and to us with respect to payments that may be made by us to these directors and executive officers pursuant to our indemnification obligations or otherwise as a matter of law. Certain of our non-employee directors may, through their relationships with their employers, be insured or indemnified against certain liabilities incurred in their capacity as members of our board of directors. We have also agreed to enter into indemnification agreements with the Founder LLC and the LTBT providing for indemnification, to the fullest extent permitted by law, of those entities and their related persons in connection with specified matters relating to, among other things, their ownership of our capital stock and the exercise of their rights and obligations under our governance documents, without limitation of other indemnification agreements to which we may be a party. The underwriting agreement will provide for indemnification by the underwriters of us and our officers and directors for certain liabilities. Insofar as indemnification for liabilities arising under the U.S. Securities Act may be permitted to directors, officers, or persons controlling the Company pursuant to the foregoing provisions, we have been informed that, in the opinion of the SEC, such indemnification is against public policy as expressed in the U.S. Securities Act and is therefore unenforceable. 11.6.12 Policies and Procedures for Related Person Transactions Following the completion of the global offering, our audit committee will have the primary responsibility for reviewing and approving or disapproving “related person transactions,” which are transactions between us and related persons in which the aggregate amount involved exceeds or may be expected to exceed $120,000 and in which a related person has or will have a direct or indirect material interest. Upon completion of the global offering, our policy regarding transactions between us and related persons will provide that a related person is defined as a director, executive officer, nominee for director, or greater than 5% beneficial owner of any class of our outstanding voting securities, in each case since the beginning of the most recently completed year, and any of their immediate family members. Our audit committee charter that will be in effect upon completion of the global offering will provide that our audit committee shall review and approve or disapprove any related person transactions. 11.7 Board of Directors’ and Executive Officers’ Conflicts of Interest Dario Amodei, our Chief Executive Officer and a member of our board of directors, and Daniela Amodei, our President and Chairperson of our board of directors, are siblings, which could give rise to conflicts of interest. Family relationships among members of a board of directors may give rise to conflicts of interest because directors who are related by blood or marriage may be inclined to prioritize the personal, financial, or professional interests of their family members over the best interests of the company and its stockholders. Such relationships may impair the objectivity and independence of board decision-making, particularly in matters involving compensation, succession planning, related party transactions, or the evaluation of executive performance. Directors with familial ties may find it difficult to exercise independent judgment when assessing the conduct, compensation, or continued service of a relative, which could undermine the board’s ability to fulfill its fiduciary duties. Other than that, there are no potential or actual conflicts of interest between any duties of the Company and the members of our board of directors and executive officers. For arrangements with our shareholders under which the members of our board of directors were elected, see the sections titled “9.1 Management” and “11.6.3 Voting Agreement,” and the board of directors’ assessment of director independence, see the section titled “9.8 Director Independence.” For lock-up arrangements entered into by the members of our board of directors and executive officers, see the section titled “8.6 Lock-Up and Market Standoff Agreements.”

 
289 11.8 Legal and Arbitration Proceedings We are currently involved in, and may in the future be involved in, legal proceedings and claims that arise in the ordinary course of business, including those involving intellectual property disputes, compliance with legal or regulatory regimes, government approvals and authorizations, labor and employment, anti-discrimination, commercial disputes, competition, data privacy, customer complaints, and other matters relating to our technology, products, and services. In addition, third parties may from time to time assert claims against us in the form of letters and other communications. Future litigation may be necessary or warranted to defend ourselves or our partners or to establish or assert our rights. The results of any current or future legal proceedings or litigation cannot be predicted with certainty, and regardless of the outcome, legal proceedings or litigation can have an adverse impact on us because of defense and settlement costs, diversion of management resources, and other factors. Other than set forth below, the Group has not been involved in any governmental, legal or arbitration proceedings (including any such proceedings which are pending of which the Company is aware), during a period covering the previous 12 months to the date of this prospectus which may have, or have had in the recent past, material effects on the Company and/or the Group’s financial position or profitability. For more information regarding legal proceedings and other claims in which we are involved, see the section titled “Legal Matters” in Note 13 to our consolidated financial statements, which are incorporated by reference in, and form part of, this prospectus (see “10.1 Consolidated Financial Statements”). 11.8.1 Intellectual Property Matters A series of lawsuits has been filed against us in federal and international courts by plaintiffs asserting copyright infringement based on the use of copyrighted material to train our models. For example, in August 2024, a group of authors filed suit against us claiming infringement of copyrighted books in Bartz. Specifically, the class action plaintiffs alleged that in the process of building and operating our models, we unlawfully copied copyrighted works controlled by the authors. Though we dispute any allegation of wrongdoing, in September 2025, we entered into a settlement agreement with the plaintiffs to settle the case for $1.5 billion, which was approved by the district court in July 2026. In each of the actions, we believe we have meritorious defenses and dispute any allegation of wrongdoing. Legal proceedings related to these matters can have an adverse effect on us because of defense and settlement costs individually and in the aggregate, diversion of management resources, and other factors. 11.8.2 Other Matters In February 2026, in response to our publicly stated position that our technology should not be used for mass domestic surveillance or fully autonomous weapons, the President of the United States stated that he had directed that all federal executive agencies cease using our technology. At the same time, the Secretary of War directed the Department of War to designate Anthropic as a “supply-chain risk to national security” and stated that “effective immediately, no contractor, supplier, or partner that does business with the United States military may conduct any commercial activity” with us. On March 4, 2026, the Department of War sent us two letters—one pursuant to 10 U.S.C. § 3252 and the other pursuant to Section 4713 of the FASCSA—asserting that our models, platform, and applications present a supply chain risk. These actions referenced above are defined herein as “Challenged Actions.” We vigorously challenged the Challenged Actions in Anthropic PBC v. Department of War, et al. (N.D. Cal.) and Anthropic PBC v. Department of War, et al. (D.C. Cir.). After first obtaining an order from the United States District Court for the Northern District of California that preliminarily enjoined the Department of War’s directive and Section 3252 supply-chain risk designation of us and preliminarily enjoined the other defendant agencies from implementing the Presidential directive until final resolution of the lawsuit, we subsequently, on August 27, 2026, obtained an order from the United States District Court for the Northern District of California that largely granted summary judgment in our favor. The court ruled that the Challenged Actions were retaliatory acts meant to punish us for speech protected under the First Amendment to the United States Constitution and violated our rights under the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution. The court also held that the Secretary of War’s actions, particularly with respect to 10 U.S.C. § 3252, violated the Administrative Procedure Act because they were in excess of statutory authority, contrary to law, and arbitrary and capricious. The court entered final judgment largely in our favor. The defendants filed notices of appeal of the preliminary injunction order and of the court’s final judgment. The D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, however, denied our motion to stay the Secretary of War’s Section 4713 designation of us as a supply-chain risk pending review on the merits. On September 25, 2026, in a 2-1 split decision, the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals denied our petition for review, ruling that the Department of War’s Section 4713 supply-chain risk designation was proper, and that our rights under the First Amendment and Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment were not violated. We filed a petition for rehearing and rehearing en banc asking the full D.C. Circuit to review the panel’s decision. We cannot predict the

 
290 ultimate outcome of these lawsuits. While we continue to work with government agencies, we cannot be certain that the resolution of these lawsuits will not adversely affect our ability to sell to government agencies and other customers that sell products and services to the U.S. government, and thus on our business, financial condition, and results of operations. In September 2026, media reports citing a senior FTC official indicated that the FTC has opened non-public investigations into the potential risks that increasingly autonomous AI systems may pose to consumers. In October 2026, the FTC issued a civil investigative demand to us seeking information about our consumer protection, data protection, and privacy practices, as well as the safety and security of our products. The civil investigative demand does not assert any claims against us, and we cannot predict the outcome of any investigation of us, including whether it will result in any proceeding. For more information, see the section titled “1.1.15 If we are unable to manage the risks related to our focus on and commitment to AI safety, our brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.” 11.9 Material Contracts For information on our material contracts, see “5.12.1 Revolving Credit Agreement,” “5.12.3 Convertible Notes” and “9.12.2.18 Equity Plans.”

 
291 12. Dividend Policy We have never declared or paid any cash dividends on our capital stock. We currently intend to retain all available funds and any future earnings to finance the operation and expansion of our business and do not expect to pay any dividends in the foreseeable future. Any future determination to declare cash dividends will be made at the discretion of our board of directors, subject to applicable laws, and will depend on a number of factors, including our financial condition, results of operations, capital requirements, contractual restrictions, general business conditions, and other factors that our board of directors may deem relevant. In addition, the terms of the A&R Credit Agreement place certain limitations on the amount of cash dividends we can pay, even if no amounts are currently outstanding under the credit facility.

G-1 G 14. Glossary The following are abbreviations, acronyms, and definitions of certain terms used in this prospectus: accelerators ................... refer to processors purpose-built or adapted for the large-scale computations required to pre-train, post-train, refine, and run super intelligence models. These processors are significantly more efficient and faster than general-purpose processors for SI workloads. agent loop ..................... refers to the iterative cycle in which an SI agent receives a task, takes an action, such as planning a project, running code, or calling a tool, observes the result, and decides its next step, with this cycle repeating until the task is complete. The agent loop is the core execution pattern underlying agentic SI behavior. agentic AI or agentic SI refer to systems that, with varying degrees of autonomy, can plan, determine, and sequence actions and execute them to accomplish defined objectives, including through interaction with external tools, services, datasets, and environments on behalf of a user. alignment ...................... refers to the extent to which AI models behave as intended and do not take unwanted actions of their own accord. API ................................ refers to application programming interface, a standardized interface that allows external software to access a system’s capabilities programmatically. SI model providers may offer APIs that allow software developers to send inputs to a model and receive outputs, enabling integration into the software developers’ products and workflows. Applied AI ..................... refers to a discipline and organizational function focused on embedding SI capabilities directly into production business environments to address specific customer requirements. Applied AI teams, which include forward-deployed engineers, work with enterprises to design and deploy custom solutions, specialized workflows, and domain- specific implementations tailored to a customer’s own systems and processes. artificial intelligence or AI ................................ refers to a machine-based system that learns or is trained from data and, for explicit or implicit objectives and with varying levels of autonomy, processes that data to infer patterns, generate outputs—such as predictions, content, recommendations, and decisions—and act upon physical or virtual environments. For purposes of this prospectus, we use the terms “artificial intelligence,” “AI,” “super intelligence,” and “SI” interchangeably. authorized .................... in respect of our capital stock refers to the maximum number of shares which we are authorized by our shareholders to create and sell under our amended and restated certificate of incorporation and includes any issued and unissued shares from time to time. closing the loop ............. refers to a development cycle in which successive versions of an SI model assist in building the next, with the goal of compounding capability gains over time. compute ........................ refers to the computational processing resources used to train and run SI models, including, without limitation, specialized accelerators, memory, networking, storage, and power systems that are deployed in data centers or other physical computing environments. compute multipliers ..... refer to algorithmic and methodological improvements in training and inference that increase the effective output of a given amount of compute. computer use ................ refers to an SI capability that allows a model to observe and interact with a graphical user interface, such as clicking, typing, and navigating applications, similar to how a human operator would. Constitutional AI .......... refers to an approach to training AI models using a set of written principles, which we refer to as Claude’s constitution, currently organized around four priorities: being broadly safe, broadly ethical, compliant with our guidelines, and genuinely helpful. Under Constitutional AI, our models evaluate, critique, and revise their own responses against these principles, enabling us to define and control model behavior through auditable principles, rather than relying solely on fixed rule-based instructions or human reviewers. context window ............ refers to the maximum amount of text, code, or other content, measured in tokens, that an SI model can process in a given request, encompassing instructions, prior conversation history, user input, and the model’s output. CSP ................................ refers to a cloud service provider, a technology company that owns and operates large- scale cloud computing infrastructure and provides on-demand compute, storage, and networking. CSPs may also serve as distribution channels through which SI products and services are made available to customers. The largest CSPs, sometimes referred to as

 
G-2 hyperscalers, operate at global scale with significant infrastructure and market concentration. customer ....................... refers to a prosumer or an organization that uses our models, platform, or applications. customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis, customers with $1 million or more of revenue on a TTM basis, and customers with $10 million or more of revenue on a TTM basis .................. each refer to customers contributing revenue equal to or greater than the applicable dollar amount during the trailing twelve-month (“TTM”) period ending on the measurement date. For purposes of this metric, we define a customer as a distinct organization, identified by aggregating the accounts that we determine belong to the same organization based on internal records and available data. We do not separately define or internally track a category of “enterprise” customers, and our customers are not segmented or measured internally by reference to whether a given customer is an “enterprise.” Because spending $100,000 or more on our products is generally characteristic of organizational rather than individual usage, we use the number of and revenue from customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis as our measure of enterprise adoption and engagement with Claude throughout this prospectus, including in references to “enterprise customers” and “enterprise adoption.” EDGAR (Electronic Data Gathering, Analysis, and Retrieval) ................... is the database system operated by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) for electronic filings of regulated information. frontier intelligence ...... refers to systems at the current leading edge of capability and safety, performing at or near the highest levels of any existing system across a broad range of tasks. hallucinations ............... refer to outputs in which an SI model generates factually incorrect or fabricated information with apparent confidence. inference ....................... refers to the process by which a trained SI model processes an input and generates an output. Inference occurs each time a user or agent interacts with an SI system. interleaved thinking ..... refers to a capability whereby an SI model interposes discrete reasoning steps between successive tool calls within a single response, rather than confining its reasoning to a single planning phase at the outset. interpretability ............. refers to research into how and why SI models produce specific outputs, with the goal of making model behavior more transparent and verifiable, especially in high-stakes applications. investment grade .......... refers to a debt security, other financial product or issuer considered to have a relatively low risk of default, as reflected in a high credit rating from a recognized rating agency. issued ............................ in respect of our capital stock refers to the number of shares which we have issued under the authorizations included in our amended and restated certificate of incorporation. knowledge work ............ refers to complex cognitive work and related professional activities, including obtaining, producing, analyzing, and communicating information through tasks such as coding, drafting analyses, synthesizing research, building financial models, and managing and automating documents and workflows. LLMs ............................. refer to large language models, or SI models trained primarily on large datasets to understand and generate natural language and computer code. mechanistic interpretability ........... refers to a subfield of interpretability research focused on reverse-engineering the internal computations of neural networks. Rather than inferring model behavior from inputs and outputs alone, mechanistic interpretability seeks to identify the specific features and circuits within a model that give rise to its behavior with the goal of making model reasoning auditable at the mechanism level and detecting failure modes, including deceptive or unsafe behavior, that may not surface in standard testing. model weights ............... refer to the numerical parameters encoding a trained SI model’s behavior, which are the primary intellectual asset of a frontier intelligence developer, representing the accumulated investment in compute, data, and research. multi-agent orchestration .............. refers to an architecture in which multiple SI agents collaborate on a shared task, with one coordinating while others execute subtasks in parallel, enabling more complex, long- horizon work than a single agent can complete alone. Net Revenue Retention reflects customer expansion, contraction, and churn as of a measurement date. We calculate Net Revenue Retention by dividing the Qualified Customers’ Current Period revenue by their Base Period revenue. A Qualified Customer is a customer with at least $1 of revenue during the Base Period, excluding subscribers to our Claude Pro, Max and Ultra plans, whose fixed-price subscriptions do not reflect the expansion and contraction behavior this metric is intended to capture. The Base Period is the three months ending a

 
G-3 year prior to the measurement date. The Current Period is the three months ending as of the measurement date. open-weight .................. refers to an SI model whose trained model weights are publicly released, allowing third parties to download, run, and modify the model, subject to the terms of the model’s license, without necessarily providing access to the underlying training data or code. outstanding ................... in respect of our capital stock refers to the number of shares which are held by third-party investors, i.e., the number of issued shares less treasury shares. pay-for-intelligence, or consumption .............. refers to our revenue model under which customers pay for their usage of our intelligence service, which is metered in tokens and priced according to the model selected. persistent ...................... in the context of SI applications refers to denoting data, state, or context that is continuously retained beyond the boundary of a single operation, session, or interaction, remaining accessible for reuse across subsequent steps, sessions, or workflows without requiring reinitialization. post-training ................. refers to the collection of techniques applied to a pre-trained model to refine its behavior, including reinforcement learning, supervised refinement methods, and other alignment methods. Post-training is the stage in which much of the work to make a frontier model helpful, accurate, and safe is performed, including the application of safety and alignment techniques. pre-training .................. refers to the initial stage of training an SI model, in which the model learns general patterns and representations from large-scale datasets of text, code, and other data, typically by predicting the next token in a sequence. The output of pre-training is a base model with broad capabilities that has not yet been adapted for any specific deployment context. primitives ...................... refer to the foundational, modular building blocks of a software system from which more complex applications and workflows are constructed. prompt injection ........... refers to an adversarial technique in which malicious instructions are embedded in content an SI model is asked to process, such as websites, documents, or tool outputs, with the aim of overriding or manipulating the model’s intended behavior, typically without the user’s knowledge. prosumers ..................... refer to individual users who subscribe to SI tools to perform knowledge work. proxy contest ................ refers to a mechanism used by a party to replace a corporation’s existing board of directors with new directors who support that party’s agenda. The initiator seeks to obtain enough proxies from the corporation’s other shareholders to vote in favor of a new slate of directors. reinforcement learning refers to a machine learning approach in which a model learns to perform a task by taking actions, receiving feedback signals called rewards, and adjusting its behavior to maximize the rewards it accrues over time. In contemporary SI development, reinforcement learning is widely used to refine model behavior after pre-training, including to improve helpfulness, accuracy, and adherence to safety guidelines. RLHF ............................ refers to reinforcement learning from human feedback, a specific form of reinforcement learning in which human evaluators rate the model’s responses, and those ratings are used as the reward signal to guide training. Run-Rate Revenue ....... is an operating metric that refers to the estimated annualized value of our revenue- generating activity as of a measurement date, calculated as the sum of (i) our consumption-based fees during the trailing 28-day period ended on the measurement date, multiplied by 13, and (ii) our aggregate monthly subscription fees as of the measurement date, multiplied by 12. For purposes of calculating Run-Rate Revenue, consumption-based fees and subscription-based fees are derived from customer usage and active subscriptions. Scaling Laws ................. refer to empirical relationships among model performance, model size, training data, and compute scale. super intelligence or SI refers to a machine-based system that learns or is trained from data and, for explicit or implicit objectives and with varying levels of autonomy, processes that data to infer patterns, generate outputs—such as predictions, content, recommendations, and decisions—and act upon physical or virtual environments. For purposes of this prospectus, to avoid confusion, we use the terms “super intelligence,” “SI,” “artificial intelligence,” and “AI” interchangeably. On September 29, 2026, the President of the United States issued Executive Order 14434, which directs federal executive departments and agencies to use the terms “Super Intelligence” and “SI” in place of “Artificial Intelligence” and “AI.”

 
G-4 systems integrators ...... refer to third-party technology and professional services firms that design, build, and deploy integrated solutions for customers by combining products and services from multiple technology vendors into unified systems tailored to customer needs. tokens ............................ refer to numeric units into which an SI model converts the data it processes, including text, images, audio, and video, the number of which varies by the model and tokenizer applied. Tokens are the smallest individual units of data a language model processes and can correspond to words, subwords, characters, or bytes. A tokenizer is the component of a model that converts customer inputs into the sequence of tokens the model processes and then converts the processed tokens into the outputs provided to customers. VIEs ............................... refer to variable interest entities. The Company evaluates its ownership, contractual, and other interests in entities to determine if it has a variable interest in an entity. These evaluations are complex, involve judgment, and the use of estimates and assumptions based on available historical and prospective information, among other factors. If the Company determines that an entity for which it holds a contractual or ownership interest is a VIE and that the Company is the primary beneficiary, the Company consolidates such entity in its consolidated financial statements. An enterprise having a controlling financial interest in a VIE must consolidate the VIE if it is considered the primary beneficiary, which is described as having both (1) the power to direct the activities of a VIE that most significantly impact the VIE’s economic performance and (2) the right to receive benefits or the obligation to absorb losses of the VIE that potentially could be significant to the VIE. The LTBT is considered a consolidated VIE as it relies on the Company for financial support. The Company is the primary beneficiary of the VIE as it has the power to direct the activities that most significantly impact the LTBT’s economic performance, provides financial support to the LTBT, and would receive the LTBT’s financial assets (other than the Class T common stock) in the event that the LTBT terminates. The Company consolidated the VIE at inception and will perform ongoing reassessments of the VIE based on any reconsideration events to reevaluate whether a change to the consolidation conclusion is required each reporting period.
